Part 7: A preview of how numbers mislead ¶ Numbers feel objective, but the same data can tell very different stories depending on how it is summarised and drawn. Here is one trap, live. Both charts below show the same two numbers . Predict, then reveal Two products have satisfaction scores of 96% and 98%. Before running the cell, decide: is that a big difference or a small one? Then see how each chart makes you feel about it. products = [ "Product A" , "Product B" ] satisfaction = [ 96 , 98 ] # made-up percentages fig , ( left , right ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 3.5 )) left . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#2a78d6" ) left . set_ylim ( 95 , 98.5 ) left . set_title ( "Axis starts at 95" ) right . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#2a78d6" ) right . set_ylim ( 0 , 100 ) right . set_title ( "Axis starts at 0" ) for ax in ( left , right ): ax . set_ylabel ( "Satisfied customers (%)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same data, two impressions (made-up numbers)" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () We judge bars by their length , so bar charts should start at zero. On the left, Product B looks several times better; on the right you see two products that are almost the same. The full list of traps is in How statistics can mislead . We return to each one later in the course. Trap One-line warning Where we meet it again Correlation is not causation Two things moving together may share a hidden cause This afternoon (correlation and confounding), Day 4 (regression) Simpson's paradox A total can reverse the story of every part This afternoon Misleading axes Where the axis starts changes the impression Day 2 (visualisation) Cherry-picked time windows The chosen start and end dates can create any trend Day 3 (forecasting) Which average? Mean and median can tell different stories This afternoon (descriptive statistics) Percentages without the base "Up 200%" means little without the counts Day 2 (dashboards and KPIs) Survivorship bias The records you see may be only the survivors Day 6 (BI case studies) A checklist for any number you are shown Compared to what? Who or what is included? What is the denominator? Could something else explain it? How is it drawn? Summary ¶ Good decisions combine data, analysis and judgement . Data gives everyone something to check instinct against; people still choose the question and own the decision. Analytics answers four kinds of question: what happened ( descriptive ), why ( diagnostic ), what next ( predictive ) and what to do ( prescriptive ). Every analysis runs question → data → analysis → validation → decision . A good question names a decision, population, period and measure. Different data can share identical summary statistics. Always plot your data. Numbers mislead through causation claims, mixed groups, axes, time windows, averages, missing bases and survivors. Closing quiz ¶ Answer in your own words, alone, in two or three minutes per question. We discuss the answers before lunch. Name the four kinds of analytics and give a one-line business example of the predictive kind. Give one reason why a decision based only on a manager's instinct can go wrong, and one thing data cannot decide for you. Rewrite "How are our stores doing?" as an analytical question that names a decision, population, period and measure. Two datasets have the same mean, standard deviation and correlation. Can you conclude they look alike? What should you do? In Anscombe's set III, what single feature of the data changes the best-fit line? Why should a bar chart's value axis start at zero? In the path question → data → analysis → validation → decision, what is the difference between analysis and validation ? docs.text: Every organisation decides things all the time: what to stock, whom to hire, which customers to target, how much to charge. Many of those decisions are still made on gut feeling , habit or the opinion of the most senior person in the room.
docs.title: Part 2: Why data-driven decisions?

docs.text: The course textbook's subtitle sums it up: good decisions combine data, analysis and judgement . Data on its own decides nothing. Analysis turns data into evidence. Judgement, from people who know the business, decides what the evidence means and what to do.
docs.title: The idea in one line

docs.text: Human judgement is valuable, but it has predictable weak spots. Psychologists have named many of them: Weak spot What happens Example at work Confirmation bias We notice evidence that agrees with us and ignore the rest A manager who believes a promotion worked only looks at the stores where sales rose Anchoring The first number we hear pulls our estimate towards it Next year's budget is "last year plus 5%" whatever has changed Availability Vivid or recent events feel more common than they are One angry customer email leads to a policy change for everyone Overconfidence We are more certain than our track record justifies Sales forecasts that are always too optimistic Data and analysis do not remove these biases, but they give everyone something to check against . A decision based on evidence can also be explained, repeated and improved, because you can see what it rested on.
docs.title: Why instinct alone is risky

docs.text: Analytics supports decisions; it does not make them. People still have to: choose the question worth answering; judge whether the data is trustworthy and relevant; weigh things the data does not capture: ethics, strategy, staff morale, reputation; take responsibility for the decision.
docs.title: Where judgement still matters

docs.text: Story What happened The habit it teaches John Snow , London, 1854 Mapping cholera deaths showed them clustered around one water pump. Its handle was removed. A simple, well-chosen picture can overturn what "everyone knows". Florence Nightingale , 1850s Her diagrams showed most soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals, not of wounds. Analysis only changes things when decision-makers understand it. Moneyball , baseball, 2002 A low-budget team found undervalued players by measuring on-base percentage. Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money. Walmart , hurricane, 2004 Sales patterns before earlier storms guided what to stock before a new one. Past patterns can guide everyday operational decisions. Google Flu Trends , 2008–2015 Estimating flu from searches worked for a while, then failed badly and was shut down. More data is not automatically better data. Every result needs validation. The full stories are in Why data analytics matters . Predict, then reveal Four of these stories are successes; one is a failure. Before reading the last row, ask yourself: what could make a model that once worked stop working? Then read the last row. Check your understanding Think of one decision at a workplace or organisation you know that was made on gut feeling. What data could have informed it, and which of the four weak spots might have affected it?
docs.title: Stories where data changed the outcome

docs.text: Analytics answers four kinds of question. Each builds on the one before. Kind Question it answers Typical methods Example Descriptive What happened? Totals, averages, tables, charts, dashboards Sales fell 8% last quarter Diagnostic Why did it happen? Breakdowns by group, comparisons, correlation The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened Predictive What is likely to happen next? Forecasting, regression, classification If nothing changes, that region will keep losing sales next quarter Prescriptive What should we do? Simulation, optimisation, scenario comparison Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices Many textbooks, including ours, group the first two together and speak of descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics. Diagnostic work is the bridge: it explains the description before anyone predicts or prescribes.

docs.text: The cell below loads the table of restaurant bills you met in the pre-class Python and Jupyter basics notebook. Each row is one table's bill and the tip it left (in US dollars, from a real restaurant study). We use it only to see the first three kinds of question in code. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd tips = pd . read_csv ( "data/tips.csv" ) tips [ "tip_percent" ] = 100 * tips [ "tip" ] / tips [ "total_bill" ] # Descriptive: what happened? Average tip on each day. print ( "Descriptive: average tip (US dollars) by day" ) print ( tips . groupby ( "day" )[ "tip" ] . mean () . round ( 2 )) Descriptive: average tip (US dollars) by day day Fri 2.73 Sat 2.99 Sun 3.26 Thur 2.77 Name: tip, dtype: float64 Predict, then reveal One day has the highest average tip. Is that because people are more generous that day, or because they spend more ? Write your guess, then run the next cell, which looks at the average bill and the tip as a percentage of the bill. # Diagnostic: why? Compare the bill size and the tip as a share of the bill. print ( "Diagnostic: average bill and tip percentage by day" ) tips . groupby ( "day" ) . agg ( average_bill = ( "total_bill" , "mean" ), average_tip_percent = ( "tip_percent" , "mean" ), ) . round ( 2 ) Diagnostic: average bill and tip percentage by day .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } average_bill average_tip_percent day Fri 17.15 16.99 Sat 20.44 15.32 Sun 21.41 16.69 Thur 17.68 16.13 Compare the two columns in the output above. Where the average tip is high, look at whether the bill or the percentage is what differs. A difference in amounts can come from a difference in spending rather than in generosity: that is a diagnostic finding. Now a prediction: the straight line that best fits tip against bill lets us estimate the tip on a new bill. # Predictive: what is likely? Fit a straight line of tip against bill. slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( tips [ "total_bill" ], tips [ "tip" ], 1 ) new_bill = 40 print ( f "Best-fit line: tip = { intercept : .2f } + { slope : .3f } x bill" ) print ( f "Predicted tip on a { new_bill } -dollar bill: { intercept + slope * new_bill : .2f } dollars" ) Best-fit line: tip = 0.92 + 0.105 x bill Predicted tip on a 40-dollar bill: 5.12 dollars Prescriptive analytics would go one step further: compare options (for example, which evening to add a second server) against an objective (service quality, wages) under constraints (staff available), and recommend one. You will build that kind of model in Excel on Day 5. Check your understanding Which kind of analytics is each statement? "Deliveries in the North got slower because the new carrier skips Saturday collections." "We expect about 400 returns in December." "Move the slow carrier's routes to the faster one for one month and measure the effect." "We shipped 12,000 parcels in October." "A customer who has not ordered for 90 days is likely to leave."
docs.title: A small live example

docs.text: A useful analysis supports a decision . It follows the same path every time: Question → Data → Analysis → Validation → Decision Stage Ask Keep as evidence 1. Question Who must decide what, and by when? The decision and a one-sentence question 2. Data What does each row represent? What is missing? How must it be prepared? The grain, units, scope, and a log of every change 3. Analysis Which comparison or metric actually answers the question? The metric definition, filters and calculation 4. Validation Do totals reconcile? Can I explain odd values? Does a chart agree with the numbers? Spot checks, counts and totals, edge cases 5. Decision What action follows, and what is still uncertain? A clear chart, the action, one caveat and a follow-up measure The course site describes the same path as seven steps , splitting out preparation and visualisation.
docs.title: Part 4: Analysis fundamentals — from question to decision

docs.text: A manager says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups." That is a feeling, not a question. A question you can answer with data names four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the sales table Period Which dates? Orders placed in the last three years Measure What will we compare? Total sales by customer segment "Which customer segment had the highest total sales over the last three years, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?"
docs.title: Step 1 in detail: a question you can answer

docs.text: A manager asks: "How many orders did we have?" The sales file has one row per order line , so an order with three products takes three rows. Counting rows counts lines , not orders. You must first know what one row represents (the table's grain ), then count distinct order numbers. You practised this in the pre-class Python and Jupyter basics notebook.
docs.title: Step 2 in detail: what does one row mean?

docs.text: A plausible number is not a checked number Before you report a result: do the parts add up to the total? Does a count match a simple manual check? Can you explain the largest and smallest values? Have you looked at the data in a chart, not only at summary numbers? Parts 5 and 6 show why that last check matters. Check your understanding A colleague asks: "Is the new website working?" Which of the four parts (decision, population, period, measure) are missing? Suggest one value for each.

Charts like this, one per group on the same axes, are called small multiples . names = dozen [ "dataset" ] . unique () fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 3 , 5 , figsize = ( 12 , 7 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) for ax in axes . flat : ax . set_visible ( False ) for ax , name in zip ( axes . flat , names ): points = dozen [ dozen [ "dataset" ] == name ] ax . set_visible ( True ) ax . scatter ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], s = 8 , color = "#2a78d6" ) ax . set_title ( name . replace ( "_" , " " )) fig . suptitle ( "The Datasaurus Dozen: same statistics, thirteen shapes (x and y have no units)" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () A report saying "x and y are essentially unrelated, centred around the same values" would be true for every panel, including the dinosaur. At work You will rarely meet a dinosaur in a sales report. You will meet the same problem in everyday forms: an average delivery time that hides a group of customers waiting weeks; one huge order that makes a quiet month look like growth; two stores with the same average sales but very different patterns. See Statistics are not enough . Check your understanding Why are the thirteen panels drawn with the same axes? What could go wrong if each panel chose its own axis range?

docs.text: Numbers feel objective, but the same data can tell very different stories depending on how it is summarised and drawn. Here is one trap, live. Both charts below show the same two numbers . Predict, then reveal Two products have satisfaction scores of 96% and 98%. Before running the cell, decide: is that a big difference or a small one? Then see how each chart makes you feel about it. products = [ "Product A" , "Product B" ] satisfaction = [ 96 , 98 ] # made-up percentages fig , ( left , right ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 3.5 )) left . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#2a78d6" ) left . set_ylim ( 95 , 98.5 ) left . set_title ( "Axis starts at 95" ) right . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#2a78d6" ) right . set_ylim ( 0 , 100 ) right . set_title ( "Axis starts at 0" ) for ax in ( left , right ): ax . set_ylabel ( "Satisfied customers (%)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same data, two impressions (made-up numbers)" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () We judge bars by their length , so bar charts should start at zero. On the left, Product B looks several times better; on the right you see two products that are almost the same. The full list of traps is in How statistics can mislead . We return to each one later in the course. Trap One-line warning Where we meet it again Correlation is not causation Two things moving together may share a hidden cause This afternoon (correlation and confounding), Day 4 (regression) Simpson's paradox A total can reverse the story of every part This afternoon Misleading axes Where the axis starts changes the impression Day 2 (visualisation) Cherry-picked time windows The chosen start and end dates can create any trend Day 3 (forecasting) Which average? Mean and median can tell different stories This afternoon (descriptive statistics) Percentages without the base "Up 200%" means little without the counts Day 2 (dashboards and KPIs) Survivorship bias The records you see may be only the survivors Day 6 (BI case studies) A checklist for any number you are shown Compared to what? Who or what is included? What is the denominator? Could something else explain it? How is it drawn?
docs.title: Part 7: A preview of how numbers mislead

docs.text: Good decisions combine data, analysis and judgement . Data gives everyone something to check instinct against; people still choose the question and own the decision. Analytics answers four kinds of question: what happened ( descriptive ), why ( diagnostic ), what next ( predictive ) and what to do ( prescriptive ). Every analysis runs question → data → analysis → validation → decision . A good question names a decision, population, period and measure. Different data can share identical summary statistics. Always plot your data. Numbers mislead through causation claims, mixed groups, axes, time windows, averages, missing bases and survivors.

docs.text: Day 1 lecture: Exploring data in Python ¶ Before anyone trusts a number, an analyst explores the table it came from. This lecture teaches a repeatable exploration routine in pandas: check the structure and data quality, describe distributions and skew, summarise groups with pivot tables, measure relationships with correlation, look for hidden confounders, and draw charts that still work with tens of thousands of rows. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . What you will be able to do ¶ Inspect a new table's structure with shape , info , dtypes and isnull , and list its data-quality problems. Describe a numeric column with the right summary, and recognise a skewed distribution. Summarise one measure across two categories with pd.pivot_table and groupby . Compute a correlation matrix , draw it as a heatmap , and read the strength and direction of each relationship. Explain confounding and Simpson's paradox , and check a comparison by holding a third variable roughly constant. Choose a violin plot or a hexbin plot when a box plot or scatter plot hides the shape of the data. Reading: Qlik, What is descriptive analytics? ; Analytics Vidhya (2015), Ultimate guide for data exploration in Python . How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words, alone or with the person next to you. Part Topic 1 The exploration routine 2 Structure and data quality 3 Distributions and skew 4 Pivot tables and groupby 5 Correlation and the heatmap 6 Confounding and Simpson's paradox 7 Charts for large datasets Recap: this morning ¶ Answer from memory, then check with the person next to you. Which kind of analytics answers "why did it happen?" Anscombe's four datasets share their means, spreads and correlation. What should you always do before trusting summary numbers? A total can reverse the story told by every one of its parts. What is that trap called? Part 1: The exploration routine ¶ Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the first look at a new dataset: what is in it, whether it can be trusted, and which patterns are worth a closer look. It is descriptive and diagnostic analytics in practice. Analysts follow roughly the same routine every time: Step Question pandas and charts 1. Structure How many rows and columns? What does one row mean? Which types? shape , info() , dtypes , head() 2. Data quality What is missing, duplicated or impossible? isnull().sum() , duplicated() , describe() (min and max) 3. Distributions What is typical? How spread out? Symmetric or skewed? describe() , skew() , histogram, box or violin plot 4. Groups How does a measure differ between categories? groupby , pd.pivot_table 5. Relationships Which numeric columns move together, and how strongly? corr() , heatmap, scatter or hexbin plot 6. Confounders Could a third variable explain the difference? Compare within groups of that variable We use two tables you have in the data folder, so everything runs without internet: Table One row is Used for mpg.csv One car model from 1970–1982 (fuel economy in miles per gallon, engine and weight) Structure, quality, correlation, confounding tips.csv One restaurant bill, with the tip (US dollars) Distributions, pivot tables The lab applies the same routine to a third table. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd import seaborn as sns cars = pd . read_csv ( "data/mpg.csv" ) tips = pd . read_csv ( "data/tips.csv" ) tips [ "tip_percent" ] = 100 * tips [ "tip" ] / tips [ "total_bill" ] print ( "cars:" , cars . shape , "| tips:" , tips . shape ) cars: (398, 9) | tips: (244, 8) Part 2: Structure and data quality ¶ Structure ¶ shape gives (rows, columns). info() lists every column with its type and its count of non-null (recorded) values. Compare that count with the number of rows: a lower number means missing values. cars . info () <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'> RangeIndex: 398 entries, 0 to 397 Data columns (total 9 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 mpg 398 non-null float64 1 cylinders 398 non-null int64 2 displacement 398 non-null float64 3 horsepower 392 non-null float64 4 weight 398 non-null int64 5 acceleration 398 non-null float64 6 model_year 398 non-null int64 7 origin 398 non-null object 8 name 398 non-null object dtypes: float64(4), int64(3), object(2) memory usage: 28.1+ KB Predict, then reveal Read the Non-Null Count column in the output above. Which column has fewer values than there are rows? Then run the next cell, which counts the missing values directly. print ( "Missing values per column:" ) print ( cars . isnull () . sum ()) Missing values per column: mpg 0 cylinders 0 displacement 0 horsepower 6 weight 0 acceleration 0 model_year 0 origin 0 name 0 dtype: int64 isnull() marks each missing cell as True ; .sum() counts the True values in each column. Let us look at the rows concerned rather than guess: cars [ cars [ "horsepower" ] . isnull ()][[ "name" , "model_year" , "weight" , "horsepower" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } name model_year weight horsepower 32 ford pinto 71 2046 NaN 126 ford maverick 74 2875 NaN 330 renault lecar deluxe 80 1835 NaN 336 ford mustang cobra 80 2905 NaN 354 renault 18i 81 2320 NaN 374 amc concord dl 82 3035 NaN A missing value is not available , not zero. Filling it with 0 would invent engines with no power and pull every average down. Common choices are: Choice When it makes sense Keep and note Few rows are affected and pandas skips missing values in means and correlations anyway Drop the rows for an analysis that needs the column The rows are a small share and missing for no particular reason Fill in (impute) with a typical value Only with a stated reason, and never silently Here we keep the rows and note it: pandas ignores missing values when it computes a mean or a correlation. Other quality checks ¶ Missing values are only one problem. Check for duplicated rows and impossible values . describe() shows each column's minimum and maximum, which is the fastest way to spot a weight of zero or a year of 2099. print ( "Fully duplicated rows:" , cars . duplicated () . sum ()) cars . describe () . round ( 1 ) Fully duplicated rows: 0 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mpg cylinders displacement horsepower weight acceleration model_year count 398.0 398.0 398.0 392.0 398.0 398.0 398.0 mean 23.5 5.5 193.4 104.5 2970.4 15.6 76.0 std 7.8 1.7 104.3 38.5 846.8 2.8 3.7 min 9.0 3.0 68.0 46.0 1613.0 8.0 70.0 25% 17.5 4.0 104.2 75.0 2223.8 13.8 73.0 50% 23.0 4.0 148.5 93.5 2803.5 15.5 76.0 75% 29.0 8.0 262.0 126.0 3608.0 17.2 79.0 max 46.6 8.0 455.0 230.0 5140.0 24.8 82.0 Read the min and max rows in the output above. Are they plausible for cars of that era (fuel economy, weight in pounds, model year as two digits)? Data-quality checklist Row count and grain: what does one row mean? Types: are numbers stored as numbers and categories as text? Missing values: how many, where, and why? Duplicates: genuine repeats or double entries? Impossible values: zeros, negatives or extremes that cannot be true? Write down what you found and what you did about it. Check your understanding A colleague replaces every missing horsepower with 0 and reports the average horsepower. What goes wrong? What would you do instead? Part 3: Distributions and skew ¶ A distribution describes how the values of one column are spread out. Three questions describe it: what is typical (centre), how spread out it is, and what shape it has. Predict, then reveal Restaurant bills cannot be negative, and most are modest, but a few parties spend a lot. Will the mean bill be above, below or equal to the median bill? Write your guess, then run the next cell. bill = tips [ "total_bill" ] print ( f "Mean bill: { bill . mean () : .2f } US dollars" ) print ( f "Median bill: { bill . median () : .2f } US dollars" ) print ( f "Skewness: { bill . skew () : .2f } " ) Mean bill: 19.79 US dollars Median bill: 17.80 US dollars Skewness: 1.13 Skewness measures how lopsided a distribution is: Skewness Shape Mean compared with median Typical business examples Close to 0 Roughly symmetric About equal Heights, measurement errors Clearly positive (about 1 or more) Right-skewed : a long tail of large values Mean above the median Bills, incomes, prices, order sizes Clearly negative Left-skewed : a long tail of small values Mean below the median Scores on an easy test With a right-skewed column, a few large values pull the mean up, so the median is the better "typical" value to report. The histogram shows the tail: fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) ax . hist ( bill , bins = 25 , color = "#2a78d6" , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . axvline ( bill . median (), color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Median" ) ax . axvline ( bill . mean (), color = "#1baf7a" , linewidth = 2 , linestyle = "--" , label = "Mean" ) ax . set_title ( "Most bills are modest; a long tail of large bills pulls the mean up" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Total bill (US dollars)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of bills" ) ax . legend () plt . show () Comparing distributions across groups: the violin plot ¶ A box plot summarises each group with five numbers. A violin plot draws the whole shape: the width at each height shows how many values lie there, like a histogram turned on its side and mirrored. The thin box inside marks the middle half and the median. cut=0 stops each violin at the smallest and largest real value, so it never suggests a negative bill. Violins are useful when a group has two peaks or a long tail, which a box plot hides. day_order = [ "Thur" , "Fri" , "Sat" , "Sun" ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) sns . violinplot ( data = tips , x = "day" , y = "total_bill" , order = day_order , color = "#2a78d6" , cut = 0 , ax = ax ) ax . set_title ( "Bills on every day are right-skewed: most are modest, a few are large" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Day of the week" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Total bill (US dollars)" ) plt . show () Each violin is wide near the bottom (many modest bills) and has a thin neck reaching upwards (a few large bills): the right-skewed shape again, on every day. Check your understanding A manager reads that the average house price in a city is far above what most families paid. Using the words skew , mean and median , explain how both statements can be true. Which number should the report lead with? Part 4: Pivot tables and groupby ¶ Business questions often compare a measure across two categories at once: tip percentage by day and by time (lunch or dinner), sales by region and by product, price by quality and by grade. A pivot table puts one category in the rows, another in the columns, and a summary of the measure in each cell. It is the same idea as a pivot table in Excel. pd.pivot_table needs four things: Argument Meaning Here values The measure to summarise tip_percent index The category for the rows day columns The category for the columns time aggfunc The summary for each cell "mean" tip_pivot = pd . pivot_table ( data = tips , values = "tip_percent" , index = "day" , columns = "time" , aggfunc = "mean" , ) . reindex ( day_order ) print ( "Average tip ( % o f the bill) by day and time" ) tip_pivot . round ( 1 ) Average tip (% of the bill) by day and time .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } time Dinner Lunch day Thur 16.0 16.1 Fri 15.9 18.9 Sat 15.3 NaN Sun 16.7 NaN .reindex(day_order) puts the rows in calendar order instead of alphabetical order. Predict, then reveal Some cells in the output above show NaN . Is that a tip percentage of zero? Before reading on, guess what it means. NaN means not available : there were no bills in that combination (the restaurant served no weekend lunches in this data). An empty cell is not a zero. A pivot table of averages should always be read next to the counts behind each cell, because an average of three bills is far less reliable than an average of eighty: count_pivot = pd . pivot_table ( data = tips , values = "tip_percent" , index = "day" , columns = "time" , aggfunc = "count" , ) . reindex ( day_order ) print ( "Number of bills behind each average" ) count_pivot Number of bills behind each average .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } time Dinner Lunch day Thur 1.0 61.0 Fri 12.0 7.0 Sat 87.0 NaN Sun 76.0 NaN The same summary with groupby ¶ groupby with two columns gives the same numbers in a long table: one row per combination. Use whichever is easier to read. observed=True keeps only combinations that actually occur. tips . groupby ([ "day" , "time" ], observed = True ) . agg ( bills = ( "tip_percent" , "count" ), average_tip_percent = ( "tip_percent" , "mean" ), ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } bills average_tip_percent day time Fri Dinner 12 15.9 Lunch 7 18.9 Sat Dinner 87 15.3 Sun Dinner 76 16.7 Thur Dinner 1 16.0 Lunch 61 16.1 Check your understanding Write the pd.pivot_table call that shows the median total bill with sex in the rows and smoker in the columns. Which argument changes, and why might the median suit bills better than the mean? Part 5: Correlation and the heatmap ¶ The correlation coefficient r measures how closely two numeric columns follow a straight line : r Reading +1 Perfect straight line going up about +0.7 or more Strong positive relationship about 0 No straight-line relationship (there may still be a curve) about −0.7 or less Strong negative relationship −1 Perfect straight line going down corr() computes r for every pair of numeric columns at once: a correlation matrix . select_dtypes(include="number") keeps only the numeric columns, because a correlation needs numbers. numeric_cars = cars . select_dtypes ( include = "number" ) corr_matrix = numeric_cars . corr () corr_matrix . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mpg cylinders displacement horsepower weight acceleration model_year mpg 1.00 -0.78 -0.80 -0.78 -0.83 0.42 0.58 cylinders -0.78 1.00 0.95 0.84 0.90 -0.51 -0.35 displacement -0.80 0.95 1.00 0.90 0.93 -0.54 -0.37 horsepower -0.78 0.84 0.90 1.00 0.86 -0.69 -0.42 weight -0.83 0.90 0.93 0.86 1.00 -0.42 -0.31 acceleration 0.42 -0.51 -0.54 -0.69 -0.42 1.00 0.29 model_year 0.58 -0.35 -0.37 -0.42 -0.31 0.29 1.00 A table of 49 numbers is hard to scan. A heatmap colours each cell by its value, with a diverging colour scale fixed from −1 to +1 so that colour means the same thing in every heatmap: one colour for positive, another for negative, pale near zero. annot=True prints the value in each cell. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6.5 )) sns . heatmap ( corr_matrix , annot = True , fmt = ".2f" , cmap = "RdBu_r" , vmin =- 1 , vmax = 1 , linewidths = 0.5 , ax = ax , cbar_kws = { "label" : "Correlation coefficient r" }, ) ax . set_title ( "Heavier, more powerful cars have lower fuel economy (mpg)" ) plt . show () Read the mpg row of the heatmap above: which column has the strongest relationship with fuel economy, and in which direction? Notice also the dark block of engine columns ( cylinders , displacement , horsepower , weight ) that are strongly correlated with each other : they largely measure the same thing, the size of the car. Three warnings about correlation Straight lines only. A strong curve can have r near 0 (remember Anscombe's set II). Plot before you conclude. Association is not causation. Two columns can move together because a third drives both. The diagonal is always 1. Every column correlates perfectly with itself; ignore it. Check your understanding The correlation between model_year and mpg is positive. Does that prove that newer car designs caused better fuel economy? Name one other column that could be part of the explanation. Part 6: Confounding and Simpson's paradox ¶ A comparison that misleads ¶ A confounder is a third variable that is related to both things you compare, and so distorts the comparison. Let us compare fuel economy of cars from the three regions of origin in the data. cars . groupby ( "origin" ) . agg ( cars = ( "mpg" , "count" ), average_mpg = ( "mpg" , "mean" ), average_weight_lb = ( "weight" , "mean" ), ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } cars average_mpg average_weight_lb origin europe 70 27.9 2423.3 japan 79 30.5 2221.2 usa 249 20.1 3361.9 Predict, then reveal The output above shows a large gap in average fuel economy between regions. Look also at the weight column. Is the gap mostly about where the car was built, or about something else? Write your answer, then run the next cell. To check, we hold the suspected confounder roughly constant : cut weight into bands with pd.cut , then compare regions within each band. cars [ "weight_band" ] = pd . cut ( cars [ "weight" ], bins = [ 0 , 2500 , 3000 , 3500 , 6000 ], labels = [ "under 2,500 lb" , "2,500-3,000 lb" , "3,000-3,500 lb" , "over 3,500 lb" ], ) within_band = pd . pivot_table ( data = cars , values = "mpg" , index = "origin" , columns = "weight_band" , aggfunc = "mean" , observed = True , ) print ( "Average mpg by origin, within weight bands (NaN = no cars of that origin and weight)" ) within_band . round ( 1 ) Average mpg by origin, within weight bands (NaN = no cars of that origin and weight) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } weight_band under 2,500 lb 2,500-3,000 lb 3,000-3,500 lb over 3,500 lb origin europe 30.7 22.8 23.5 21.0 japan 31.7 26.0 NaN NaN usa 29.0 24.3 19.4 15.1 Compare the overall gap from the previous output with the gap inside each weight band above. Within a band, cars of similar weight from different regions are much closer than the overall averages suggested. A large part of the overall gap comes from the mix : one region's cars are mostly heavy, the others' mostly light. Weight is a confounder : it is related to origin and it drives fuel economy. The chart shows the mix directly: origin_colours = { "europe" : "#1baf7a" , "japan" : "#eb6834" , "usa" : "#2a78d6" } fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) for origin , group in cars . groupby ( "origin" ): ax . scatter ( group [ "weight" ], group [ "mpg" ], s = 18 , alpha = 0.7 , color = origin_colours [ origin ], label = origin ) ax . set_title ( "Fuel economy falls with weight for cars from every region" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Weight (pounds)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Fuel economy (miles per gallon)" ) ax . legend ( title = "Origin" ) plt . show () Simpson's paradox: when the total reverses every part ¶ Sometimes a confounder does not just shrink a gap; it reverses it. A well-known medical study (Charig and colleagues, 1986) compared two treatments for kidney stones. The counts below are from that study. stones = pd . DataFrame ({ "treatment" : [ "A" , "A" , "B" , "B" ], "stone_size" : [ "small" , "large" , "small" , "large" ], "patients" : [ 87 , 263 , 270 , 80 ], "successes" : [ 81 , 192 , 234 , 55 ], }) by_size = stones . assign ( success_rate = 100 * stones [ "successes" ] / stones [ "patients" ]) print ( "Success rate (%) within each stone size" ) print ( by_size . pivot_table ( values = "success_rate" , index = "treatment" , columns = "stone_size" ) . round ( 1 )) overall = stones . groupby ( "treatment" )[[ "patients" , "successes" ]] . sum () overall [ "success_rate" ] = 100 * overall [ "successes" ] / overall [ "patients" ] print () print ( "Success rate (%) overall" ) print ( overall . round ( 1 )) Success rate (%) within each stone size stone_size large small treatment A 73.0 93.1 B 68.8 86.7 Success rate (%) overall patients successes success_rate treatment A 350 273 78.0 B 350 289 82.6 Predict, then reveal Before reading on: in the output above, which treatment wins for small stones? For large stones? And overall ? Treatment A has the higher success rate for small stones and for large stones, yet B looks better overall. The reason is the mix: doctors gave A mostly to large , difficult stones and B mostly to small, easy ones. Stone size affects both the treatment chosen and the chance of success, so it is a confounder, and adding the groups together reverses the story. This reversal is Simpson's paradox . How to protect yourself When a comparison between groups surprises you, ask: what else differs between these groups? Then compare within levels of that variable (bands, as above), or compare a ratio that removes it (for example fuel used per pound, or price per unit of size). You will meet a confounder in the lab. Check your understanding A hospital's overall death rate is higher than a nearby clinic's. Name a likely confounder, and say how you would check whether the hospital is really worse. Part 7: Charts for large datasets ¶ With a few hundred rows a scatter plot works well. With tens of thousands, the dots pile on top of each other ( overplotting ): a solid blob hides where most of the data actually is. To show this, the next cell creates synthetic (made-up) data for 50,000 deliveries: the distance in kilometres and the delivery time in minutes. The random generator is seeded, so everyone gets the same numbers. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 300 ) n = 50_000 distance_km = rng . gamma ( shape = 2.0 , scale = 3.0 , size = n ) delivery_min = 10 + 4 * distance_km + rng . gamma ( shape = 2.0 , scale = 5.0 , size = n ) deliveries = pd . DataFrame ({ "distance_km" : distance_km , "delivery_min" : delivery_min }) print ( "Synthetic deliveries:" , deliveries . shape ) deliveries . describe () . round ( 1 ) Synthetic deliveries: (50000, 2) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } distance_km delivery_min count 50000.0 50000.0 mean 6.0 44.0 std 4.2 18.3 min 0.0 10.8 25% 2.9 30.6 50% 5.0 40.6 75% 8.1 53.7 max 39.7 179.0 Predict, then reveal In a plain scatter plot of 50,000 deliveries, will you be able to see where most deliveries lie? Run the next cell and compare the two panels. fig , ( left , right ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4.5 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) left . scatter ( deliveries [ "distance_km" ], deliveries [ "delivery_min" ], s = 4 , color = "#2a78d6" ) left . set_title ( "Scatter plot: 50,000 dots overlap into a blob" ) hb = right . hexbin ( deliveries [ "distance_km" ], deliveries [ "delivery_min" ], gridsize = 40 , cmap = "Blues" , mincnt = 1 ) fig . colorbar ( hb , ax = right , label = "Deliveries in the hexagon" ) right . set_title ( "Hexbin plot: colour shows where deliveries concentrate" ) for ax in ( left , right ): ax . set_xlabel ( "Distance (km)" ) left . set_ylabel ( "Delivery time (minutes)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Synthetic data: the same 50,000 deliveries, two charts" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () A hexbin plot divides the chart into hexagons and colours each one by how many points fall inside it, like a two-dimensional histogram. The darkest hexagons show where the data is densest : here, short deliveries of modest duration. gridsize sets how many hexagons fit across; mincnt=1 leaves empty hexagons blank. Chart Best for Weakness Scatter plot Up to a few thousand rows; individual outliers Overplotting with many rows Hexbin plot Two numeric columns with many rows Hides individual points Box plot Comparing centre and spread across groups Hides the shape (two peaks, gaps) Violin plot Comparing the full shape across groups Harder for a non-technical audience to read Check your understanding In the hexbin plot, where is the densest region, roughly (a distance range and a time range)? How would you describe it to an operations manager in one sentence? Summary ¶ Explore before you analyse: structure → quality → distributions → groups → relationships → confounders . info() and isnull().sum() find missing values; a missing value is not available , never zero. Check duplicates and impossible values with duplicated() and the min and max in describe() . Prices, bills and incomes are usually right-skewed : the mean sits above the median, so report the median as the typical value. pd.pivot_table(values=, index=, columns=, aggfunc=) compares a measure across two categories; always read the counts behind each average. corr() and a heatmap show straight-line relationships from −1 to +1; correlation is not causation. A confounder can shrink, inflate or reverse a comparison ( Simpson's paradox ). Compare within bands of the suspected confounder. With many rows, use a hexbin plot instead of a scatter plot, and a violin plot to see the full shape of each group. Quick reference ¶ You want to… Code Columns, types and non-null counts df.info() Missing values per column df.isnull().sum() Duplicated rows df.duplicated().sum() Skewness of a column df["col"].skew() Pivot table pd.pivot_table(data=df, values="y", index="a", columns="b", aggfunc="mean") Correlation matrix df.select_dtypes(include="number").corr() Heatmap sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1) Bands of a number pd.cut(df["col"], bins=[...]) Violin plot sns.violinplot(data=df, x="group", y="value") Hexbin plot plt.hexbin(df["x"], df["y"], gridsize=40, cmap="Blues", mincnt=1) Quiz: ready for the lab? ¶ Which two pandas calls tell you whether a table has missing values, and how? A column of prices has a mean of 4,000 and a median of 2,400. What shape is its distribution, and which number would you report as the typical price? Write the pd.pivot_table call that shows the average price with cut in the rows and color in the columns of a table called diamonds . In a correlation heatmap, one column has r = 0.92 with price and another r = −0.01. Describe each relationship in words. A cheaper product grade sells for a higher average price than a better grade. Suggest one reason based on confounding, and one way to check it. Why would you draw a hexbin plot instead of a scatter plot for 50,000 rows, and what does the darkest hexagon tell you? docs.text: Before anyone trusts a number, an analyst explores the table it came from. This lecture teaches a repeatable exploration routine in pandas: check the structure and data quality, describe distributions and skew, summarise groups with pivot tables, measure relationships with correlation, look for hidden confounders, and draw charts that still work with tens of thousands of rows. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter .

docs.text: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the first look at a new dataset: what is in it, whether it can be trusted, and which patterns are worth a closer look. It is descriptive and diagnostic analytics in practice. Analysts follow roughly the same routine every time: Step Question pandas and charts 1. Structure How many rows and columns? What does one row mean? Which types? shape , info() , dtypes , head() 2. Data quality What is missing, duplicated or impossible? isnull().sum() , duplicated() , describe() (min and max) 3. Distributions What is typical? How spread out? Symmetric or skewed? describe() , skew() , histogram, box or violin plot 4. Groups How does a measure differ between categories? groupby , pd.pivot_table 5. Relationships Which numeric columns move together, and how strongly? corr() , heatmap, scatter or hexbin plot 6. Confounders Could a third variable explain the difference? Compare within groups of that variable We use two tables you have in the data folder, so everything runs without internet: Table One row is Used for mpg.csv One car model from 1970–1982 (fuel economy in miles per gallon, engine and weight) Structure, quality, correlation, confounding tips.csv One restaurant bill, with the tip (US dollars) Distributions, pivot tables The lab applies the same routine to a third table. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd import seaborn as sns cars = pd . read_csv ( "data/mpg.csv" ) tips = pd . read_csv ( "data/tips.csv" ) tips [ "tip_percent" ] = 100 * tips [ "tip" ] / tips [ "total_bill" ] print ( "cars:" , cars . shape , "| tips:" , tips . shape ) cars: (398, 9) | tips: (244, 8)
docs.title: Part 1: The exploration routine

docs.text: shape gives (rows, columns). info() lists every column with its type and its count of non-null (recorded) values. Compare that count with the number of rows: a lower number means missing values. cars . info () <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'> RangeIndex: 398 entries, 0 to 397 Data columns (total 9 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 mpg 398 non-null float64 1 cylinders 398 non-null int64 2 displacement 398 non-null float64 3 horsepower 392 non-null float64 4 weight 398 non-null int64 5 acceleration 398 non-null float64 6 model_year 398 non-null int64 7 origin 398 non-null object 8 name 398 non-null object dtypes: float64(4), int64(3), object(2) memory usage: 28.1+ KB Predict, then reveal Read the Non-Null Count column in the output above. Which column has fewer values than there are rows? Then run the next cell, which counts the missing values directly. print ( "Missing values per column:" ) print ( cars . isnull () . sum ()) Missing values per column: mpg 0 cylinders 0 displacement 0 horsepower 6 weight 0 acceleration 0 model_year 0 origin 0 name 0 dtype: int64 isnull() marks each missing cell as True ; .sum() counts the True values in each column. Let us look at the rows concerned rather than guess: cars [ cars [ "horsepower" ] . isnull ()][[ "name" , "model_year" , "weight" , "horsepower" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } name model_year weight horsepower 32 ford pinto 71 2046 NaN 126 ford maverick 74 2875 NaN 330 renault lecar deluxe 80 1835 NaN 336 ford mustang cobra 80 2905 NaN 354 renault 18i 81 2320 NaN 374 amc concord dl 82 3035 NaN A missing value is not available , not zero. Filling it with 0 would invent engines with no power and pull every average down. Common choices are: Choice When it makes sense Keep and note Few rows are affected and pandas skips missing values in means and correlations anyway Drop the rows for an analysis that needs the column The rows are a small share and missing for no particular reason Fill in (impute) with a typical value Only with a stated reason, and never silently Here we keep the rows and note it: pandas ignores missing values when it computes a mean or a correlation.
docs.title: Structure

docs.text: Missing values are only one problem. Check for duplicated rows and impossible values . describe() shows each column's minimum and maximum, which is the fastest way to spot a weight of zero or a year of 2099. print ( "Fully duplicated rows:" , cars . duplicated () . sum ()) cars . describe () . round ( 1 ) Fully duplicated rows: 0 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mpg cylinders displacement horsepower weight acceleration model_year count 398.0 398.0 398.0 392.0 398.0 398.0 398.0 mean 23.5 5.5 193.4 104.5 2970.4 15.6 76.0 std 7.8 1.7 104.3 38.5 846.8 2.8 3.7 min 9.0 3.0 68.0 46.0 1613.0 8.0 70.0 25% 17.5 4.0 104.2 75.0 2223.8 13.8 73.0 50% 23.0 4.0 148.5 93.5 2803.5 15.5 76.0 75% 29.0 8.0 262.0 126.0 3608.0 17.2 79.0 max 46.6 8.0 455.0 230.0 5140.0 24.8 82.0 Read the min and max rows in the output above. Are they plausible for cars of that era (fuel economy, weight in pounds, model year as two digits)? Data-quality checklist Row count and grain: what does one row mean? Types: are numbers stored as numbers and categories as text? Missing values: how many, where, and why? Duplicates: genuine repeats or double entries? Impossible values: zeros, negatives or extremes that cannot be true? Write down what you found and what you did about it. Check your understanding A colleague replaces every missing horsepower with 0 and reports the average horsepower. What goes wrong? What would you do instead?
docs.title: Other quality checks

docs.text: A distribution describes how the values of one column are spread out. Three questions describe it: what is typical (centre), how spread out it is, and what shape it has. Predict, then reveal Restaurant bills cannot be negative, and most are modest, but a few parties spend a lot. Will the mean bill be above, below or equal to the median bill? Write your guess, then run the next cell. bill = tips [ "total_bill" ] print ( f "Mean bill: { bill . mean () : .2f } US dollars" ) print ( f "Median bill: { bill . median () : .2f } US dollars" ) print ( f "Skewness: { bill . skew () : .2f } " ) Mean bill: 19.79 US dollars Median bill: 17.80 US dollars Skewness: 1.13 Skewness measures how lopsided a distribution is: Skewness Shape Mean compared with median Typical business examples Close to 0 Roughly symmetric About equal Heights, measurement errors Clearly positive (about 1 or more) Right-skewed : a long tail of large values Mean above the median Bills, incomes, prices, order sizes Clearly negative Left-skewed : a long tail of small values Mean below the median Scores on an easy test With a right-skewed column, a few large values pull the mean up, so the median is the better "typical" value to report. The histogram shows the tail: fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) ax . hist ( bill , bins = 25 , color = "#2a78d6" , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . axvline ( bill . median (), color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Median" ) ax . axvline ( bill . mean (), color = "#1baf7a" , linewidth = 2 , linestyle = "--" , label = "Mean" ) ax . set_title ( "Most bills are modest; a long tail of large bills pulls the mean up" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Total bill (US dollars)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of bills" ) ax . legend () plt . show ()
docs.title: Part 3: Distributions and skew

docs.text: A box plot summarises each group with five numbers. A violin plot draws the whole shape: the width at each height shows how many values lie there, like a histogram turned on its side and mirrored. The thin box inside marks the middle half and the median. cut=0 stops each violin at the smallest and largest real value, so it never suggests a negative bill. Violins are useful when a group has two peaks or a long tail, which a box plot hides. day_order = [ "Thur" , "Fri" , "Sat" , "Sun" ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) sns . violinplot ( data = tips , x = "day" , y = "total_bill" , order = day_order , color = "#2a78d6" , cut = 0 , ax = ax ) ax . set_title ( "Bills on every day are right-skewed: most are modest, a few are large" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Day of the week" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Total bill (US dollars)" ) plt . show () Each violin is wide near the bottom (many modest bills) and has a thin neck reaching upwards (a few large bills): the right-skewed shape again, on every day. Check your understanding A manager reads that the average house price in a city is far above what most families paid. Using the words skew , mean and median , explain how both statements can be true. Which number should the report lead with?
docs.title: Comparing distributions across groups: the violin plot

docs.text: Business questions often compare a measure across two categories at once: tip percentage by day and by time (lunch or dinner), sales by region and by product, price by quality and by grade. A pivot table puts one category in the rows, another in the columns, and a summary of the measure in each cell. It is the same idea as a pivot table in Excel. pd.pivot_table needs four things: Argument Meaning Here values The measure to summarise tip_percent index The category for the rows day columns The category for the columns time aggfunc The summary for each cell "mean" tip_pivot = pd . pivot_table ( data = tips , values = "tip_percent" , index = "day" , columns = "time" , aggfunc = "mean" , ) . reindex ( day_order ) print ( "Average tip ( % o f the bill) by day and time" ) tip_pivot . round ( 1 ) Average tip (% of the bill) by day and time .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } time Dinner Lunch day Thur 16.0 16.1 Fri 15.9 18.9 Sat 15.3 NaN Sun 16.7 NaN .reindex(day_order) puts the rows in calendar order instead of alphabetical order. Predict, then reveal Some cells in the output above show NaN . Is that a tip percentage of zero? Before reading on, guess what it means. NaN means not available : there were no bills in that combination (the restaurant served no weekend lunches in this data). An empty cell is not a zero. A pivot table of averages should always be read next to the counts behind each cell, because an average of three bills is far less reliable than an average of eighty: count_pivot = pd . pivot_table ( data = tips , values = "tip_percent" , index = "day" , columns = "time" , aggfunc = "count" , ) . reindex ( day_order ) print ( "Number of bills behind each average" ) count_pivot Number of bills behind each average .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } time Dinner Lunch day Thur 1.0 61.0 Fri 12.0 7.0 Sat 87.0 NaN Sun 76.0 NaN
docs.title: Part 4: Pivot tables and groupby

docs.text: groupby with two columns gives the same numbers in a long table: one row per combination. Use whichever is easier to read. observed=True keeps only combinations that actually occur. tips . groupby ([ "day" , "time" ], observed = True ) . agg ( bills = ( "tip_percent" , "count" ), average_tip_percent = ( "tip_percent" , "mean" ), ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } bills average_tip_percent day time Fri Dinner 12 15.9 Lunch 7 18.9 Sat Dinner 87 15.3 Sun Dinner 76 16.7 Thur Dinner 1 16.0 Lunch 61 16.1 Check your understanding Write the pd.pivot_table call that shows the median total bill with sex in the rows and smoker in the columns. Which argument changes, and why might the median suit bills better than the mean?
docs.title: The same summary with groupby

docs.text: The correlation coefficient r measures how closely two numeric columns follow a straight line : r Reading +1 Perfect straight line going up about +0.7 or more Strong positive relationship about 0 No straight-line relationship (there may still be a curve) about −0.7 or less Strong negative relationship −1 Perfect straight line going down corr() computes r for every pair of numeric columns at once: a correlation matrix . select_dtypes(include="number") keeps only the numeric columns, because a correlation needs numbers. numeric_cars = cars . select_dtypes ( include = "number" ) corr_matrix = numeric_cars . corr () corr_matrix . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mpg cylinders displacement horsepower weight acceleration model_year mpg 1.00 -0.78 -0.80 -0.78 -0.83 0.42 0.58 cylinders -0.78 1.00 0.95 0.84 0.90 -0.51 -0.35 displacement -0.80 0.95 1.00 0.90 0.93 -0.54 -0.37 horsepower -0.78 0.84 0.90 1.00 0.86 -0.69 -0.42 weight -0.83 0.90 0.93 0.86 1.00 -0.42 -0.31 acceleration 0.42 -0.51 -0.54 -0.69 -0.42 1.00 0.29 model_year 0.58 -0.35 -0.37 -0.42 -0.31 0.29 1.00 A table of 49 numbers is hard to scan. A heatmap colours each cell by its value, with a diverging colour scale fixed from −1 to +1 so that colour means the same thing in every heatmap: one colour for positive, another for negative, pale near zero. annot=True prints the value in each cell. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6.5 )) sns . heatmap ( corr_matrix , annot = True , fmt = ".2f" , cmap = "RdBu_r" , vmin =- 1 , vmax = 1 , linewidths = 0.5 , ax = ax , cbar_kws = { "label" : "Correlation coefficient r" }, ) ax . set_title ( "Heavier, more powerful cars have lower fuel economy (mpg)" ) plt . show () Read the mpg row of the heatmap above: which column has the strongest relationship with fuel economy, and in which direction? Notice also the dark block of engine columns ( cylinders , displacement , horsepower , weight ) that are strongly correlated with each other : they largely measure the same thing, the size of the car. Three warnings about correlation Straight lines only. A strong curve can have r near 0 (remember Anscombe's set II). Plot before you conclude. Association is not causation. Two columns can move together because a third drives both. The diagonal is always 1. Every column correlates perfectly with itself; ignore it. Check your understanding The correlation between model_year and mpg is positive. Does that prove that newer car designs caused better fuel economy? Name one other column that could be part of the explanation.
docs.title: Part 5: Correlation and the heatmap

docs.text: A confounder is a third variable that is related to both things you compare, and so distorts the comparison. Let us compare fuel economy of cars from the three regions of origin in the data. cars . groupby ( "origin" ) . agg ( cars = ( "mpg" , "count" ), average_mpg = ( "mpg" , "mean" ), average_weight_lb = ( "weight" , "mean" ), ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } cars average_mpg average_weight_lb origin europe 70 27.9 2423.3 japan 79 30.5 2221.2 usa 249 20.1 3361.9 Predict, then reveal The output above shows a large gap in average fuel economy between regions. Look also at the weight column. Is the gap mostly about where the car was built, or about something else? Write your answer, then run the next cell. To check, we hold the suspected confounder roughly constant : cut weight into bands with pd.cut , then compare regions within each band. cars [ "weight_band" ] = pd . cut ( cars [ "weight" ], bins = [ 0 , 2500 , 3000 , 3500 , 6000 ], labels = [ "under 2,500 lb" , "2,500-3,000 lb" , "3,000-3,500 lb" , "over 3,500 lb" ], ) within_band = pd . pivot_table ( data = cars , values = "mpg" , index = "origin" , columns = "weight_band" , aggfunc = "mean" , observed = True , ) print ( "Average mpg by origin, within weight bands (NaN = no cars of that origin and weight)" ) within_band . round ( 1 ) Average mpg by origin, within weight bands (NaN = no cars of that origin and weight) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } weight_band under 2,500 lb 2,500-3,000 lb 3,000-3,500 lb over 3,500 lb origin europe 30.7 22.8 23.5 21.0 japan 31.7 26.0 NaN NaN usa 29.0 24.3 19.4 15.1 Compare the overall gap from the previous output with the gap inside each weight band above. Within a band, cars of similar weight from different regions are much closer than the overall averages suggested. A large part of the overall gap comes from the mix : one region's cars are mostly heavy, the others' mostly light. Weight is a confounder : it is related to origin and it drives fuel economy. The chart shows the mix directly: origin_colours = { "europe" : "#1baf7a" , "japan" : "#eb6834" , "usa" : "#2a78d6" } fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) for origin , group in cars . groupby ( "origin" ): ax . scatter ( group [ "weight" ], group [ "mpg" ], s = 18 , alpha = 0.7 , color = origin_colours [ origin ], label = origin ) ax . set_title ( "Fuel economy falls with weight for cars from every region" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Weight (pounds)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Fuel economy (miles per gallon)" ) ax . legend ( title = "Origin" ) plt . show ()
docs.title: A comparison that misleads

docs.text: Sometimes a confounder does not just shrink a gap; it reverses it. A well-known medical study (Charig and colleagues, 1986) compared two treatments for kidney stones. The counts below are from that study. stones = pd . DataFrame ({ "treatment" : [ "A" , "A" , "B" , "B" ], "stone_size" : [ "small" , "large" , "small" , "large" ], "patients" : [ 87 , 263 , 270 , 80 ], "successes" : [ 81 , 192 , 234 , 55 ], }) by_size = stones . assign ( success_rate = 100 * stones [ "successes" ] / stones [ "patients" ]) print ( "Success rate (%) within each stone size" ) print ( by_size . pivot_table ( values = "success_rate" , index = "treatment" , columns = "stone_size" ) . round ( 1 )) overall = stones . groupby ( "treatment" )[[ "patients" , "successes" ]] . sum () overall [ "success_rate" ] = 100 * overall [ "successes" ] / overall [ "patients" ] print () print ( "Success rate (%) overall" ) print ( overall . round ( 1 )) Success rate (%) within each stone size stone_size large small treatment A 73.0 93.1 B 68.8 86.7 Success rate (%) overall patients successes success_rate treatment A 350 273 78.0 B 350 289 82.6 Predict, then reveal Before reading on: in the output above, which treatment wins for small stones? For large stones? And overall ? Treatment A has the higher success rate for small stones and for large stones, yet B looks better overall. The reason is the mix: doctors gave A mostly to large , difficult stones and B mostly to small, easy ones. Stone size affects both the treatment chosen and the chance of success, so it is a confounder, and adding the groups together reverses the story. This reversal is Simpson's paradox . How to protect yourself When a comparison between groups surprises you, ask: what else differs between these groups? Then compare within levels of that variable (bands, as above), or compare a ratio that removes it (for example fuel used per pound, or price per unit of size). You will meet a confounder in the lab. Check your understanding A hospital's overall death rate is higher than a nearby clinic's. Name a likely confounder, and say how you would check whether the hospital is really worse.
docs.title: Simpson's paradox: when the total reverses every part

docs.text: With a few hundred rows a scatter plot works well. With tens of thousands, the dots pile on top of each other ( overplotting ): a solid blob hides where most of the data actually is. To show this, the next cell creates synthetic (made-up) data for 50,000 deliveries: the distance in kilometres and the delivery time in minutes. The random generator is seeded, so everyone gets the same numbers. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 300 ) n = 50_000 distance_km = rng . gamma ( shape = 2.0 , scale = 3.0 , size = n ) delivery_min = 10 + 4 * distance_km + rng . gamma ( shape = 2.0 , scale = 5.0 , size = n ) deliveries = pd . DataFrame ({ "distance_km" : distance_km , "delivery_min" : delivery_min }) print ( "Synthetic deliveries:" , deliveries . shape ) deliveries . describe () . round ( 1 ) Synthetic deliveries: (50000, 2) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } distance_km delivery_min count 50000.0 50000.0 mean 6.0 44.0 std 4.2 18.3 min 0.0 10.8 25% 2.9 30.6 50% 5.0 40.6 75% 8.1 53.7 max 39.7 179.0 Predict, then reveal In a plain scatter plot of 50,000 deliveries, will you be able to see where most deliveries lie? Run the next cell and compare the two panels. fig , ( left , right ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4.5 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) left . scatter ( deliveries [ "distance_km" ], deliveries [ "delivery_min" ], s = 4 , color = "#2a78d6" ) left . set_title ( "Scatter plot: 50,000 dots overlap into a blob" ) hb = right . hexbin ( deliveries [ "distance_km" ], deliveries [ "delivery_min" ], gridsize = 40 , cmap = "Blues" , mincnt = 1 ) fig . colorbar ( hb , ax = right , label = "Deliveries in the hexagon" ) right . set_title ( "Hexbin plot: colour shows where deliveries concentrate" ) for ax in ( left , right ): ax . set_xlabel ( "Distance (km)" ) left . set_ylabel ( "Delivery time (minutes)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Synthetic data: the same 50,000 deliveries, two charts" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () A hexbin plot divides the chart into hexagons and colours each one by how many points fall inside it, like a two-dimensional histogram. The darkest hexagons show where the data is densest : here, short deliveries of modest duration. gridsize sets how many hexagons fit across; mincnt=1 leaves empty hexagons blank. Chart Best for Weakness Scatter plot Up to a few thousand rows; individual outliers Overplotting with many rows Hexbin plot Two numeric columns with many rows Hides individual points Box plot Comparing centre and spread across groups Hides the shape (two peaks, gaps) Violin plot Comparing the full shape across groups Harder for a non-technical audience to read Check your understanding In the hexbin plot, where is the densest region, roughly (a distance range and a time range)? docs.text: Explore before you analyse: structure → quality → distributions → groups → relationships → confounders . info() and isnull().sum() find missing values; a missing value is not available , never zero. Check duplicates and impossible values with duplicated() and the min and max in describe() . Prices, bills and incomes are usually right-skewed : the mean sits above the median, so report the median as the typical value. pd.pivot_table(values=, index=, columns=, aggfunc=) compares a measure across two categories; always read the counts behind each average. corr() and a heatmap show straight-line relationships from −1 to +1; correlation is not causation. A confounder can shrink, inflate or reverse a comparison ( Simpson's paradox ). Compare within bands of the suspected confounder. With many rows, use a hexbin plot instead of a scatter plot, and a violin plot to see the full shape of each group.

Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Applied Lab 2 (Dashboard creation). Instructions rewritten for this classroom. Graded work: Applied Lab 2 (3%, CLO 1, 2 and 3) Tools: Tableau Desktop (student licence) with the built-in Sample – Superstore data, and Word (or another editor that saves PDF). Its regional managers say two things are hard to see in their current reports: how their own state's sales are moving from month to month, and which product sub-categories make or lose money in their state. Your job is to build one interactive Executive Summary Dashboard . A manager clicks their state on a map, and the other charts immediately show that state's monthly sales trend and its sub-categories, coloured by profit. This is this morning's dashboard design in practice: one audience (regional managers), one decision (which products to look at), a few views, and an action that filters every view. Before you start ¶ Open Tableau Desktop . If it asks for a licence, use your student licence key. On the start page, check that Sample – Superstore appears under Saved Data Sources . If it does not, ask your facilitator for the course copy of the Superstore file; then connect with Connect → To a File → Microsoft Excel and drag the Orders sheet onto the canvas. Make a folder for this lab, for example Lab2 , to keep your files together. Your numbers may differ from your neighbour's Tableau ships different versions of Sample – Superstore with different releases (different years, and sometimes Canadian provinces as well as US states). Answer from your dashboard. If a field is called State/Province instead of State , use that; the steps are the same. Part 1: Connect to the data (Core) ¶ On the start page, under Saved Data Sources , click Sample – Superstore . Tableau opens a blank worksheet called Sheet 1 . The Data pane on the left lists the fields. You are connected. Check: you can see Order Date , State (or State/Province ), Sub-Category , Sales and Profit in the Data pane. Part 2: Build three worksheets (Core) ¶ A dashboard is assembled from separate worksheets. Build and name each one first. Sheet 1: Monthly Sales Trend (a line chart) ¶ Rename the sheet: right-click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom → Rename → type Monthly Sales Trend . Drag Order Date from the Data pane to the Columns shelf. Tableau shows a blue pill, YEAR(Order Date) : one column per year. Right-click that pill. The menu shows two lists of date options. In the second list (the continuous date values, which show an example such as May 2015 ), choose Month . The pill turns green : the dates now form one continuous timeline, month by month. Drag Sales to the Rows shelf. A line chart of total sales per month appears. Check: the pill on Columns is green and reads MONTH(Order Date) ; the x-axis is a timeline across several years, not twelve month names. Sheet 2: Profitability by State (a filled map) ¶ Click the New Worksheet icon (the first small icon to the right of the sheet tabs). Rename the new tab Profitability by State . In the Data pane, double-click State (or State/Province ). Tableau draws a map with one dot per state. On the Marks card, open the mark-type dropdown (it says Automatic ) and choose Map . Each state is now filled. Drag Profit onto Color on the Marks card. Tableau colours states on a diverging scale: blue for profit, orange for loss . Check: most states are blue, and a few are orange. If the map is empty or shows "unknown" locations, click the grey unknown indicator at the bottom right of the map and ask your facilitator. Sheet 3: Sales by Sub-Category (a bar chart coloured by profit) ¶ Create another New Worksheet and rename it Sales by Sub-Category . Drag Sub-Category to Rows . Drag Sales to Columns . You see horizontal bars. Click the Sort Descending button in the toolbar so the biggest sub-category is at the top. Drag Profit onto Color on the Marks card. Now the length of each bar is sales and its colour is profit. Check: 17 bars, sorted from largest to smallest sales, most of them blue and a few orange. Part 3: Assemble the interactive dashboard (Core) ¶ Click the New Dashboard icon (the second small icon next to the sheet tabs). In the Size section on the left, change the size setting to Automatic so the dashboard fills the screen. Under Sheets on the left you see your three worksheets. Drag them onto the canvas: Profitability by State across the top half ; Monthly Sales Trend in the bottom left ; Sales by Sub-Category in the bottom right . Make the map a filter. Click once on the map inside the dashboard so a grey border appears around it. At the top right of that border, click the small funnel icon ( Use as Filter ). It changes colour when it is on. Test it: click Texas on the map. The trend and the bar chart should change to show Texas only. Click Texas again (or press Esc ) to clear the selection. Check: clicking any state changes both bottom charts; clearing the selection brings back the national totals. Rename the dashboard tab to Executive Summary Dashboard , then save your work: File → Save As → Tableau Packaged Workbook ( .twbx ) in your Lab2 folder. Part 4: Answer the business questions (Core) ¶ Use your dashboard to answer these questions in a Word document (one or two sentences each, in full sentences). Put your name and student ID at the top. National view (no state selected) ¶ Question 1. Looking at the whole country, which sub-category has the highest total sales ? Is it profitable? (Is its bar blue or orange?) Question 2. On the national map, name two states that make an overall loss (coloured orange). Using the dashboard filter ¶ Question 3. Click Texas on the map. (a) In Sales by Sub-Category , which sub-category makes the largest loss in Texas (the darkest orange)? (b) In Monthly Sales Trend , in which month and year did Texas have an unusually large spike in sales? Question 4. Now click California . Compare its Sales by Sub-Category chart with Texas's. Are the top three best-selling sub-categories the same in both states? If not, name California's top three. Visual design ¶ Question 5. Why is it more useful to colour the Sales by Sub-Category bars by Profit rather than by Sales? What business insight does showing two measures in one chart (length = sales, colour = profit) reveal that a plain sales bar chart would hide?
