Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Assignment 4 (Final Comprehensive Assignment, Capstone). Brief rewritten for this classroom; the text mining runs offline in local JupyterLab. Graded work: Assignment 4 (25%, CLO 4 and 5) Set: Thursday 19 November (Day 7), in the afternoon lab. Due: Sunday 29 November 2026, 23:59 China Standard Time . Submit: the report PDF, the notebook PDF and the Excel workbook (Part 5) to the DATA 300: Assignment 4 drop-box on GAP (Moodle) . Work: individual. Online support is available during the post-class week. This notebook is both the brief (read it all first) and your starter notebook for Part 1. Save your own copy before you change anything: File → Save Notebook As… → YourLastName_DATA300_Capstone.ipynb , in the same folder as this notebook so that the data folder is found. The outcomes this capstone assesses: Outcome What it means here CLO 4 : develop predictive models (forecasting, regression, spreadsheet simulation) to project future outcomes A sentiment-adjusted five-year demand projection and a profit model for two supply-chain scenarios CLO 5 : evaluate the impact of BI tools within a case study to produce managerial reports that consider ethical and societal contexts A board recommendation that balances the profit gap against ethics and brand, and an evaluation of the Python → Excel → Tableau workflow The scenario ¶ EcoVate is an electronics company about to launch a smart-home energy manager , a device that cuts household electricity use. Before it signs a five-year manufacturing contract , the executive team needs answers to two questions: Question What the board needs to know 1. Demand Focus groups have tried the product. Judging by what they said, should the sales forecast be raised, and by how much? 2. Ethical supply chain Should EcoVate use a standard overseas manufacturer, which is cheaper but has a record of carbon-emission violations, or a Fair-Trade Green Certified manufacturer, which costs more per unit but meets ethical and environmental standards? You are the lead BI analyst. You will carry the evidence through three tools, as BI teams do in practice: Python (JupyterLab): turn the focus groups' free-text comments into a single demand multiplier . Excel: apply the multiplier to a five-year demand plan and compute the profit under each supplier. Tableau: chart the two profit paths for the board. Then you write the managerial report . What you must do ¶ Part Tool Task Output 1 JupyterLab Score the focus-group comments and compute the demand multiplier Executed notebook (PDF) 2 Excel Build the five-year demand and profit model for both suppliers YourLastName_DATA300_Capstone.xlsx 3 Tableau Chart standard against ethical profit by year and export the chart Image in your Word report 4 Word Write the executive summary: introduction plus answers to two questions YourLastName_Capstone_Report.pdf 5 GAP Submit the three deliverables The code in Part 1 already works. Run it, read the output, and write down your multiplier. The cells after it help you check your Excel results and give you numbers you may quote in your report. Part 1: Text mining in JupyterLab (from sentiment to strategy) ¶ Setup ¶ The first cell points NLTK, the Natural Language Toolkit, to the word lists bundled in the data folder, so nothing is downloaded from the internet. import zipfile from pathlib import Path import nltk NLTK_DIR = Path ( "data/nltk_data" ) . resolve () if not ( NLTK_DIR / "tokenizers" / "punkt_tab" ) . exists (): with zipfile . ZipFile ( NLTK_DIR / "tokenizers" / "punkt_tab.zip" ) as z : z . extractall ( NLTK_DIR / "tokenizers" ) nltk . data . path . insert ( 0 , str ( NLTK_DIR )) Load the focus-group comments ¶ The five comments come from the focus groups that tested the product. One row is one participant's comment. They are bundled in data/ecovate_focus_group.csv . import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd from nltk.sentiment.vader import SentimentIntensityAnalyzer pd . set_option ( "display.max_colwidth" , 100 ) pd . set_option ( "display.width" , 140 ) reviews = pd . read_csv ( "data/ecovate_focus_group.csv" ) print ( "Comments:" , len ( reviews )) reviews Comments: 5 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Review_ID Review_Text 0 1 I absolutely love the energy-saving features. It looks sleek and works perfectly. 1 2 Good product, but the mobile app is a little bit confusing to set up. 2 3 Incredible! I saved $40 on my electric bill the first month. Highly recommend. 3 4 It is an okay device. Kind of expensive for what it actually does. 4 5 Brilliant integration with my other smart devices. A must-buy for green homes. Score the sentiment and compute the demand multiplier ¶ VADER gives each comment a compound sentiment score from −1 (very negative) to +1 (very positive), as in Lab 3. The business rule that turns sentiment into a forecast adjustment: Step Rule Baseline A multiplier of 1.0 means "keep the original demand plan" Adjustment Add up to 20% : multiplier = 1.0 + (average compound score × 0.20) Example An average score of +0.5 gives 1.0 + 0.5 × 0.20 = 1.10, so demand is raised by 10% Run the cell and read the table and the multiplier in the output. analyser = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () reviews [ "Sentiment_Score" ] = reviews [ "Review_Text" ] . apply ( lambda text : analyser . polarity_scores ( text )[ "compound" ]) avg_sentiment = reviews [ "Sentiment_Score" ] . mean () demand_multiplier = 1.0 + avg_sentiment * 0.20 print ( "--- Step 1: Sentiment analysis results ---" ) display ( reviews ) print ( f " \n Average sentiment score: { avg_sentiment : .3f } " ) print ( f "--> YOUR DEMAND MULTIPLIER (use in Excel, 3 decimals): { demand_multiplier : .3f } <--" ) --- Step 1: Sentiment analysis results --- .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Review_ID Review_Text Sentiment_Score 0 1 I absolutely love the energy-saving features. It looks sleek and works perfectly. 0.8655 1 2 Good product, but the mobile app is a little bit confusing to set up. 0.0045 2 3 Incredible! I saved $40 on my electric bill the first month. Highly recommend. 0.7082 3 4 It is an okay device. Kind of expensive for what it actually does. 0.2263 4 5 Brilliant integration with my other smart devices. A must-buy for green homes. 0.7579 Average sentiment score: 0.512 --> YOUR DEMAND MULTIPLIER (use in Excel, 3 decimals): 1.102 <-- fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.5 )) ordered = reviews . sort_values ( "Sentiment_Score" ) ax . barh ( ordered [ "Review_ID" ] . astype ( str ), ordered [ "Sentiment_Score" ], color = "#2a78d6" ) ax . axvline ( avg_sentiment , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = f "Average = { avg_sentiment : .3f } " ) ax . set_xlim ( - 1 , 1 ) ax . set_title ( "Focus-group comments are positive overall, but not all equally" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "VADER compound score (−1 very negative, +1 very positive)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Comment ID" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "lower left" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Read before you move on Write down your multiplier, rounded to 3 decimals as printed above; you type it into Excel in Part 2. Read the two lowest-scoring comments: what do they complain about? A good report mentions what the multiplier hides (five comments is a very small sample; mixed comments score close to neutral). Part 2: Five-year financial model in Excel ¶ Apply the multiplier to the demand plan and compare the profit of the two suppliers. Amounts are in US dollars. Assumptions Item Value Selling price per unit 200 Fixed costs per year 500,000 Standard supplier: cost to build one unit 120, so the margin is 80 per unit Ethical (Fair-Trade Green Certified) supplier: cost to build one unit 140, so the margin is 60 per unit Base demand plan, years 1–5 (units) 10,000; 15,000; 22,000; 30,000; 45,000 (also in data/ecovate_base_demand.csv ) Steps Open a blank Excel workbook and save it as YourLastName_DATA300_Capstone.xlsx . In row 1, type these headers in cells A1 to F1 : Year , Base_Demand , Demand_Multiplier , Adjusted_Demand , Standard_Profit , Ethical_Profit . In A2:A6 type the years 1 to 5. In B2:B6 type the base demand for each year from the table above. In C2:C6 type your demand multiplier from Part 1 (the same 3-decimal number in every row). In D2 type =ROUND(B2*C2, 0) and fill it down to D6. This is the sentiment-adjusted demand in whole units. In E2 type =(D2*80)-500000 and fill down to E6: profit with the standard supplier (units × margin − fixed costs). In F2 type =(D2*60)-500000 and fill down to F6: profit with the ethical supplier. Format columns E and F as currency. Save and close the workbook (Tableau cannot read a file that is open in Excel on some computers). Better practice (optional, recommended) Professional models keep assumptions in labelled cells, not inside formulas. You may put the price, costs and fixed costs in an assumptions block (for example in H1:I5) and refer to them with absolute references such as $I$3 . Your results must be the same. Check your Excel model ¶ The next cell builds the same table in Python from the bundled demand plan and your multiplier. Your Excel sheet should match it exactly . If it does not, check that you typed the multiplier rounded to 3 decimals and that the formulas were filled down. PRICE , FIXED = 200 , 500_000 MARGIN_STANDARD , MARGIN_ETHICAL = PRICE - 120 , PRICE - 140 plan = pd . read_csv ( "data/ecovate_base_demand.csv" ) plan [ "Demand_Multiplier" ] = round ( demand_multiplier , 3 ) # Excel's ROUND rounds halves away from zero; this matches it for positive numbers plan [ "Adjusted_Demand" ] = ( plan [ "Base_Demand" ] * plan [ "Demand_Multiplier" ] + 0.5 ) . astype ( int ) plan [ "Standard_Profit" ] = plan [ "Adjusted_Demand" ] * MARGIN_STANDARD - FIXED plan [ "Ethical_Profit" ] = plan [ "Adjusted_Demand" ] * MARGIN_ETHICAL - FIXED plan .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Year Base_Demand Demand_Multiplier Adjusted_Demand Standard_Profit Ethical_Profit 0 1 10000 1.102 11020 381600 161200 1 2 15000 1.102 16530 822400 491800 2 3 22000 1.102 24244 1439520 954640 3 4 30000 1.102 33060 2144800 1483600 4 5 45000 1.102 49590 3467200 2475400 How severe is the profit gap? (evidence you may quote) ¶ Question 1 of the report asks how severe the profit loss from the ethical supplier is. The cell below measures it in three ways: in money each year, in per cent, and as the extra demand the ethical option would need to earn the same profit as the standard one. You do not have to use all of these; choose what helps your argument. gap = plan [[ "Year" ]] . copy () gap [ "Gap" ] = plan [ "Standard_Profit" ] - plan [ "Ethical_Profit" ] gap [ "Gap_%_of_Standard" ] = ( 100 * gap [ "Gap" ] / plan [ "Standard_Profit" ]) . round ( 1 ) # Units the ethical option needs so that units x 60 - fixed = the standard profit gap [ "Ethical_Units_Needed" ] = (( plan [ "Standard_Profit" ] + FIXED ) / MARGIN_ETHICAL ) . round ( 0 ) . astype ( int ) gap [ "Extra_Demand_%" ] = ( 100 * ( gap [ "Ethical_Units_Needed" ] / plan [ "Adjusted_Demand" ] - 1 )) . round ( 1 ) print ( gap . to_string ( index = False )) total_std , total_eth = plan [ "Standard_Profit" ] . sum (), plan [ "Ethical_Profit" ] . sum () print ( f " \n Five-year profit, standard: { total_std : ,.0f } | ethical: { total_eth : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "Five-year gap: { total_std - total_eth : ,.0f } ( { 100 * ( total_std - total_eth ) / total_std : .1f } % of the standard profit)" ) print ( f "Both options are profitable in every year: { bool (( plan [[ 'Standard_Profit' , 'Ethical_Profit' ]] > 0 ) . all () . all ()) } " ) Year Gap Gap_%_of_Standard Ethical_Units_Needed Extra_Demand_% 1 220400 57.8 14693 33.3 2 330600 40.2 22040 33.3 3 484880 33.7 32325 33.3 4 661200 30.8 44080 33.3 5 991800 28.6 66120 33.3 Five-year profit, standard: 8,255,520 | ethical: 5,566,640 Five-year gap: 2,688,880 (32.6% of the standard profit) Both options are profitable in every year: True What if the focus groups were wrong? (optional sensitivity check) ¶ Five comments are a thin basis for a five-year contract. A model is more useful when it shows how the answer changes if a key input is wrong. The cell below repeats the five-year totals for the whole range of multipliers the rule allows: from 0.800 (every comment as negative as possible) through 1.000 (ignore the focus groups) and your multiplier, to 1.200 (every comment as positive as possible). You may quote it in your report, or build the same what-if table in Excel with a Data Table (Day 5). rows = [] for m in sorted ({ 0.8 , 0.9 , 1.0 , round ( demand_multiplier , 3 ), 1.1 , 1.2 }): units = ( plan [ "Base_Demand" ] * m + 0.5 ) . astype ( int ) rows . append ({ "Multiplier" : m , "5-yr standard profit" : ( units * MARGIN_STANDARD - FIXED ) . sum (), "5-yr ethical profit" : ( units * MARGIN_ETHICAL - FIXED ) . sum (), "Ethical years with a loss" : int ((( units * MARGIN_ETHICAL - FIXED ) < 0 ) . sum ()), }) print ( pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . to_string ( index = False )) Multiplier 5-yr standard profit 5-yr ethical profit Ethical years with a loss 0.800 5308000 3356000 1 0.900 6284000 4088000 0 1.000 7260000 4820000 0 1.100 8236000 5552000 0 1.102 8255520 5566640 0 1.200 9212000 6284000 0 Part 3: Executive chart in Tableau ¶ Chart the two profit paths so the board sees the choice at a glance. Open Tableau Desktop . Under Connect , choose Microsoft Excel and open YourLastName_DATA300_Capstone.xlsx . Open Sheet 1 . Drag Year to Columns . Right-click the pill and choose Dimension , so each year is its own position on the axis. Drag Measure Values to Rows . On the Measure Values card (below the Marks card), remove every measure except SUM(Standard Profit) and SUM(Ethical Profit) . On the Marks card, choose Line or Bar (side-by-side bars), whichever shows the comparison more clearly. Drag Measure Names to Colour so the two suppliers are distinguished, and use two colours that colour-blind readers can tell apart (for example blue and orange). Double-click the profit axis (or right-click → Format ) and set the numbers to Currency . Replace the sheet title with a message title that states the finding, with one number (Day 2), not "Sheet 1". Export the chart: Worksheet → Export → Image… , then insert the image in a blank Word document. This document becomes your report. Part 4: Managerial report ¶ In the Word document that holds your Tableau chart, write an executive summary for the board: a short introduction (the decision, the data and the three tools), then answers to the two questions below. Write for non-technical executives: lead with your recommendation, quote numbers with units, and say what the numbers cannot tell you. Follow APA 7th edition for the cover page, headings, citations and references. As a guide, about two to three pages of text is enough, not counting the cover page, the chart and the references. Question 1: Strategic and ethical recommendation (CLO 5) ¶ Your chart shows that the ethical supplier earns less profit than the standard supplier in every year . Assume also that the focus groups showed that EcoVate's target customers care strongly about a company's carbon footprint . As lead BI analyst, recommend one supplier to the board, standard or ethical, and justify it. Your justification should: state how large the profit sacrifice is (in money and in per cent, over the five years and in the early years), and whether both options stay profitable; weigh it against the ethical and societal context : emissions, the supplier's record, the customers' values, and the risk to the brand, to future sales and from regulation; consider long-term brand value , not only the five-year profit in the model; name the main assumptions and limits (for example the small focus group, fixed prices and costs) and what you would monitor after the decision. Question 2: The value of an integrated BI workflow ¶ In this project you moved the evidence across three tools: text mining in Python → financial model in Excel → visual story in Tableau . Explain why linking these three steps gives the board a more robust and realistic plan than a single static spreadsheet would. Refer to what each step added in this case, and to at least one risk of the workflow (for example an error carried from one tool to the next) and how you controlled it. Before it signs a five-year manufacturing contract , the executive team needs answers to two questions: Question What the board needs to know 1. Demand Focus groups have tried the product. Judging by what they said, should the sales forecast be raised, and by how much? 2. Ethical supply chain Should EcoVate use a standard overseas manufacturer, which is cheaper but has a record of carbon-emission violations, or a Fair-Trade Green Certified manufacturer, which costs more per unit but meets ethical and environmental standards? You are the lead BI analyst. You will carry the evidence through three tools, as BI teams do in practice: Python (JupyterLab): turn the focus groups' free-text comments into a single demand multiplier . Excel: apply the multiplier to a five-year demand plan and compute the profit under each supplier. Tableau: chart the two profit paths for the board. Then you write the managerial report .

docs.text: VADER gives each comment a compound sentiment score from −1 (very negative) to +1 (very positive), as in Lab 3. The business rule that turns sentiment into a forecast adjustment: Step Rule Baseline A multiplier of 1.0 means "keep the original demand plan" Adjustment Add up to 20% : multiplier = 1.0 + (average compound score × 0.20) Example An average score of +0.5 gives 1.0 + 0.5 × 0.20 = 1.10, so demand is raised by 10% Run the cell and read the table and the multiplier in the output. analyser = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () reviews [ "Sentiment_Score" ] = reviews [ "Review_Text" ] . apply ( lambda text : analyser . polarity_scores ( text )[ "compound" ]) avg_sentiment = reviews [ "Sentiment_Score" ] . mean () demand_multiplier = 1.0 + avg_sentiment * 0.20 print ( "--- Step 1: Sentiment analysis results ---" ) display ( reviews ) print ( f " \n Average sentiment score: { avg_sentiment : .3f } " ) print ( f "--> YOUR DEMAND MULTIPLIER (use in Excel, 3 decimals): { demand_multiplier : .3f } <--" ) --- Step 1: Sentiment analysis results --- .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Review_ID Review_Text Sentiment_Score 0 1 I absolutely love the energy-saving features. It looks sleek and works perfectly. 0.8655 1 2 Good product, but the mobile app is a little bit confusing to set up. 0.0045 2 3 Incredible! I saved $40 on my electric bill the first month. Highly recommend. 0.7082 3 4 It is an okay device. Kind of expensive for what it actually does. 0.2263 4 5 Brilliant integration with my other smart devices. A must-buy for green homes. 0.7579 Average sentiment score: 0.512 --> YOUR DEMAND MULTIPLIER (use in Excel, 3 decimals): 1.102 <-- fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.5 )) ordered = reviews . sort_values ( "Sentiment_Score" ) ax . barh ( ordered [ "Review_ID" ] . astype ( str ), ordered [ "Sentiment_Score" ], color = "#2a78d6" ) ax . axvline ( avg_sentiment , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = f "Average = { avg_sentiment : .3f } " ) ax . set_xlim ( - 1 , 1 ) ax . set_title ( "Focus-group comments are positive overall, but not all equally" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "VADER compound score (−1 very negative, +1 very positive)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Comment ID" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "lower left" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Read before you move on Write down your multiplier, rounded to 3 decimals as printed above; you type it into Excel in Part 2. Read the two lowest-scoring comments: what do they complain about? A good report mentions what the multiplier hides (five comments is a very small sample; mixed comments score close to neutral).

docs.text: Apply the multiplier to the demand plan and compare the profit of the two suppliers. Amounts are in US dollars. Assumptions Item Value Selling price per unit 200 Fixed costs per year 500,000 Standard supplier: cost to build one unit 120, so the margin is 80 per unit Ethical (Fair-Trade Green Certified) supplier: cost to build one unit 140, so the margin is 60 per unit Base demand plan, years 1–5 (units) 10,000; 15,000; 22,000; 30,000; 45,000 (also in data/ecovate_base_demand.csv ) Steps Open a blank Excel workbook and save it as YourLastName_DATA300_Capstone.xlsx . In row 1, type these headers in cells A1 to F1 : Year , Base_Demand , Demand_Multiplier , Adjusted_Demand , Standard_Profit , Ethical_Profit . In A2:A6 type the years 1 to 5. In B2:B6 type the base demand for each year from the table above. In C2:C6 type your demand multiplier from Part 1 (the same 3-decimal number in every row). In D2 type =ROUND(B2*C2, 0) and fill it down to D6. This is the sentiment-adjusted demand in whole units. In E2 type =(D2*80)-500000 and fill down to E6: profit with the standard supplier (units × margin − fixed costs). In F2 type =(D2*60)-500000 and fill down to F6: profit with the ethical supplier. Format columns E and F as currency. Save and close the workbook (Tableau cannot read a file that is open in Excel on some computers). Better practice (optional, recommended) Professional models keep assumptions in labelled cells, not inside formulas. You may put the price, costs and fixed costs in an assumptions block (for example in H1:I5) and refer to them with absolute references such as $I$3 . Your results must be the same.

docs.text: Question 1 of the report asks how severe the profit loss from the ethical supplier is. docs.text: Chart the two profit paths so the board sees the choice at a glance. Open Tableau Desktop . Under Connect , choose Microsoft Excel and open YourLastName_DATA300_Capstone.xlsx . Open Sheet 1 . Drag Year to Columns . Right-click the pill and choose Dimension , so each year is its own position on the axis. Drag Measure Values to Rows . On the Marks card, choose Line or Bar (side-by-side bars), whichever shows the comparison more clearly. docs.title: Part 4: Managerial report

docs.text: Your chart shows that the ethical supplier earns less profit than the standard supplier in every year . Assume also that the focus groups showed that EcoVate's target customers care strongly about a company's carbon footprint . As lead BI analyst, recommend one supplier to the board, standard or ethical, and justify it. Your justification should: state how large the profit sacrifice is (in money and in per cent, over the five years and in the early years), and whether both options stay profitable; weigh it against the ethical and societal context : emissions, the supplier's record, the customers' values, and the risk to the brand, to future sales and from regulation; consider long-term brand value , not only the five-year profit in the model; name the main assumptions and limits (for example the small focus group, fixed prices and costs) and what you would monitor after the decision.

docs.text: Day 7 lecture: Course review ¶ One review of the whole course, organised by the five course learning outcomes (CLOs). For each outcome you get the key ideas in a table, one short worked example on the bundled data, and the mistakes that cost marks. A practice set at the end lets you test yourself before the final exam. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder (next to the data folder) and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . What you will be able to do ¶ Match each course topic to the outcome it serves, and explain how descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive analytics fit together ( CLO 1 ). Choose an honest chart and a correct KPI for a decision, and write a message title for it ( CLO 2 ). Find relationships in structured data (correlation) and unstructured data (sentiment scores), and state their limits ( CLO 3 ). Judge a forecast, a regression model and a simulation by the right measures: MAE and RMSE, R² on test data, and the probability of a loss ( CLO 4 ). Evaluate a business intelligence (BI) recommendation that weighs money against ethical and social effects, and write it for a manager ( CLO 5 ). How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words, alone or with the person next to you. The practice set in Part 6 is in the style of the exam but uses different questions. The course on one page ¶ Day Topics Graded work Main CLOs Pre-class Python and Jupyter basics, setup Activity 1 1–4 1 Data-driven decisions; kinds of analytics; exploring data in Python Lab 1 (diamonds) 1, 2, 3 2 Visualisation principles; storytelling; dashboards and KPIs; Tableau Lab 2, Assignment 1 (tips) 1, 2, 3 3 Text mining and sentiment; forecasting Midterm, Lab 3, Lab 4 1, 2, 3, 5 4 Predictive analytics; simple and multiple regression; model evaluation Assignment 2 1–4 5 Financial modelling; spreadsheet simulation in Excel Lab 5 (MPG regression) 4, 5 6 BI strategy; BI case studies; ethics and societal context Lab 6, Lab 7, Assignment 3 3, 4, 5 7 Review; final exam; capstone launch Final exam, Assignment 4 1–5 Part Outcome Review topic 1 CLO 1 Kinds of analytics; describing data; confounding 2 CLO 2 Charts, KPIs and messages 3 CLO 3 Data mining and text mining 4 CLO 4 Forecasting, regression and simulation 5 CLO 5 BI strategy, case evaluation and ethics 6 All Practice set 7 The final exam and this afternoon The setup cell loads the libraries and the four bundled data sources: diamonds, restaurant tips, car fuel economy (MPG) and the Mauna Loa CO₂ series that ships with statsmodels . It also points NLTK at the bundled VADER lexicon, so nothing is downloaded. import warnings from pathlib import Path import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import nltk import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from nltk.sentiment.vader import SentimentIntensityAnalyzer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , mean_squared_error , r2_score from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing warnings . filterwarnings ( "ignore" , category = FutureWarning ) # NLTK reads the VADER lexicon straight from the bundled zip file nltk . data . path . insert ( 0 , str ( Path ( "data/nltk_data" ) . resolve ())) BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" # context INK = "#55534e" # notes and labels plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 9 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) diamonds = pd . read_csv ( "data/diamonds.csv" ) tips = pd . read_csv ( "data/tips.csv" ) mpg = pd . read_csv ( "data/mpg.csv" ) co2 = sm . datasets . co2 . load_pandas () . data [ "co2" ] . resample ( "ME" ) . mean () . ffill () for name , frame in [( "diamonds" , diamonds ), ( "tips" , tips ), ( "mpg" , mpg )]: print ( f " { name : 9 } { frame . shape [ 0 ] : >6 } rows x { frame . shape [ 1 ] } columns" ) print ( f "co2 { len ( co2 ) : >6 } months, { co2 . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { co2 . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } " ) diamonds 53940 rows x 10 columns tips 244 rows x 7 columns mpg 398 rows x 9 columns co2 526 months, Mar 1958 to Dec 2001 Part 1 (CLO 1): Kinds of analytics, describing data, confounding ¶ CLO 1 asks you to describe the principles of descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics and use them on a business problem. Every analysis in this course started from a decision. Kind Question it answers Course example Typical output Descriptive What happened? Revenue by day in the tips data Tables, KPIs, charts, dashboards Diagnostic Why did it happen? Why "Ideal" diamonds look cheap (Part 1 below) Comparisons within groups, drill-down Predictive What is likely to happen? Forecast of CO₂; MPG from car specifications A forecast or prediction with its error Prescriptive What should we do? Choose a supplier or a marketing strategy from a simulation A recommended action and its trade-offs The four build on each other: you cannot recommend an action (prescriptive) without a sound prediction, and you cannot predict well without first describing and checking the data. The analytics workflow ¶ Frame the decision and the question (who decides what, by when, using which measure). Get and check the data: grain (what one row is), size, types, missing values, impossible values. Describe it: centre, spread, shape, groups. Diagnose and model : relationships, comparisons within groups, predictions. Validate : test on unseen data, reconcile totals, look for confounders. Communicate and act : one message, the evidence, the recommendation, its limits. Worked example: mean or median? ¶ A distribution with a long right tail (a few very large values) pulls the mean above the median . Prices, incomes and bill sizes usually look like this. print ( diamonds [ "price" ] . describe () . round ( 0 ) . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Mean minus median: { diamonds [ 'price' ] . mean () - diamonds [ 'price' ] . median () : ,.0f } US dollars" ) count 53940.0 mean 3933.0 std 3989.0 min 326.0 25% 950.0 50% 2401.0 75% 5324.0 max 18823.0 Mean minus median: 1,532 US dollars In the output above the mean is far above the median, so the "typical" diamond costs about the median . The middle half of the diamonds lies between the 25% and 75% values (the interquartile range ). Worked example: a confounder ¶ Predict, then reveal Diamond cut runs from Fair (worst) to Ideal (best). Which cut do you expect to have the highest median price? Write your guess, then run the next cell. CUTS = [ "Fair" , "Good" , "Very Good" , "Premium" , "Ideal" ] by_cut = diamonds . groupby ( "cut" )[[ "price" , "carat" ]] . median () . loc [ CUTS ] by_cut . columns = [ "median price ($)" , "median carat" ] by_cut .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } median price ($) median carat cut Fair 3282.0 1.00 Good 3050.5 0.82 Very Good 2648.0 0.71 Premium 3185.0 0.86 Ideal 1810.0 0.54 Ideal diamonds have the lowest median price in the table above, and also the smallest median carat (weight). Carat drives price far more than cut, and Ideal stones tend to be small. Carat is a confounder : it is related to both the group (cut) and the outcome (price). The fair comparison holds carat roughly fixed: compare cuts within carat bands. diamonds [ "carat band" ] = pd . cut ( diamonds [ "carat" ], [ 0 , 0.5 , 1.0 , 1.5 , 2.0 , 6.0 ], labels = [ "up to 0.5" , "0.5-1.0" , "1.0-1.5" , "1.5-2.0" , "over 2.0" ]) within = diamonds . pivot_table ( values = "price" , index = "carat band" , columns = "cut" , aggfunc = "median" , observed = True )[ CUTS ] print ( "Median price (US dollars) by carat band and cut" ) within . round ( 0 ) Median price (US dollars) by carat band and cut .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } cut Fair Good Very Good Premium Ideal carat band up to 0.5 1002.0 685.0 684.0 827.0 825.0 0.5-1.0 2596.0 2817.0 2652.0 2579.0 2353.0 1.0-1.5 4544.0 5232.0 5839.0 5646.0 6460.0 1.5-2.0 8621.0 9791.0 11068.0 11034.0 11536.0 over 2.0 12617.0 14962.0 15680.0 15248.0 15990.0 Within the heavier bands in the output above, better cuts generally cost more, which is what a jeweller would expect. The overall table answered "what happened?" (descriptive). The within-band table starts to answer "why?" (diagnostic). Check your understanding A manager asks: "Which of our stores will run out of stock next week?" Which kind of analytics is this, and what would the prescriptive follow-up question be? Give the general rule from this example in one sentence, in words a manager would understand. Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 1): calling a forecast "prescriptive"; reporting the mean of a skewed measure as "typical"; reading a missing value as 0; claiming a cause from a comparison that has a confounder. Part 2 (CLO 2): Charts, KPIs and messages ¶ CLO 2 asks you to design and use visualisation and modelling tools to communicate for decisions. Task Chart Avoid Compare a measure across categories Bar chart, sorted, axis from zero Pie with many slices, 3-D bars Show change over time Line chart Bars for long series; uneven time gaps Show a distribution Histogram or box plot A single average with no spread Show a relationship between two measures Scatter plot (hexbin for very many points) Two lines on two different axes Track a KPI against a target KPI tile or bullet chart, with the target and period A number with no comparison Principle Meaning Position beats area and angle Readers judge positions on a common scale most accurately Bars start at zero Bars are read by length; a cut axis exaggerates differences Highlight one thing Grey for context, one colour for the point you are making Message title The title states the finding ("Saturday brings the most revenue"), not the chart type Units and period Every axis and KPI says what it measures, in which unit, over which period Worked example: a KPI computed the right way ¶ The tip rate is tips ÷ bill. For a group of bills there are two ways to average it: Ratio of sums: total tips ÷ total bills. This is what the restaurant actually earned per dollar billed. Mean of ratios: average of each bill's tip rate. Every bill counts equally, so small bills with generous tips push it up. DAYS = [ "Thur" , "Fri" , "Sat" , "Sun" ] per_bill_rate = 100 * tips [ "tip" ] / tips [ "total_bill" ] kpi = tips . groupby ( "day" ) . agg ( bills = ( "tip" , "size" ), tips_total = ( "tip" , "sum" ), bills_total = ( "total_bill" , "sum" )) . loc [ DAYS ] kpi [ "ratio of sums %" ] = 100 * kpi [ "tips_total" ] / kpi [ "bills_total" ] kpi [ "mean of ratios %" ] = per_bill_rate . groupby ( tips [ "day" ]) . mean () . loc [ DAYS ] kpi . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } bills tips_total bills_total ratio of sums % mean of ratios % day Thur 62 171.83 1096.33 15.67 16.13 Fri 19 51.96 325.88 15.94 16.99 Sat 87 260.40 1778.40 14.64 15.32 Sun 76 247.39 1627.16 15.20 16.69 The two columns in the output above differ on every day. Neither is "wrong", but they answer different questions, so a dashboard must say which one it shows. For "how much of our revenue goes to tips?", use the ratio of sums . In Tableau, SUM([Tip]) / SUM([Total Bill]) gives the ratio of sums at the level of the view. The chart below follows the rules in the table: sorted bars, an axis from zero, one highlight colour, and a message title computed from the data rather than typed by hand. revenue = tips . groupby ( "day" )[ "total_bill" ] . sum () . loc [ DAYS ] . sort_values () top_day = revenue . idxmax () colours = [ ORANGE if day == top_day else GREY for day in revenue . index ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.5 )) ax . barh ( revenue . index , revenue . values , color = colours ) ax . set_title ( f " { top_day } brought in the most revenue: { revenue . max () : ,.0f } dollars " f "( { 100 * revenue . max () / revenue . sum () : .0f } % of the total)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Total of bills (US dollars), all weeks in the data" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Day" ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , None ) plt . show () Check your understanding A colleague's chart compares two branches' sales with a vertical axis starting at 95,000. What two changes would you ask for? A dashboard tile says "Conversion 4.2%". What is missing for a manager to act on it? Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 2): a title that names the chart instead of the finding; no units or period; averaging percentages that have different denominators; a dashboard with many charts and no question. Part 3 (CLO 3): Data mining and text mining ¶ CLO 3 asks you to apply computational problem-solving to find relationships in structured data (tables of numbers and categories) and unstructured data (free text). Method Data What it gives you Watch out for Group comparison, pivot table Structured Differences between groups Confounders; small groups Correlation r Structured, two numeric measures Direction and strength of a straight-line relationship, from −1 to +1 Curves, outliers, causation Tokenising, stopwords, word frequency Unstructured The topics people mention most Domain words that every text contains Lexicon sentiment (VADER) Unstructured A compound score from −1 (very negative) to +1 (very positive) Sarcasm, domain words, mixed opinions Text feature in a model Both A number (for example a sentiment score) used as a predictor The score is only as good as the lexicon Worked example: correlation in the car data ¶ mpg is fuel economy in miles per US gallon, so higher is better . Six cars have no horsepower value; we leave them out of each pair rather than filling them with 0. cols = [ "mpg" , "weight" , "horsepower" , "displacement" , "acceleration" , "model_year" ] print ( "Correlation of each measure with mpg" ) print ( mpg [ cols ] . corr ()[ "mpg" ] . drop ( "mpg" ) . sort_values () . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) Correlation of each measure with mpg weight -0.83 displacement -0.80 horsepower -0.78 acceleration 0.42 model_year 0.58 fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) ax . scatter ( mpg [ "weight" ], mpg [ "mpg" ], s = 12 , alpha = 0.6 , color = BLUE ) r = mpg [ "weight" ] . corr ( mpg [ "mpg" ]) ax . set_title ( f "Heavier cars travel fewer miles per gallon (r = { r : .2f } )" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Weight (pounds)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Fuel economy (miles per gallon)" ) plt . show () Weight, horsepower and displacement all correlate strongly and negatively with mpg in the output above, and they also correlate strongly with each other (heavy cars have big engines). That matters in Part 4: in a regression, predictors that move together share the credit, so their individual coefficients are less stable. Worked example: VADER sentiment rules ¶ VADER looks up each word in a lexicon of rated words and then applies rules for negation ("not"), intensifiers ("very"), "but" (the second half counts more), capital letters and exclamation marks. Predict, then reveal Rank the five sentences below from most negative to most positive before you run the cell. analyser = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () sentences = [ "The delivery was good." , "The delivery was very good!" , "The delivery was not good." , "The delivery was good, but the driver was rude." , "The delivery arrived on Tuesday." , ] scores = pd . DataFrame ({ "sentence" : sentences , "compound" : [ analyser . polarity_scores ( s )[ "compound" ] for s in sentences ]}) pd . set_option ( "display.max_colwidth" , 60 ) scores . sort_values ( "compound" ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sentence compound 3 The delivery was good, but the driver was rude. -0.4678 2 The delivery was not good. -0.3412 4 The delivery arrived on Tuesday. 0.0000 0 The delivery was good. 0.4404 1 The delivery was very good! 0.5400 In the output above, negation flips the score, the intensifier and "!" raise it, "but" lets the complaint dominate, and a neutral fact scores 0. VADER cannot read context: "the battery died" or "it's sick" may be scored wrongly, so always read a sample of texts next to their scores before you trust an average. Check your understanding Two measures have r = 0.05. Can you conclude they are unrelated? What should you do first? In Assignment 2 a sentiment score became a predictor of house price. Name one reason the score might mislead the model. Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 3): "correlation proves cause"; keeping words like the product name, which appear in every review; reporting an average sentiment without reading any of the texts. Part 4 (CLO 4): Forecasting, regression and simulation ¶ CLO 4 asks you to develop predictive models with three tools. All three answer "what is likely to happen?" and all three must be judged honestly. Tool Use when Judge it by Course work Time-series forecasting One measure over time; the future follows the past pattern Error on a later test period (MAE, RMSE, MAPE) against a baseline Lab 4 (CO₂), Lab 7 (Excel forecast sheet) Linear regression An outcome explained by several measures R², RMSE and MAE on test data; residuals Lab 5 (MPG), Assignment 2 Spreadsheet simulation Inputs are uncertain; you need the range of outcomes, not one number Distribution of the outcome: mean, percentiles, probability of a loss Lab 6, Assignment 3 4a. Forecasting: test on the future, beat a baseline ¶ We hide the last 24 months of CO₂, fit on the earlier months, and compare a seasonal naive baseline (same month last year) with Holt-Winters (level + trend + season). def errors ( actual , forecast ): e = np . asarray ( actual ) - np . asarray ( forecast ) return { "MAE" : np . mean ( np . abs ( e )), "RMSE" : np . sqrt ( np . mean ( e ** 2 )), "MAPE %" : 100 * np . mean ( np . abs ( e / np . asarray ( actual )))} H = 24 train , test = co2 . iloc [: - H ], co2 . iloc [ - H :] seasonal_naive = np . tile ( train . iloc [ - 12 :] . values , H // 12 ) hw = ExponentialSmoothing ( train , trend = "add" , seasonal = "add" , seasonal_periods = 12 , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit () hw_forecast = hw . forecast ( H ) print ( f "Train: { train . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { train . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } | test: { test . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { test . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } " ) pd . DataFrame ({ "seasonal naive" : errors ( test , seasonal_naive ), "Holt-Winters" : errors ( test , hw_forecast )}) . T . round ( 3 ) Train: Mar 1958 to Dec 1999 | test: Jan 2000 to Dec 2001 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE MAPE % seasonal naive 1.882 2.066 0.508 Holt-Winters 0.231 0.304 0.062 fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1997" :] . index , train [ "1997" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Actual (test)" ) ax . plot ( test . index , seasonal_naive , color = ORANGE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Seasonal naive" ) ax . plot ( test . index , hw_forecast , color = BLUE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Holt-Winters" ) ax . set_title ( "Holt-Winters follows the trend that the seasonal naive baseline misses" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () Idea Remember MAE Average size of the miss, in the data's units RMSE Like MAE but punishes big misses more; always at least as large as MAE MAPE Average miss as a % of the actual; misleading when actual values are near zero Baseline A model is only useful if it beats a simple baseline on the test period Never shuffle The test period must come after the training period Forecast interval The range widens with the horizon because uncertainty adds up Stationarity (ARIMA) ARIMA needs a stable mean; differencing removes a trend; ADF p ≤ 0.05 suggests stationary 4b. Regression: interpret coefficients, judge on test data ¶ We predict mpg from weight, horsepower and model year. Rows with no horsepower are dropped (6 cars). We hold back 20% of cars as a test set with a fixed random_state , so the split is the same each time. cars = mpg . dropna ( subset = [ "horsepower" ]) features = [ "weight" , "horsepower" , "model_year" ] X_train , X_test , y_train , y_test = train_test_split ( cars [ features ], cars [ "mpg" ], test_size = 0.2 , random_state = 42 ) model = LinearRegression () . fit ( X_train , y_train ) pred_train , pred_test = model . predict ( X_train ), model . predict ( X_test ) print ( f "Cars used: { len ( cars ) } | train: { len ( X_train ) } | test: { len ( X_test ) } " ) print ( f "Intercept: { model . intercept_ : .2f } " ) for name , coef in zip ( features , model . coef_ ): print ( f "Coefficient for { name : 11 } : { coef : +.4f } " ) print ( f " \n R² train: { r2_score ( y_train , pred_train ) : .3f } | R² test: { r2_score ( y_test , pred_test ) : .3f } " ) print ( f "Test MAE: { mean_absolute_error ( y_test , pred_test ) : .2f } mpg | " f "test RMSE: { np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( y_test , pred_test )) : .2f } mpg" ) Cars used: 392 | train: 313 | test: 79 Intercept: -13.99 Coefficient for weight : -0.0065 Coefficient for horsepower : -0.0088 Coefficient for model_year : +0.7594 R² train: 0.810 | R² test: 0.792 Test MAE: 2.51 mpg | test RMSE: 3.26 mpg How to read the output above, in words a manager understands: Coefficient of weight: holding horsepower and model year fixed, each extra pound of weight goes with a change in mpg equal to the coefficient. That is tiny per pound, so say it per 1,000 pounds (multiply by 1,000). Coefficient of model year: cars one model year newer, at the same weight and horsepower, travel this many more miles per gallon on average. R² on test data: the share of the variation in mpg, among cars the model never saw, that the model explains. A test R² close to the training R² means the model generalises ; a much lower test R² signals overfitting . Test RMSE and MAE: a typical prediction misses by about this many mpg. Coefficients describe association in this data , not what would happen if an engineer changed one feature. A residual plot (actual minus predicted against predicted) should look like a shapeless cloud around zero. A curve means the straight-line model misses a pattern. residuals = y_test - pred_test fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) ax . scatter ( pred_test , residuals , s = 18 , color = BLUE , alpha = 0.7 ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = INK , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_title ( "Test residuals: a slight curve, and larger misses for efficient cars" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Predicted fuel economy (mpg)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Actual minus predicted (mpg)" ) plt . show () The plot above is not a perfect cloud: the misses are larger for the most fuel-efficient cars, and the middle of the range is slightly over-predicted. A straight line is a good first model here, not a perfect one. Say so in a report, together with the test error. 4c. Simulation: the range of outcomes, not one number ¶ Excel simulation on Days 5–6 used random inputs to see how uncertain inputs produce uncertain profit. The same idea in Python makes the steps explicit. A synthetic example: a pop-up shop sells a product for 40 currency units. Monthly demand is uncertain (normal, mean 3,000, standard deviation 600 units). The unit cost is somewhere between 22 and 28 (uniform). Fixed costs are 30,000 a month. Excel Python here Meaning =RAND() rng.uniform(0, 1) A random number between 0 and 1 =NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd) rng.normal(mean, sd) A random draw from a normal distribution =RANDBETWEEN(a, b) rng.integers(a, b + 1) A random whole number from a to b Fill down 10,000 rows size=10_000 Many trials Paste values / a fixed seed np.random.default_rng(7) Freeze the random numbers so results can be checked Data Table (what-if) A loop over input values Outcome for each scenario rng = np . random . default_rng ( 7 ) TRIALS = 10_000 demand = np . clip ( rng . normal ( 3000 , 600 , TRIALS ), 0 , None ) . round () unit_cost = rng . uniform ( 22 , 28 , TRIALS ) profit = demand * ( 40 - unit_cost ) - 30_000 summary = pd . Series ({ "mean profit" : profit . mean (), "5th percentile" : np . percentile ( profit , 5 ), "median" : np . median ( profit ), "95th percentile" : np . percentile ( profit , 95 ), "probability of a loss (%)" : 100 * ( profit < 0 ) . mean (), }) print ( summary . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) mean profit 14814.0 5th percentile -1287.4 median 14353.9 95th percentile 32520.4 probability of a loss (%) 6.6 fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . hist ( profit / 1000 , bins = 50 , color = BLUE , alpha = 0.85 ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 ) ax . set_title ( f "About { 100 * ( profit < 0 ) . mean () : .0f } % of simulated months make a loss (left of the orange line)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Monthly profit (thousand currency units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of simulated months" ) plt . show () The mean in the output above looks healthy, but the risk is in the left tail. A manager should hear both: "we expect about the mean, but there is roughly this percentage chance of a loss, and in a bad month (5th percentile) we lose about this much". That sentence is the bridge from predictive to prescriptive . Check your understanding Why must the CO₂ test period come after the training period, but the car test set can be a random 20%? The simulation's mean profit doubles if fixed costs fall. Does the probability of a loss necessarily fall to zero? Why not? Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 4): judging a model on its training data; quoting R² with no error in units; "each extra pound causes …"; reporting only the mean of a simulation; forgetting to freeze random numbers before charting them. Part 5 (CLO 5): BI strategy, case evaluation and ethics ¶ CLO 5 asks you to evaluate the impact of BI tools within a case and write a managerial report that considers ethical and societal contexts. Element of a BI strategy Questions to ask Business goals Which decisions will the BI tools improve, and how will we measure the improvement? People Who uses the dashboards? What skills and training do they need? Who owns each KPI? Process How do insights reach decisions (meetings, alerts, approvals)? Data and governance Single source of truth, definitions, data quality checks, access rights, privacy Technology Which tools (Python, Excel, Tableau) for which job, and how they connect Value and adoption Is the dashboard used? Did the decision or the KPI improve? Ethical and societal issue Example from the course Mitigation Privacy and consent Reviews, customer or employee records Collect the minimum, anonymise, state the purpose Bias and fairness A model trained on past decisions repeats their bias Check results by group; involve the people affected Transparency A score nobody can explain Document the method and its limits Supply chain and environment Cheaper supplier with labour or emission violations Price the risk; include brand, regulation and social cost Honest communication Cut axes, selective time windows Show the full picture and the uncertainty Worked example: pricing an ethical choice ¶ A synthetic case. A product sells 20,000 units a year. A standard supplier leaves a margin of 50 currency units per unit; a certified supplier with fair labour and lower emissions leaves 44. Fixed costs are 600,000 a year. How large is the profit gap, and how much extra demand would the certified option need to break even with the standard one? units , fixed = 20_000 , 600_000 margin_standard , margin_certified = 50 , 44 profit_standard = units * margin_standard - fixed profit_certified = units * margin_certified - fixed gap = profit_standard - profit_certified # Demand at which the certified option earns the same profit as the standard option break_even_units = ( profit_standard + fixed ) / margin_certified print ( f "Profit, standard supplier: { profit_standard : >10,.0f } " ) print ( f "Profit, certified supplier: { profit_certified : >10,.0f } " ) print ( f "Gap: { gap : ,.0f } ( { 100 * gap / profit_standard : .1f } % of the standard profit)" ) print ( f "Certified option breaks even with standard at { break_even_units : ,.0f } units " f "(+ { 100 * ( break_even_units / units - 1 ) : .1f } % demand)" ) Profit, standard supplier: 400,000 Profit, certified supplier: 280,000 Gap: 120,000 (30.0% of the standard profit) Certified option breaks even with standard at 22,727 units (+13.6% demand) A small cut in the margin becomes a large cut in profit when fixed costs are high (operating leverage). The break-even line turns an ethical debate into a testable question for the board: "Is it plausible that the certified option wins this much extra demand, or protects us from losses of this size (fines, boycotts, lost contracts)?" The answer still needs judgement, but now it is an informed judgement. A managerial report in five moves ¶ Bottom line first: the recommendation in one sentence. Evidence: two or three numbers that support it, with units and the period. Trade-offs: what is given up (money, risk, ethics, time) and why it is worth it. Limits: what the data cannot show; key assumptions. Next steps: what to monitor, and the KPI that will show whether the decision worked. Check your understanding A company has many dashboards but decisions have not changed. Which element of a BI strategy would you examine first, and why? Name one stakeholder outside the company who is affected by the supplier choice above, and how. Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 5): a recommendation with no numbers; ethics mentioned in one sentence at the end instead of weighed against the money; no limits or next steps; "the data proves" instead of "the data suggests". Part 6: Practice set ¶ Answer on paper first, then check with the person next to you. These questions are practice : they are in the style of the exam, but the exam questions are different. Answers are discussed at the end of the review. P1 (CLO 1). Label each question as descriptive, diagnostic, predictive or prescriptive: (a) How many tablets did we return last quarter? (b) How many staff should we roster each evening next week to keep waiting times under 10 minutes? (c) Why did returns rise in March? (d) How many tablets will we sell in December? P2 (CLO 1). From the confounding example in Part 1, explain to a jewellery buyer, in two sentences, why the table "median price by cut" alone would lead to a wrong conclusion. P3 (CLO 2). Choose a chart for each task and name one design rule for it: (a) monthly revenue for the last three years; (b) the spread of delivery times for four couriers; (c) the relationship between advertising spend and sales for 200 stores. P4 (CLO 2). A shop had 30 sales from 600 visits on Monday and 90 sales from 1,200 visits on Saturday. Compute the overall conversion rate correctly, and the (incorrect) average of the two daily rates. P5 (CLO 3). VADER scores "The app is not bad at all" as positive. Explain why, and give one example of a review VADER would probably score wrongly. P6 (CLO 3). Using the correlation output in Part 3, which single measure has the strongest relationship with mpg? Does this mean reducing a car's weight will raise its mpg by a predictable amount? Explain. P7 (CLO 4). A shop forecast weekly sales of 100, 120, 110 and 90 units; actual sales were 110, 115, 100 and 95. Compute the MAE and the RMSE (show the errors). Which is larger, and why must it be? P8 (CLO 4). Using the regression output in Part 4, (a) state the effect of 1,000 extra pounds of weight on predicted mpg, holding the other two measures fixed; (b) compare the training and test R² and say what the comparison tells you. P9 (CLO 4). Using the simulation output in Part 4, write one sentence for a manager that gives the expected monthly profit and the risk of a loss. Then say why a fixed seed (or Paste Values in Excel) matters before you chart the results. P10 (CLO 4). Why does a forecast interval get wider for months further in the future? P11 (CLO 5). A hospital wants to use a BI dashboard that flags nurses whose overtime is "too high". Name two ethical risks and one safeguard for each. P12 (CLO 5). Using the worked example in Part 5, write the bottom-line sentence of a recommendation for the certified supplier, with two numbers from the output. Part 7: The final exam and this afternoon ¶ The final exam (20% of the course grade, CLO 1–5) When: today, periods 3–4, straight after this review. Length: 90 minutes, 100 marks, all five learning outcomes, including forecasting, regression, simulation, and BI and ethics. Format: multiple-choice questions, short written answers, and a data-interpretation section in which you read printed Python output; no computer is needed. Closed book. Bring a pen and a basic calculator . No notes, laptops, phones or internet. How to score well: quote the numbers you use, with units; say "is associated with", not "causes"; judge models on test data; give recommendations with their trade-offs. This afternoon (lab, 13:45–17:20): the launch of Assignment 4, the capstone (25%, due Sunday 29 November, 23:59 China Standard Time ), followed by a studio session with feedback checkpoints. Support for Assignments 2 and 3 (due Sunday 22 November) is available in the same session. All deadlines are on the schedule .

It also points NLTK at the bundled VADER lexicon, so nothing is downloaded. import warnings from pathlib import Path import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import nltk import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from nltk.sentiment.vader import SentimentIntensityAnalyzer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , mean_squared_error , r2_score from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing warnings . filterwarnings ( "ignore" , category = FutureWarning ) # NLTK reads the VADER lexicon straight from the bundled zip file nltk . data . path . insert ( 0 , str ( Path ( "data/nltk_data" ) . resolve ())) BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" # context INK = "#55534e" # notes and labels plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 9 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) diamonds = pd . read_csv ( "data/diamonds.csv" ) tips = pd . read_csv ( "data/tips.csv" ) mpg = pd . read_csv ( "data/mpg.csv" ) co2 = sm . datasets . co2 . load_pandas () . data [ "co2" ] . resample ( "ME" ) . mean () . ffill () for name , frame in [( "diamonds" , diamonds ), ( "tips" , tips ), ( "mpg" , mpg )]: print ( f " { name : 9 } { frame . shape [ 0 ] : >6 } rows x { frame . shape [ 1 ] } columns" ) print ( f "co2 { len ( co2 ) : >6 } months, { co2 . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { co2 . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } " ) diamonds 53940 rows x 10 columns tips 244 rows x 7 columns mpg 398 rows x 9 columns co2 526 months, Mar 1958 to Dec 2001
