docs.text: CLO 1 asks you to describe the principles of descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics and use them on a business problem. Every analysis in this course started from a decision. Kind Question it answers Course example Typical output Descriptive What happened? Revenue by day in the tips data Tables, KPIs, charts, dashboards Diagnostic Why did it happen? Why "Ideal" diamonds look cheap (Part 1 below) Comparisons within groups, drill-down Predictive What is likely to happen? Forecast of CO₂; MPG from car specifications A forecast or prediction with its error Prescriptive What should we do? Choose a supplier or a marketing strategy from a simulation A recommended action and its trade-offs The four build on each other: you cannot recommend an action (prescriptive) without a sound prediction, and you cannot predict well without first describing and checking the data.
docs.title: Part 1 (CLO 1): Kinds of analytics, describing data, confounding

docs.text: Frame the decision and the question (who decides what, by when, using which measure). Get and check the data: grain (what one row is), size, types, missing values, impossible values. Describe it: centre, spread, shape, groups. Diagnose and model : relationships, comparisons within groups, predictions. Validate : test on unseen data, reconcile totals, look for confounders. Communicate and act : one message, the evidence, the recommendation, its limits.
docs.title: The analytics workflow

docs.text: A distribution with a long right tail (a few very large values) pulls the mean above the median . Prices, incomes and bill sizes usually look like this. print ( diamonds [ "price" ] . describe () . round ( 0 ) . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Mean minus median: { diamonds [ 'price' ] . mean () - diamonds [ 'price' ] . median () : ,.0f } US dollars" ) count 53940.0 mean 3933.0 std 3989.0 min 326.0 25% 950.0 50% 2401.0 75% 5324.0 max 18823.0 Mean minus median: 1,532 US dollars In the output above the mean is far above the median, so the "typical" diamond costs about the median . The middle half of the diamonds lies between the 25% and 75% values (the interquartile range ).
docs.title: Worked example: mean or median?

docs.text: Predict, then reveal Diamond cut runs from Fair (worst) to Ideal (best). Which cut do you expect to have the highest median price? Write your guess, then run the next cell. CUTS = [ "Fair" , "Good" , "Very Good" , "Premium" , "Ideal" ] by_cut = diamonds . groupby ( "cut" )[[ "price" , "carat" ]] . median () . loc [ CUTS ] by_cut . columns = [ "median price ($)" , "median carat" ] by_cut .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } median price ($) median carat cut Fair 3282.0 1.00 Good 3050.5 0.82 Very Good 2648.0 0.71 Premium 3185.0 0.86 Ideal 1810.0 0.54 Ideal diamonds have the lowest median price in the table above, and also the smallest median carat (weight). Carat drives price far more than cut, and Ideal stones tend to be small. Carat is a confounder : it is related to both the group (cut) and the outcome (price). The fair comparison holds carat roughly fixed: compare cuts within carat bands. diamonds [ "carat band" ] = pd . cut ( diamonds [ "carat" ], [ 0 , 0.5 , 1.0 , 1.5 , 2.0 , 6.0 ], labels = [ "up to 0.5" , "0.5-1.0" , "1.0-1.5" , "1.5-2.0" , "over 2.0" ]) within = diamonds . pivot_table ( values = "price" , index = "carat band" , columns = "cut" , aggfunc = "median" , observed = True )[ CUTS ] print ( "Median price (US dollars) by carat band and cut" ) within . round ( 0 ) Median price (US dollars) by carat band and cut .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } cut Fair Good Very Good Premium Ideal carat band up to 0.5 1002.0 685.0 684.0 827.0 825.0 0.5-1.0 2596.0 2817.0 2652.0 2579.0 2353.0 1.0-1.5 4544.0 5232.0 5839.0 5646.0 6460.0 1.5-2.0 8621.0 9791.0 11068.0 11034.0 11536.0 over 2.0 12617.0 14962.0 15680.0 15248.0 15990.0 Within the heavier bands in the output above, better cuts generally cost more, which is what a jeweller would expect. The overall table answered "what happened?" (descriptive). The within-band table starts to answer "why?" (diagnostic). Check your understanding A manager asks: "Which of our stores will run out of stock next week?" Which kind of analytics is this, and what would the prescriptive follow-up question be? Give the general rule from this example in one sentence, in words a manager would understand. Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 1): calling a forecast "prescriptive"; reporting the mean of a skewed measure as "typical"; reading a missing value as 0; claiming a cause from a comparison that has a confounder.
docs.title: Worked example: a confounder

docs.text: CLO 2 asks you to design and use visualisation and modelling tools to communicate for decisions. Task Chart Avoid Compare a measure across categories Bar chart, sorted, axis from zero Pie with many slices, 3-D bars Show change over time Line chart Bars for long series; uneven time gaps Show a distribution Histogram or box plot A single average with no spread Show a relationship between two measures Scatter plot (hexbin for very many points) Two lines on two different axes Track a KPI against a target KPI tile or bullet chart, with the target and period A number with no comparison Principle Meaning Position beats area and angle Readers judge positions on a common scale most accurately Bars start at zero Bars are read by length; a cut axis exaggerates differences Highlight one thing Grey for context, one colour for the point you are making Message title The title states the finding ("Saturday brings the most revenue"), not the chart type Units and period Every axis and KPI says what it measures, in which unit, over which period
docs.title: Part 2 (CLO 2): Charts, KPIs and messages

docs.text: The tip rate is tips ÷ bill. For a group of bills there are two ways to average it: Ratio of sums: total tips ÷ total bills. This is what the restaurant actually earned per dollar billed. Mean of ratios: average of each bill's tip rate. Every bill counts equally, so small bills with generous tips push it up. DAYS = [ "Thur" , "Fri" , "Sat" , "Sun" ] per_bill_rate = 100 * tips [ "tip" ] / tips [ "total_bill" ] kpi = tips . groupby ( "day" ) . agg ( bills = ( "tip" , "size" ), tips_total = ( "tip" , "sum" ), bills_total = ( "total_bill" , "sum" )) . loc [ DAYS ] kpi [ "ratio of sums %" ] = 100 * kpi [ "tips_total" ] / kpi [ "bills_total" ] kpi [ "mean of ratios %" ] = per_bill_rate . groupby ( tips [ "day" ]) . mean () . loc [ DAYS ] kpi . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } bills tips_total bills_total ratio of sums % mean of ratios % day Thur 62 171.83 1096.33 15.67 16.13 Fri 19 51.96 325.88 15.94 16.99 Sat 87 260.40 1778.40 14.64 15.32 Sun 76 247.39 1627.16 15.20 16.69 The two columns in the output above differ on every day. Neither is "wrong", but they answer different questions, so a dashboard must say which one it shows. For "how much of our revenue goes to tips?", use the ratio of sums . In Tableau, SUM([Tip]) / SUM([Total Bill]) gives the ratio of sums at the level of the view. The chart below follows the rules in the table: sorted bars, an axis from zero, one highlight colour, and a message title computed from the data rather than typed by hand. revenue = tips . groupby ( "day" )[ "total_bill" ] . sum () . loc [ DAYS ] . sort_values () top_day = revenue . idxmax () colours = [ ORANGE if day == top_day else GREY for day in revenue . index ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.5 )) ax . barh ( revenue . index , revenue . values , color = colours ) ax . set_title ( f " { top_day } brought in the most revenue: { revenue . max () : ,.0f } dollars " f "( { 100 * revenue . max () / revenue . sum () : .0f } % of the total)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Total of bills (US dollars), all weeks in the data" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Day" ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , None ) plt . show () Check your understanding A colleague's chart compares two branches' sales with a vertical axis starting at 95,000. What two changes would you ask for? A dashboard tile says "Conversion 4.2%". What is missing for a manager to act on it? Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 2): a title that names the chart instead of the finding; no units or period; averaging percentages that have different denominators; a dashboard with many charts and no question.
docs.title: Worked example: a KPI computed the right way

docs.text: CLO 3 asks you to apply computational problem-solving to find relationships in structured data (tables of numbers and categories) and unstructured data (free text). Method Data What it gives you Watch out for Group comparison, pivot table Structured Differences between groups Confounders; small groups Correlation r Structured, two numeric measures Direction and strength of a straight-line relationship, from −1 to +1 Curves, outliers, causation Tokenising, stopwords, word frequency Unstructured The topics people mention most Domain words that every text contains Lexicon sentiment (VADER) Unstructured A compound score from −1 (very negative) to +1 (very positive) Sarcasm, domain words, mixed opinions Text feature in a model Both A number (for example a sentiment score) used as a predictor The score is only as good as the lexicon
docs.title: Part 3 (CLO 3): Data mining and text mining

docs.text: mpg is fuel economy in miles per US gallon, so higher is better . Six cars have no horsepower value; we leave them out of each pair rather than filling them with 0. cols = [ "mpg" , "weight" , "horsepower" , "displacement" , "acceleration" , "model_year" ] print ( "Correlation of each measure with mpg" ) print ( mpg [ cols ] . corr ()[ "mpg" ] . drop ( "mpg" ) . sort_values () . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) Correlation of each measure with mpg weight -0.83 displacement -0.80 horsepower -0.78 acceleration 0.42 model_year 0.58 fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) ax . scatter ( mpg [ "weight" ], mpg [ "mpg" ], s = 12 , alpha = 0.6 , color = BLUE ) r = mpg [ "weight" ] . corr ( mpg [ "mpg" ]) ax . set_title ( f "Heavier cars travel fewer miles per gallon (r = { r : .2f } )" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Weight (pounds)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Fuel economy (miles per gallon)" ) plt . show () Weight, horsepower and displacement all correlate strongly and negatively with mpg in the output above, and they also correlate strongly with each other (heavy cars have big engines). That matters in Part 4: in a regression, predictors that move together share the credit, so their individual coefficients are less stable.
docs.title: Worked example: correlation in the car data

docs.text: VADER looks up each word in a lexicon of rated words and then applies rules for negation ("not"), intensifiers ("very"), "but" (the second half counts more), capital letters and exclamation marks. Predict, then reveal Rank the five sentences below from most negative to most positive before you run the cell. analyser = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () sentences = [ "The delivery was good." , "The delivery was very good!" , "The delivery was not good." , "The delivery was good, but the driver was rude." , "The delivery arrived on Tuesday." , ] scores = pd . DataFrame ({ "sentence" : sentences , "compound" : [ analyser . polarity_scores ( s )[ "compound" ] for s in sentences ]}) pd . set_option ( "display.max_colwidth" , 60 ) scores . sort_values ( "compound" ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sentence compound 3 The delivery was good, but the driver was rude. -0.4678 2 The delivery was not good. -0.3412 4 The delivery arrived on Tuesday. 0.0000 0 The delivery was good. 0.4404 1 The delivery was very good! 0.5400 In the output above, negation flips the score, the intensifier and "!" raise it, "but" lets the complaint dominate, and a neutral fact scores 0. VADER cannot read context: "the battery died" or "it's sick" may be scored wrongly, so always read a sample of texts next to their scores before you trust an average. Check your understanding Two measures have r = 0.05. Can you conclude they are unrelated? What should you do first? In Assignment 2 a sentiment score became a predictor of house price. Name one reason the score might mislead the model. Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 3): "correlation proves cause"; keeping words like the product name, which appear in every review; reporting an average sentiment without reading any of the texts.
docs.title: Worked example: VADER sentiment rules

docs.text: CLO 4 asks you to develop predictive models with three tools. All three answer "what is likely to happen?" and all three must be judged honestly. Tool Use when Judge it by Course work Time-series forecasting One measure over time; the future follows the past pattern Error on a later test period (MAE, RMSE, MAPE) against a baseline Lab 4 (CO₂), Lab 7 (Excel forecast sheet) Linear regression An outcome explained by several measures R², RMSE and MAE on test data; residuals Lab 5 (MPG), Assignment 2 Spreadsheet simulation Inputs are uncertain; you need the range of outcomes, not one number Distribution of the outcome: mean, percentiles, probability of a loss Lab 6, Assignment 3
docs.title: Part 4 (CLO 4): Forecasting, regression and simulation

docs.text: We hide the last 24 months of CO₂, fit on the earlier months, and compare a seasonal naive baseline (same month last year) with Holt-Winters (level + trend + season). def errors ( actual , forecast ): e = np . asarray ( actual ) - np . asarray ( forecast ) return { "MAE" : np . mean ( np . abs ( e )), "RMSE" : np . sqrt ( np . mean ( e ** 2 )), "MAPE %" : 100 * np . mean ( np . abs ( e / np . asarray ( actual )))} H = 24 train , test = co2 . iloc [: - H ], co2 . iloc [ - H :] seasonal_naive = np . tile ( train . iloc [ - 12 :] . values , H // 12 ) hw = ExponentialSmoothing ( train , trend = "add" , seasonal = "add" , seasonal_periods = 12 , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit () hw_forecast = hw . forecast ( H ) print ( f "Train: { train . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { train . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } | test: { test . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { test . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } " ) pd . DataFrame ({ "seasonal naive" : errors ( test , seasonal_naive ), "Holt-Winters" : errors ( test , hw_forecast )}) . T . round ( 3 ) Train: Mar 1958 to Dec 1999 | test: Jan 2000 to Dec 2001 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE MAPE % seasonal naive 1.882 2.066 0.508 Holt-Winters 0.231 0.304 0.062 fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1997" :] . index , train [ "1997" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Actual (test)" ) ax . plot ( test . index , seasonal_naive , color = ORANGE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Seasonal naive" ) ax . plot ( test . index , hw_forecast , color = BLUE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Holt-Winters" ) ax . set_title ( "Holt-Winters follows the trend that the seasonal naive baseline misses" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () Idea Remember MAE Average size of the miss, in the data's units RMSE Like MAE but punishes big misses more; always at least as large as MAE MAPE Average miss as a % of the actual; misleading when actual values are near zero Baseline A model is only useful if it beats a simple baseline on the test period Never shuffle The test period must come after the training period Forecast interval The range widens with the horizon because uncertainty adds up Stationarity (ARIMA) ARIMA needs a stable mean; differencing removes a trend; ADF p ≤ 0.05 suggests stationary
docs.title: 4a. Forecasting: test on the future, beat a baseline

docs.text: We predict mpg from weight, horsepower and model year. Rows with no horsepower are dropped (6 cars). We hold back 20% of cars as a test set with a fixed random_state , so the split is the same each time. cars = mpg . dropna ( subset = [ "horsepower" ]) features = [ "weight" , "horsepower" , "model_year" ] X_train , X_test , y_train , y_test = train_test_split ( cars [ features ], cars [ "mpg" ], test_size = 0.2 , random_state = 42 ) model = LinearRegression () . fit ( X_train , y_train ) pred_train , pred_test = model . predict ( X_train ), model . predict ( X_test ) print ( f "Cars used: { len ( cars ) } | train: { len ( X_train ) } | test: { len ( X_test ) } " ) print ( f "Intercept: { model . intercept_ : .2f } " ) for name , coef in zip ( features , model . coef_ ): print ( f "Coefficient for { name : 11 } : { coef : +.4f } " ) print ( f " \n R² train: { r2_score ( y_train , pred_train ) : .3f } | R² test: { r2_score ( y_test , pred_test ) : .3f } " ) print ( f "Test MAE: { mean_absolute_error ( y_test , pred_test ) : .2f } mpg | " f "test RMSE: { np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( y_test , pred_test )) : .2f } mpg" ) Cars used: 392 | train: 313 | test: 79 Intercept: -13.99 Coefficient for weight : -0.0065 Coefficient for horsepower : -0.0088 Coefficient for model_year : +0.7594 R² train: 0.810 | R² test: 0.792 Test MAE: 2.51 mpg | test RMSE: 3.26 mpg How to read the output above, in words a manager understands: Coefficient of weight: holding horsepower and model year fixed, each extra pound of weight goes with a change in mpg equal to the coefficient. That is tiny per pound, so say it per 1,000 pounds (multiply by 1,000). Coefficient of model year: cars one model year newer, at the same weight and horsepower, travel this many more miles per gallon on average. R² on test data: the share of the variation in mpg, among cars the model never saw, that the model explains. A test R² close to the training R² means the model generalises ; a much lower test R² signals overfitting . Test RMSE and MAE: a typical prediction misses by about this many mpg. Coefficients describe association in this data , not what would happen if an engineer changed one feature. A residual plot (actual minus predicted against predicted) should look like a shapeless cloud around zero. A curve means the straight-line model misses a pattern. residuals = y_test - pred_test fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) ax . scatter ( pred_test , residuals , s = 18 , color = BLUE , alpha = 0.7 ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = INK , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_title ( "Test residuals: a slight curve, and larger misses for efficient cars" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Predicted fuel economy (mpg)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Actual minus predicted (mpg)" ) plt . show () The plot above is not a perfect cloud: the misses are larger for the most fuel-efficient cars, and the middle of the range is slightly over-predicted. A straight line is a good first model here, not a perfect one. Say so in a report, together with the test error.
docs.title: 4b. Regression: interpret coefficients, judge on test data

docs.text: Excel simulation on Days 5–6 used random inputs to see how uncertain inputs produce uncertain profit. The same idea in Python makes the steps explicit. A synthetic example: a pop-up shop sells a product for 40 currency units. Monthly demand is uncertain (normal, mean 3,000, standard deviation 600 units). The unit cost is somewhere between 22 and 28 (uniform). Fixed costs are 30,000 a month. Excel Python here Meaning =RAND() rng.uniform(0, 1) A random number between 0 and 1 =NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd) rng.normal(mean, sd) A random draw from a normal distribution =RANDBETWEEN(a, b) rng.integers(a, b + 1) A random whole number from a to b Fill down 10,000 rows size=10_000 Many trials Paste values / a fixed seed np.random.default_rng(7) Freeze the random numbers so results can be checked Data Table (what-if) A loop over input values Outcome for each scenario rng = np . random . default_rng ( 7 ) TRIALS = 10_000 demand = np . clip ( rng . normal ( 3000 , 600 , TRIALS ), 0 , None ) . round () unit_cost = rng . uniform ( 22 , 28 , TRIALS ) profit = demand * ( 40 - unit_cost ) - 30_000 summary = pd . Series ({ "mean profit" : profit . mean (), "5th percentile" : np . percentile ( profit , 5 ), "median" : np . median ( profit ), "95th percentile" : np . percentile ( profit , 95 ), "probability of a loss (%)" : 100 * ( profit < 0 ) . mean (), }) print ( summary . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) mean profit 14814.0 5th percentile -1287.4 median 14353.9 95th percentile 32520.4 probability of a loss (%) 6.6 fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . hist ( profit / 1000 , bins = 50 , color = BLUE , alpha = 0.85 ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 ) ax . set_title ( f "About { 100 * ( profit < 0 ) . mean () : .0f } % of simulated months make a loss (left of the orange line)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Monthly profit (thousand currency units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of simulated months" ) plt . show () The mean in the output above looks healthy, but the risk is in the left tail. A manager should hear both: "we expect about the mean, but there is roughly this percentage chance of a loss, and in a bad month (5th percentile) we lose about this much". That sentence is the bridge from predictive to prescriptive . Check your understanding Why must the CO₂ test period come after the training period, but the car test set can be a random 20%? The simulation's mean profit doubles if fixed costs fall. Does the probability of a loss necessarily fall to zero? Why not? Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 4): judging a model on its training data; quoting R² with no error in units; "each extra pound causes …"; reporting only the mean of a simulation; forgetting to freeze random numbers before charting them.
docs.title: 4c. Simulation: the range of outcomes, not one number

docs.text: CLO 5 asks you to evaluate the impact of BI tools within a case and write a managerial report that considers ethical and societal contexts. Element of a BI strategy Questions to ask Business goals Which decisions will the BI tools improve, and how will we measure the improvement? People Who uses the dashboards? What skills and training do they need? Who owns each KPI? Process How do insights reach decisions (meetings, alerts, approvals)? Data and governance Single source of truth, definitions, data quality checks, access rights, privacy Technology Which tools (Python, Excel, Tableau) for which job, and how they connect Value and adoption Is the dashboard used? Did the decision or the KPI improve? Ethical and societal issue Example from the course Mitigation Privacy and consent Reviews, customer or employee records Collect the minimum, anonymise, state the purpose Bias and fairness A model trained on past decisions repeats their bias Check results by group; involve the people affected Transparency A score nobody can explain Document the method and its limits Supply chain and environment Cheaper supplier with labour or emission violations Price the risk; include brand, regulation and social cost Honest communication Cut axes, selective time windows Show the full picture and the uncertainty
docs.title: Part 5 (CLO 5): BI strategy, case evaluation and ethics

docs.text: A synthetic case. A product sells 20,000 units a year. A standard supplier leaves a margin of 50 currency units per unit; a certified supplier with fair labour and lower emissions leaves 44. Fixed costs are 600,000 a year. How large is the profit gap, and how much extra demand would the certified option need to break even with the standard one? units , fixed = 20_000 , 600_000 margin_standard , margin_certified = 50 , 44 profit_standard = units * margin_standard - fixed profit_certified = units * margin_certified - fixed gap = profit_standard - profit_certified # Demand at which the certified option earns the same profit as the standard option break_even_units = ( profit_standard + fixed ) / margin_certified print ( f "Profit, standard supplier: { profit_standard : >10,.0f } " ) print ( f "Profit, certified supplier: { profit_certified : >10,.0f } " ) print ( f "Gap: { gap : ,.0f } ( { 100 * gap / profit_standard : .1f } % of the standard profit)" ) print ( f "Certified option breaks even with standard at { break_even_units : ,.0f } units " f "(+ { 100 * ( break_even_units / units - 1 ) : .1f } % demand)" ) Profit, standard supplier: 400,000 Profit, certified supplier: 280,000 Gap: 120,000 (30.0% of the standard profit) Certified option breaks even with standard at 22,727 units (+13.6% demand) A small cut in the margin becomes a large cut in profit when fixed costs are high (operating leverage). The break-even line turns an ethical debate into a testable question for the board: "Is it plausible that the certified option wins this much extra demand, or protects us from losses of this size (fines, boycotts, lost contracts)?" The answer still needs judgement, but now it is an informed judgement.
docs.title: Worked example: pricing an ethical choice

docs.text: Bottom line first: the recommendation in one sentence. Evidence: two or three numbers that support it, with units and the period. Trade-offs: what is given up (money, risk, ethics, time) and why it is worth it. Limits: what the data cannot show; key assumptions. Next steps: what to monitor, and the KPI that will show whether the decision worked. Check your understanding A company has many dashboards but decisions have not changed. Which element of a BI strategy would you examine first, and why? Name one stakeholder outside the company who is affected by the supplier choice above, and how. Mistakes that cost marks (CLO 5): a recommendation with no numbers; ethics mentioned in one sentence at the end instead of weighed against the money; no limits or next steps; "the data proves" instead of "the data suggests".
docs.title: A managerial report in five moves

docs.text: Answer on paper first, then check with the person next to you. These questions are practice : they are in the style of the exam, but the exam questions are different. Answers are discussed at the end of the review. P1 (CLO 1). Label each question as descriptive, diagnostic, predictive or prescriptive: (a) How many tablets did we return last quarter? (b) How many staff should we roster each evening next week to keep waiting times under 10 minutes? (c) Why did returns rise in March? (d) How many tablets will we sell in December? P2 (CLO 1). From the confounding example in Part 1, explain to a jewellery buyer, in two sentences, why the table "median price by cut" alone would lead to a wrong conclusion. P3 (CLO 2). Choose a chart for each task and name one design rule for it: (a) monthly revenue for the last three years; (b) the spread of delivery times for four couriers; (c) the relationship between advertising spend and sales for 200 stores. P4 (CLO 2). A shop had 30 sales from 600 visits on Monday and 90 sales from 1,200 visits on Saturday. Compute the overall conversion rate correctly, and the (incorrect) average of the two daily rates. P5 (CLO 3). VADER scores "The app is not bad at all" as positive. Explain why, and give one example of a review VADER would probably score wrongly. P6 (CLO 3). Using the correlation output in Part 3, which single measure has the strongest relationship with mpg? Does this mean reducing a car's weight will raise its mpg by a predictable amount? Explain. P7 (CLO 4). A shop forecast weekly sales of 100, 120, 110 and 90 units; actual sales were 110, 115, 100 and 95. Compute the MAE and the RMSE (show the errors). Which is larger, and why must it be? P8 (CLO 4). Using the regression output in Part 4, (a) state the effect of 1,000 extra pounds of weight on predicted mpg, holding the other two measures fixed; (b) compare the training and test R² and say what the comparison tells you. P9 (CLO 4). Using the simulation output in Part 4, write one sentence for a manager that gives the expected monthly profit and the risk of a loss. Then say why a fixed seed (or Paste Values in Excel) matters before you chart the results. P10 (CLO 4). Why does a forecast interval get wider for months further in the future? P11 (CLO 5). A hospital wants to use a BI dashboard that flags nurses whose overtime is "too high". Name two ethical risks and one safeguard for each. P12 (CLO 5). Using the worked example in Part 5, write the bottom-line sentence of a recommendation for the certified supplier, with two numbers from the output.
docs.title: Part 6: Practice set

docs.text: The final exam (20% of the course grade, CLO 1–5) When: today, periods 3–4, straight after this review. Length: 90 minutes, 100 marks, all five learning outcomes, including forecasting, regression, simulation, and BI and ethics. Format: multiple-choice questions, short written answers, and a data-interpretation section in which you read printed Python output; no computer is needed. Closed book. Bring a pen and a basic calculator . No notes, laptops, phones or internet. How to score well: quote the numbers you use, with units; say "is associated with", not "causes"; judge models on test data; give recommendations with their trade-offs. This afternoon (lab, 13:45–17:20): the launch of Assignment 4, the capstone (25%, due Sunday 29 November, 23:59 China Standard Time ), followed by a studio session with feedback checkpoints. Support for Assignments 2 and 3 (due Sunday 22 November) is available in the same session. All deadlines are on the schedule .

docs.text: Setup ¶ Everything in this course runs on your own computer, without needing Google or GitHub. Set it up before the first day and check it with the setup notebook. What you need ¶ A laptop (Windows or macOS), or a classroom lab PC Anaconda , which gives you Python and Jupyter Tableau (for Lab 2 and the readiness check) Microsoft Excel (for Labs 6–7 and Assignment 3) The course folder of notebooks and data, provided by your facilitator 1. Install Anaconda ¶ Download the Anaconda Distribution installer for your computer and run it with the default options. Open Anaconda Navigator and launch JupyterLab . (Or open "Anaconda Prompt" / Terminal and type jupyter lab .) A browser tab opens with JupyterLab. This is where you run every notebook. Two extra packages Lab 3 needs wordcloud . Open Anaconda Prompt (Windows) or Terminal (macOS) and run: pip install wordcloud Your facilitator may provide an offline installer if the internet connection is slow. 2. Unzip the course folder ¶ Copy the course folder you receive (for example China_Classroom.zip ) to your Documents folder and unzip it. Inside you will find the notebooks and a data folder. Keep them together : the notebooks load data from that folder, so they work without internet. In JupyterLab, use the file browser on the left to open the folder. 3. Run the setup check ¶ Open the setup check notebook from the course folder and run all cells ( Run → Run All Cells ). It confirms that Python and every package the course needs are installed, and that the data files load. If any line says MISSING , show it to your facilitator. 4. Tableau ¶ Claim the free Tableau for Students licence with your university email, then download and activate Tableau Desktop. Open it and check that you can open the Sample – Superstore data source. 5. Excel ¶ Labs 6–7 and Assignment 3 use Microsoft Excel ( RAND() , NORM.INV() and Data Table ). It is installed on the lab PCs; if you use your own laptop, check that Excel opens before Day 5 (Tuesday 17 November). Running and submitting a notebook ¶ Open a notebook, then choose Run → Run All Cells , or run cells one by one with Shift + Enter . Save often with Ctrl + S (Windows) or Cmd + S (macOS). To submit, follow the instructions in each lab. Most labs ask you to export the notebook to PDF ( File → Print , then Save as PDF ) and upload it to the matching assignment on GAP (Moodle) . Combining PDFs without internet ¶ Several labs and assignments ask for one PDF made from two parts, for example your written answers and a dashboard or notebook. Online PDF tools are often blocked, so combine them on your own computer: Word (any computer): put everything in one Word document. Paste the dashboard or notebook output as pictures on new pages after your answers (in Tableau, Dashboard → Export Image ), then File → Save As → PDF . macOS Preview: open the first PDF, choose View → Thumbnails , drag the second PDF into the sidebar below the last page, then File → Export as PDF . Adobe Acrobat (if installed): Tools → Combine Files . Check that the final PDF has the parts in the order the lab asks for and the exact file name it gives. Only use course data Never use private company, customer or personal data in course work.

docs.text: Learning roadmap ¶ The course has sixteen Python sessions, followed by a Tableau section. Every session has two parts: a Lecture that teaches the theory with worked examples, and a Lab where you practise it yourself on real and synthetic data. This is the planned sequence Lecture and lab materials are released only after they have been checked. Sessions marked with a link already have draft material. How each session works ¶ Lecture. A short recap quiz, then the theory, explained with examples and questions where you predict the answer before seeing it. It ends with a worked case in code. Lab. Three levels of practice in a Colab notebook: Guided: step-by-step, everyone together. Independent: the same skill applied to a new question. Challenge: a harder problem or a deliberate mistake to debug. You keep the evidence from every lab in your portfolio. Part A: Thinking with data ¶ Session Lecture Lab 1. Why data analytics matters Why data analytics matters : the four levels of analytics, decision-driven questions, and why statistics alone can mislead Python, Colab and always plotting your data : recreate Anscombe's quartet and the Datasaurus 2. Data, grain and the DataFrame Data, grain and the DataFrame : types of data, tidy data, grain and keys, data dictionaries, data quality Can we trust the sales table? 3. Cleaning and preparing data Cleaning and preparing data : missing data, duplicates, outliers, dates, joins and their pitfalls, reshaping Clean World Cup and mobile-OS data; merge tables safely Part B: Describing and measuring ¶ Session Lecture Lab 4. Descriptive statistics and distributions Descriptive statistics and distributions : centre, spread, percentiles, skew, outliers, histograms and box plots Distributions of order value and shipping time; median vs mean house prices 5. Metrics and KPIs Metrics and KPIs : designing metrics, ratios of totals, weighted rates, Simpson's paradox Which segment deserves a closer look? ; the Berkeley admissions paradox 6. Visualisation principles Visualisation principles : choosing charts, perception, data-ink, Gestalt, colour and accessibility ( Designing clear visuals ) Redesign bad charts; one-, two- and many-variable views Part C: Relationships, change and uncertainty ¶ Session Lecture Lab 7. Time series and trends Time series and trends : trend and seasonality, month-on-month vs year-on-year, moving averages Trends, returns and a decision dashboard ; construction spending 8. Correlation and regression Correlation and regression : correlation, confounding, simple linear regression, residuals Discount vs profit; advertising spend vs revenue 9. Sampling, uncertainty and experiments Sampling, uncertainty and experiments : samples and populations, confidence intervals, A/B tests, practical vs statistical significance Simulate sampling; bootstrap a confidence interval; analyse an A/B test Part D: Business cases ¶ Session Lecture Lab 10. Finance Budget accountability : budget vs actual, variance, reconciliation Which spending needs review? 11. Operations Service performance : service levels, open shipments, delay distributions Are deliveries on time? 12. Marketing Campaign evaluation : funnels, weighted conversion, cost per acquisition, attribution limits Which campaigns deserve the budget? 13. HR Workforce analytics : headcount, turnover, recruitment, fairness and privacy Is workforce change creating a capacity problem? Part E: Communicating and bringing it together ¶ Session Lecture Lab 14. Dashboards and storytelling Dashboards and storytelling : audience, the big idea, dashboard design, the Challenger case From analysis to a decision dashboard 15. Capstone studio Combining evidence : evidence registers, no false joins, validation, trade-offs Build your capstone 16. Executive briefings Executive briefings : recommendation first, uncertainty, handling questions Brief, critique, revise Part F: Tableau ¶ Session Lecture Lab T1. Tableau fundamentals How Tableau thinks: dimensions, measures, aggregation Rebuild earlier views ( T1 lab ) T2. Calculations and KPIs Calculated fields, distinct counts, table calculations Rebuild the segment KPIs and growth measures T3. Dashboards in Tableau Layout, filters, actions, accessibility Rebuild your decision dashboard T4. Publishing and portfolio Tableau Public and privacy Your Tableau portfolio piece What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of the course you should be able to: Turn a business request into a clear question with a decision, population, period and measure. Load, inspect, clean and reshape data in Python, keeping a record of every change. Describe data with the right statistics and charts, and explain distributions, outliers and skew. Define metrics precisely and avoid the common traps. Measure relationships and change over time, and explain what correlation and regression can and cannot show. Express uncertainty with confidence intervals and simple experiments. Design clear charts and dashboards, and tell a decision-focused story. Apply all of this to retail, finance, operations, marketing and HR, and defend a recommendation to executives. Rebuild key analyses in Tableau. How you will be assessed ¶ Theory quizzes at the start of each lecture help you check your understanding. They are for feedback. Your lab portfolio collects your evidence from every session and covers all five business areas. You submit each lab on Moodle . Your capstone combines findings from at least three areas into a dashboard and an individual executive briefing, presented in Session 16. Everything is assessed for feedback , using the rubric shown in Session 16. It is not a graded exam. Feedback rewards correct reasoning, careful checking and honest statements of uncertainty, not only attractive charts. Extra practice topics ¶ Selected datasets from the Tableau sample-data catalog give you practice in sports, technology, government and more. Each keeps its own real dates, units and context.

docs.text: Setup and practice ¶ What you need before you start, how to run the lessons in Google Colab, how to stay safe with data, and how to keep a simple evidence log. What you need ¶ A laptop with a modern web browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari), brought to every class: all sessions are in person A Google account , to use Google Colab Your login for the course Moodle page, where you submit your work Before teaching starts Nothing needs to be installed for the Python lessons. Tell your facilitator before the first session if you need any accessibility support or cannot bring a laptop. Open a lesson in Google Colab ¶ Every Python lesson page has an Open in Colab button near the top. Click Open in Colab . The lesson notebook opens in Google Colab; sign in with your Google account if asked. Run the cells from top to bottom: click a cell and press Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive , so your changes are kept. The notebook opens with the facilitator's outputs already visible. Running it yourself replaces them with your own results. The first code cell in each lesson downloads the course data from Tableau's sample-data page and checks that it is exactly the version the lesson was written for. If it prints a warning, tell your facilitator. If something goes wrong Choose Runtime → Restart session and run all . This runs everything again from the top and fixes most problems. New to Python? Start with the Session 1 lab: Python, Colab and always plotting your data . Submit your work on Moodle ¶ Each session has a Moodle assignment for its lab, and there is one for the capstone. In Colab, finish the lab and run all cells so your outputs are visible. Choose File → Download → Download .ipynb . Open the matching assignment on the course Moodle page and upload the .ipynb file. If the lab asks for a written answer or an image (for example a dashboard), upload it to the same assignment. Name your files clearly Use SessionNN_lab_YourName.ipynb , for example Session05_lab_AnitaShrestha.ipynb . Keep your data safe ¶ Only use course data Use only the datasets supplied for this course. Never upload private employer, customer or employee files to Colab or any other online tool. Notebooks you save in Google Drive are private to you unless you choose to share them. Check the sharing setting before sending a link to anyone. If something does not work ¶ No internet or no Google account Follow the demonstration or pair with a classmate, and keep writing your metric and checking notes. Run the notebook yourself later, once access is back. Tableau (later) ¶ You do not need Tableau for the Python lessons. The Tableau sessions come after the Python sessions. When you reach them, you will install Tableau Desktop Public Edition from the official Tableau Public page ; the sessions explain what to set up. The labs need the Desktop edition because it saves .twbx files on your own computer, and Moodle needs those files. In the Tableau Public web editor, saving publishes the workbook and its data, so never use the web editor with Superstore. Anything you publish to Tableau Public is public Published workbooks and their data can be seen by anyone. Hiding an item on your profile does not make it private. Tableau Public also lets you save workbooks on your own computer, so publishing online is optional. Keep an evidence log ¶ For every task, write down a few short notes. They make your portfolio much easier to build. Record Example prompt Data release Which file and version did I use? Question What decision is this for? Grain What does one row represent? Date window and filters Which records are included? Metric definition What is the numerator and denominator? Checks How did I confirm the number is right? Chart and recommendation What should the stakeholder do next? Save your notebook and your notes together. When two numbers disagree Compare their populations and denominators before changing the chart.

docs.text: From business question to recommendation ¶ A useful analysis supports a decision. A chart becomes trustworthy when its population, calculations and limitations are clear. We follow the same seven steps in every lesson and case. The seven steps ¶ 1. Business question ¶ Ask: Who must decide what, and by when? Keep: the decision and a one-sentence question. 2. Data understanding ¶ Ask: What does each row represent? What is missing? Keep: the grain, keys, units, data dictionary and scope. 3. Preparation ¶ Ask: What changes are needed, and could someone else repeat them? Keep: an untouched copy of the original data and a log of every change. 4. Analysis ¶ Ask: Which comparison or metric actually answers the question? Keep: the metric definition, filters and calculation. 5. Validation ¶ Ask: Do totals reconcile? Can I explain any odd values? Keep: a manual spot check, count and total checks, and edge cases. 6. Visualization ¶ Ask: Can the audience see the important comparison at a glance? Keep: a labelled chart showing the period, units and population. 7. Recommendation ¶ Ask: What action follows, and what is still uncertain? Keep: an action linked to evidence, one caveat and a follow-up measure. A worked example ¶ Why are orders falling? A manager asks: "Why are orders falling?" The data file has one row per order line , so a single order with three products takes up three rows. Counting rows would count lines , not orders. First, define what an order is, which period to look at and which orders are eligible. Then count distinct order IDs in that population. docs.text: Why data analytics matters ¶ Every organisation makes decisions. Data analytics is the discipline of making those decisions with evidence instead of guesswork, and of explaining that evidence so other people act on it. Before we write any code or build any charts, this Foundations section answers a simple question: why bother? You will see how analysis has changed real outcomes, how numbers can mislead, and why the way we present evidence matters as much as the evidence itself. What is data analytics? ¶ Data analytics turns raw records into answers to business questions. It usually works at four levels: Level Question it answers Everyday example Descriptive What happened? Sales fell 8% last quarter. Diagnostic Why did it happen? The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened. Predictive What is likely to happen next? If nothing changes, the region will lose a further 5% next quarter. Prescriptive What should we do about it? Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices. This course focuses mostly on the first two levels, done properly : a clear question, trustworthy data, correct calculations, honest charts and a recommendation a manager can act on. Real stories where data changed the outcome ¶ A map that changed how we think about disease (London, 1854) ¶ During a cholera outbreak in Soho, physician John Snow investigated where the victims lived and where they drew their water. The cases clustered around one public water pump on Broad Street. At the time, most experts blamed "bad air". Snow persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle. His famous dot map of the deaths, drawn shortly afterwards, became the classic demonstration that cholera spreads through water, though it took years for that view to be widely accepted. Lesson A simple, well-chosen picture of the data can overturn what "everyone knows". A chart that reformed hospitals (1850s) ¶ After the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale showed with her "rose" diagrams that far more soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals than of battle wounds. Her charts were designed for politicians, not statisticians, and helped drive major sanitary reforms. Lesson Analysis only changes things when the people who decide can understand it. Winning on a small budget (baseball, 2002) ¶ The Oakland Athletics , with one of the lowest payrolls in Major League Baseball, used statistics such as on-base percentage to find undervalued players. They competed with teams spending far more. The story became the book and film Moneyball , and data-driven scouting spread across sport. Lesson Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money. Preparing for a hurricane (retail, 2004) ¶ Before a hurricane reached Florida, Walmart analysts looked at what shoppers had bought before earlier storms. Alongside torches and water, sales of strawberry Pop-Tarts and beer reportedly jumped well above normal. Stores were stocked accordingly. Lesson Past patterns can guide practical, everyday operational decisions. When big data got it wrong (public health, 2008–2015) ¶ Google Flu Trends tried to estimate flu levels from search queries. It worked for a while, then missed the 2009 swine-flu pandemic and badly overestimated later flu seasons, and was shut down. People's search habits and Google's own search algorithms changed, and the model was not re-checked against official flu data often enough. Lesson More data is not automatically better data. Every result still needs validation. Where you meet analytics every day ¶ Banking: a card payment is flagged as possible fraud because it does not fit your normal pattern. Streaming and shopping: recommendations are based on what similar customers watched or bought. Transport: ride-hailing prices rise when demand outstrips available drivers. Healthcare: hospitals plan staff rotas using predicted admission levels. Workplaces: HR teams track hiring time and staff turnover to spot problems early. Why presentation is part of analysis ¶ An analysis that nobody understands has no effect. The most important finding in a report can be lost in a cluttered table, a misleading chart or a slide with too much text. Good analysts therefore do three jobs: Find what is true in the data. Check that it really is true. Show it so the right person understands it quickly and acts on it. The rest of this Foundations section covers each of these. What comes next ¶ Work through these pages in order: Statistics are not enough : why you must always look at the data, not just the summary numbers. How statistics can mislead : correlation versus causation, misleading charts and other traps. Types of analysis : looking at one, two or many variables at once. Designing clear visuals : data-ink, how the eye groups things, and using colour with purpose. Storytelling with data : the Challenger disaster, and how to turn analysis into a message people act on. Try this before moving on Think of one decision at your own workplace that was made on gut feeling. Write down: what data could have informed it, who would have needed to understand that data, what could have gone wrong if the data had been misread.

docs.text: How statistics can mislead ¶ Numbers feel objective, but the same data can support very different stories depending on how it is summarised, compared and drawn. Learn the common traps so you never fall into them, and can spot them in other people's work. In 1954, Darrell Huff wrote a short, famous book called How to Lie with Statistics . Its point was not to teach lying. It was to show readers how easily numbers mislead, often by accident. The traps below are the ones you will meet most often at work. 1. Correlation is not causation ¶ Two things that move together are correlated . That does not mean one causes the other. A classic example: in many cities, ice cream sales and crime both rise in summer and fall in winter. Plot one against the other and you see a strong relationship. Does ice cream cause crime? Of course not. Both are plausibly driven by a third factor, warm weather , when more people are outside. The chart uses synthetic data made up for illustration. The hidden third factor is called a confounder . Whenever you see two things moving together, ask: Could a third factor be driving both? Could the cause run the other way? Could it be coincidence, especially if I searched through many variables? Spurious correlations If you compare enough unrelated series, some will match by pure chance. Tyler Vigen's Spurious Correlations project collects amusing examples, such as films featuring a particular actor tracking the number of swimming-pool drownings in the same years. At work "Customers who used our app spent 30% more." Perhaps the app made them spend more. Or perhaps the customers who already spent the most were the ones who bothered to download the app. Only a fair comparison or a test can tell you which. 2. Simpson's paradox: the total can reverse the parts ¶ In 1973, the University of California, Berkeley, looked at graduate admissions. Overall, 44% of men but only 35% of women were admitted. It looked like clear bias against women. But when the figures were split by department, the picture changed. The chart and table show the six largest departments; the overall row covers all departments. Department Men admitted Women admitted A 62% 82% B 63% 68% C 37% 34% D 33% 35% E 28% 24% F 6% 7% All departments (overall) 44% 35% What happened? Women applied mostly to departments that were very competitive for everyone (C to F). Men applied mostly to departments that admitted many applicants (A and B). The overall rate mixed together very different groups. The lesson Before comparing two overall rates, check whether the groups being compared have a different mix underneath. A total can tell the opposite story to every one of its parts. 3. Misleading axes ¶ The same two numbers can look dramatically different depending on where the axis starts. Synthetic data for illustration. Bar charts should start at zero, because we judge bars by their length. Line charts may start elsewhere, because we judge lines by their slope, but label the axis clearly. Watch for two different y-axes on one chart. They let the author make any two lines appear to move together. 4. Cherry-picked time windows ¶ Choose the start and end dates carefully and almost any trend can be made to look like growth or decline. "Sales up 40% since March!" (March was the worst month in five years.) "Complaints halved this quarter!" (Last quarter included a one-off system outage.) Synthetic data for illustration. The left chart is true, but the right chart shows the real story: March was an unusual low, and sales have been falling for five years. Ask Why does the chart start and end there ? What does the longer history look like? 5. Which average? ¶ The word "average" can mean different things: The mean adds everything up and divides by the count. The median is the middle value when everything is sorted. If a few values are extremely large, the mean is pulled upward. Imagine nine employees earning 40,000 and one director earning 1,000,000. The mean salary is 136,000; the median is 40,000. Both are "the average salary", but only one describes a typical employee. Synthetic data for illustration. Which to use Use the median for things with a few very large values, such as salaries, house prices or delivery delays. Report both when the difference matters. 6. Percentages without the base ¶ "Complaints rose 200%!" sounds alarming. From 1 to 3, it is not. From 10,000 to 30,000, it is a crisis. Synthetic data for illustration. Notice that the two charts look exactly the same. Only the axis numbers reveal how different the situations are. Always ask for the count behind a percentage. Be wary of averaging percentages from groups of very different sizes. You will meet this trap in the marketing case. 7. Survivorship bias ¶ As the story is usually told, during the Second World War analysts studied bombers returning from missions and mapped where they had been hit. The obvious idea was to add armour where the bullet holes were. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out the flaw: these were the planes that survived . Planes hit in other places, such as the engines, never came back to be counted. The armour belonged where the returning planes had no holes. Simplified illustration, not real wartime data. At work Surveying only current customers about why they like you tells you nothing about why others left. Studying only successful projects hides the reasons projects fail. A checklist for any number you are shown ¶ Before you trust a figure, ask: Compared to what? A number without a comparison means little. Who or what is included? Which records, which dates, which filters? What is the denominator? Out of how many? Could something else explain it? A confounder, a different mix, chance? How is it drawn? Where does the axis start? Is the time window fair? Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: name the confounder For each claim, suggest a third factor that could explain the link: Towns with more fire engines have more fire damage. Employees who attend more training get promoted more often. Stores with more staff have more customer complaints. Exercise 2: fix the chart Find a chart in a news article or a company report. Check where its axis starts, which time period it covers and whether the counts behind its percentages are shown. Rewrite its headline so it is fair. Exercise 3: spot the paradox A sales manager says: "Team A's overall conversion rate is lower than Team B's, so Team A is weaker." What extra breakdown would you ask for before agreeing?

docs.text: Statistics are not enough ¶ Averages, spreads and correlations are useful summaries. But very different data can produce exactly the same summary numbers. The only safe habit is to look at the data as well. Anscombe's quartet ¶ In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe created four small datasets. Each has eleven points. Look at their summary statistics: Statistic Dataset I Dataset II Dataset III Dataset IV Mean of x 9.0 9.0 9.0 9.0 Mean of y 7.50 7.50 7.50 7.50 Variance of x 11.0 11.0 11.0 11.0 Variance of y 4.13 4.13 4.12 4.12 Correlation of x and y 0.816 0.816 0.816 0.817 Best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x If you only read this table, you would say the four datasets are the same. Now look at them: Dataset What the picture shows What the statistics hide I A loose, roughly straight-line relationship Nothing. This is the case the summary describes well. II A smooth curve The relationship is not a straight line at all. III A perfect straight line, except for one outlier A single unusual point drags the trend line. IV Almost all points share one x value; one extreme point creates the "trend" Remove that one point and every x is the same, so there is no trend left to measure. The lesson Summary statistics compress data. Compression throws information away. A chart lets you see what was thrown away. The raw data, if you want to plot it yourself x (I, II, III) y I y II y III x IV y IV 10 8.04 9.14 7.46 8 6.58 8 6.95 8.14 6.77 8 5.76 13 7.58 8.74 12.74 8 7.71 9 8.81 8.77 7.11 8 8.84 11 8.33 9.26 7.81 8 8.47 14 9.96 8.10 8.84 8 7.04 6 7.24 6.13 6.08 8 5.25 4 4.26 3.10 5.39 19 12.50 12 10.84 9.13 8.15 8 5.56 7 4.82 7.26 6.42 8 7.91 5 5.68 4.74 5.73 8 6.89 The Datasaurus Dozen ¶ In 2017, researchers Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice took the idea further. Starting from a dinosaur drawing made of data points (originally created by Alberto Cairo), they nudged points step by step into new shapes while keeping the summary statistics nearly identical, to about two decimal places. Every one of these thirteen datasets has: mean of x ≈ 54.3 and mean of y ≈ 47.8 standard deviation of x ≈ 16.8 and of y ≈ 26.9 correlation between x and y between −0.06 and −0.07 A report that said "x and y are essentially unrelated, centred around 54 and 48" would be technically correct for all of them, including the dinosaur. Data source Datasaurus Dozen data from the open-source datasauRus package (MIT licence), based on Matejka and Fitzmaurice, Same Stats, Different Graphs , ACM CHI 2017. What this means at work ¶ You will rarely meet a dinosaur in a sales report. But you will meet the same problems in everyday forms: An average hides two very different groups. Average delivery time looks fine, because most deliveries are fast while a few customers wait weeks. One outlier drives the trend. A single huge order makes a quiet month look like growth. A relationship is curved, not straight. Discounts raise sales up to a point, then only cut profit. Rule of thumb Never report a summary number you have not also looked at in a chart, at least once, yourself. Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: predict, then check Cover the Anscombe chart above. Using only the statistics table, sketch what you think each dataset looks like. Then uncover the chart. Which of your sketches was furthest off, and why? Exercise 2: find a hidden shape at work Think of a number you see regularly in your job, for example average monthly sales or average response time. Write down two different situations that would produce the same average but would need different decisions . DataFrame ({ "x" : [ 10 , 8 , 13 , 9 , 11 , 14 , 6 , 4 , 12 , 7 , 5 ], "y" : [ 9.14 , 8.14 , 8.74 , 8.77 , 9.26 , 8.10 , 6.13 , 3.10 , 9.13 , 7.26 , 4.74 ], }) print ( d . mean ()) print ( "Correlation:" , d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) d . plot ( kind = "scatter" , x = "x" , y = "y" , title = "Anscombe dataset II" ) plt . show () Then replace the y values with Dataset III from the table above. The printed statistics barely change. Does the chart?

Every one of these thirteen datasets has: mean of x ≈ 54.3 and mean of y ≈ 47.8 standard deviation of x ≈ 16.8 and of y ≈ 26.9 correlation between x and y between −0.06 and −0.07 A report that said "x and y are essentially unrelated, centred around 54 and 48" would be technically correct for all of them, including the dinosaur. Data source Datasaurus Dozen data from the open-source datasauRus package (MIT licence), based on Matejka and Fitzmaurice, Same Stats, Different Graphs , ACM CHI 2017.
docs.title: The Datasaurus Dozen

docs.text: You will rarely meet a dinosaur in a sales report. But you will meet the same problems in everyday forms: An average hides two very different groups. Average delivery time looks fine, because most deliveries are fast while a few customers wait weeks. One outlier drives the trend. A single huge order makes a quiet month look like growth. A relationship is curved, not straight. Discounts raise sales up to a point, then only cut profit. Rule of thumb Never report a summary number you have not also looked at in a chart, at least once, yourself.

docs.text: Storytelling with data ¶ A correct analysis that nobody understands changes nothing. Storytelling with data means shaping evidence into a clear message, for a specific audience, that leads to a decision. The Challenger disaster: right data, wrong presentation ¶ On 28 January 1986 , the space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing all seven crew. The investigation found that rubber O-ring seals in a booster rocket had failed. They had become stiff in the unusually cold weather: the air temperature at launch was about 36°F (2°C) , far colder than any previous launch. The night before, engineers at the contractor Morton Thiokol were worried. They had data on O-ring damage from earlier flights and recommended not launching below 53°F, the coldest temperature previously flown. In a tense teleconference, their recommendation was challenged, managers reversed it, and the launch went ahead. What did the data show? ¶ Discussion that night focused on flights where O-rings had been damaged , the view later highlighted by the Rogers Commission investigation. Looked at alone, those flights do not show an obvious temperature pattern: damage appeared at both cool and warm temperatures. The picture changes completely when you include the flights with no damage: What you see Only damaged flights All 23 flights Pattern with temperature Unclear Every flight below 65°F had O-ring damage Launches near 36°F None None. Challenger was far outside all experience Every launch below 65°F had damage. Most warm launches had none. And Challenger would launch more than 15 degrees colder than anything ever tried. Two views of the lesson Edward Tufte argued in Visual Explanations (1997) that the engineers' charts failed to show this relationship clearly. Others have pointed out that the engineers did raise temperature as the key concern, and that the decision was also shaped by schedule and organisational pressure. Both views lead to the same lesson for analysts: when the stakes are high, the evidence must be presented so the risk is impossible to miss. Data source O-ring data for the 23 flights before Challenger: UCI Machine Learning Repository, Challenger USA Space Shuttle O-Ring dataset (erosion or blow-by version), based on Draper (1995) and Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley (1989). What makes a data story ¶ The ideas in this section draw on Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's book Storytelling with Data (2015), paraphrased for this course. A data story is not a decorated chart. It has three parts: Context: who is the audience, what do they already know, and what decision do they face? Evidence: the few charts and numbers that matter, checked and clearly drawn. Action: what you recommend, what is uncertain, and how success will be measured. Start with the "big idea" ¶ Before building any chart, write your main message in one sentence that: states your point of view, says what is at stake, and is written for your audience. Example: "Delivery delays in the North region are costing us repeat customers, so we should trial a second carrier there next quarter before the peak season." If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to build the presentation. A simple process ¶ Know your audience. A finance director and a warehouse team need different levels of detail. Write the big idea in one sentence. Choose the right chart for each point (see Types of analysis ). Remove clutter (see Designing clear visuals ). Direct attention with one colour, a clear title and a short annotation. Build the flow: situation, complication, resolution. What is happening, why it is a problem, what we should do. Test it on someone who has not seen it. Can they repeat your message in one sentence? Titles that tell Replace descriptive titles with message titles. Instead of "Monthly sales by region" write "North region sales have fallen for three months while all others grew." Exploratory versus explanatory ¶ Exploratory Explanatory Purpose Find out what is in the data Tell others what you found Audience You Decision-makers Number of charts Many As few as possible Style Rough, quick Clean, titled, annotated Most of your time in analysis is exploratory. Only the few findings that matter make it into the explanatory story. Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: rescue the Challenger chart Look at the left-hand Challenger chart. Write a one-sentence title for the right-hand chart that a manager could not misunderstand. Exercise 2: write a big idea Choose a recent finding from your own work, or from any chart on these Foundations pages. Write a big-idea sentence with a point of view, the stakes and the audience. Exercise 3: three slides, one story Plan a three-slide story about the ice cream and crime example on How statistics can mislead : Situation: what the raw correlation seems to say. Complication: what it hides. Resolution: what a decision-maker should do instead. Exercise 4: the one-sentence test Show any chart you have made to a colleague for ten seconds. Ask them what it says. If their answer differs from your intended message, revise the title, the highlight or the chart type.

docs.text: Types of analysis: one, two or many variables ¶ Most questions start with one variable, then ask how it relates to a second, and finally how several factors work together. Each step needs different summaries and different charts. Synthetic data for illustration. Univariate analysis: one variable at a time ¶ Question: What does this one variable look like? You describe its centre (mean, median), spread (range, standard deviation) and shape (symmetric, skewed, any outliers). Kind of variable Good summaries Good charts Numbers (sales, days, age) Mean, median, minimum, maximum, spread Histogram, box plot Categories (region, product type) Counts and percentages Bar chart sorted by size Dates Counts per day, week or month Line chart over time Business examples: How long do deliveries usually take, and how long do the slowest ones take? Which product category sells most often? How many customer complaints arrive each week? Watch for A skewed shape. In the histogram above, most orders arrive within 1 to 5 days, but a long tail stretches past two weeks. The median (3 days) describes a typical order better than the mean (about 4 days), which the slow tail pulls upward. Bivariate analysis: two variables together ¶ Question: How does one variable change with another? The two variables are… Good summaries Good charts Number and number Correlation, trend line Scatter plot Category and number Mean or median per group Bar chart, box plot per group Category and category Counts in a cross-table Heat map, stacked or grouped bar Date and number Change over time Line chart Business examples: Does higher advertising spend go with higher revenue? Do some regions have longer delivery times than others? Which customer segments buy which product categories? Remember A relationship between two variables is a correlation , not proof of cause. See How statistics can mislead . Multivariate analysis: three or more variables ¶ Question: Does the relationship change when we account for something else? You add a third variable by using colour , size , small multiples (one small chart per group) or filters . Business examples: Does the link between ad spend and revenue differ by sales channel? Do delivery times by region change once we separate standard and express shipping? Is a profit drop explained by a change in the product mix? The second and third panels show exactly the same points. Colouring by channel in the third panel shows that "Store" tends to sit above the others at the same spend, on average. That pattern is invisible in the two-variable chart. Rule of thumb Add one variable at a time. If a chart needs a long explanation, split it into small multiples instead. Choosing a chart: quick guide ¶ I want to show… Try How values are distributed Histogram or box plot A ranking Sorted bar chart Change over time Line chart Parts of a whole (few parts) Stacked bar; a pie only for two or three slices Relationship between two numbers Scatter plot Comparison across many groups Small multiples or a heat map A single headline number Just the number, large and clearly labelled Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: classify the question Is each question univariate, bivariate or multivariate? What is the typical order value? Do larger discounts go with lower profit? Does the discount–profit relationship differ between furniture and office supplies? How many orders were placed each month? Exercise 2: pick the chart For each question in Exercise 1, choose a chart type from the quick guide and say in one sentence why. Exercise 3: your own data Pick one variable from your own work. Write one univariate, one bivariate and one multivariate question you could ask about it.

docs.text: Designing clear visuals ¶ A good chart lets the reader see the important comparison in seconds. That depends on removing what does not help, and on using what we know about how the eye and brain read pictures. The data-ink ratio ¶ Information designer Edward Tufte suggested a simple test. Of all the ink on a chart, how much actually shows data ? Everything else (heavy gridlines, borders, shading, 3D effects, decorative colours) is non-data ink. Tufte called unnecessary decoration chartjunk . Aim: increase the share of ink that carries data, without removing anything the reader needs. Synthetic data for illustration. What changed between the two versions: Removed the background shading, borders and hatching. Removed the gridlines and the value axis, and wrote the values directly on the bars. Sorted the bars, so the ranking is obvious. Used colour once , to point at the bar that matters. Turned the bars horizontal , so labels are easy to read. Do not overdo it Removing axis labels, units or context to make a chart "clean" makes it less useful. The goal is clarity, not minimalism. Pre-attentive attributes: what the eye sees first ¶ Some visual differences are noticed almost instantly, before we consciously think. These are called pre-attentive attributes . They include colour, size, position, orientation and boldness. Try it: count the number 3 in the top grid, then in the bottom grid. The bottom grid takes a second. The top one takes much longer. The only difference is one attribute: colour. Use this deliberately Make most of the chart grey, then use one strong colour or bold label for the thing you want the reader to see. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. Gestalt principles: how we group things ¶ Our brains automatically group what we see. Designers use these Gestalt principles to make related items look related. Principle What it means Use it in a chart or dashboard Proximity Things close together seem related Put related charts next to each other; leave space between unrelated ones Similarity Things that look alike (colour, shape) seem related Use the same colour for the same category on every chart Enclosure Things inside a shared border or shaded area seem grouped Shade a time period, such as a promotion, on a line chart Connection Things joined by a line seem related Lines connect points in a time series; avoid lines between unrelated categories Closure We complete incomplete shapes in our minds Charts rarely need full borders; the eye fills them in Continuity We follow smooth paths Align charts and labels so the eye flows across the page Colour with purpose ¶ One colour for one meaning. If "East" is blue in one chart, keep it blue in every chart. Grey for context, colour for focus. Do not rely on colour alone. Around one in twelve men has some colour-vision deficiency. Add labels or patterns too. Avoid rainbow palettes for numbers. Use light-to-dark shades of one colour for "more" and "less". Avoid red and green as the only difference. It is the most common pair people cannot tell apart. A clean-chart checklist ¶ Does the title say what the reader should notice, not just what is plotted? Are axes labelled with units, and do bars start at zero? Is everything that is not data as light as possible? Is colour used only where it means something? Can someone who cannot see colour still read it? Would a sorted table or a single number be clearer than a chart? Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: declutter Take a chart from a recent report at work, or any chart from the news. List every element that is not data. For each, decide: keep , lighten or remove . Sketch the improved version. Exercise 2: one highlight Sketch a bar chart of five products where only one product needs attention. Use grey for four bars and one colour for the fifth. Write a title that tells the reader what to notice. Exercise 3: spot the Gestalt Open any dashboard you use at work. Find one place where proximity or similarity helps you, and one place where it confuses you.
