docs.text: Session 1 lab: Python, Colab and always plotting your data ¶ Learn just enough Python to run every notebook in this course, then use it to recreate the lecture's main lesson yourself: summary statistics are not enough, so always plot your data. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . How this lab works ¶ Part Level What you do A. Guided practice Core Follow step by step: Colab, variables, lists, tables, filters, groups and a chart B. Independent tasks Core and Stretch Use the same skills on a new question: Anscombe's quartet and your own analytical question C. Challenge Challenge Investigate the Datasaurus Dozen Core tasks are for everyone and are enough for your portfolio. Stretch tasks are for when you finish early. Challenge tasks are optional and need more reasoning. How the course uses code Every notebook gives you working code with explanations. You read it, run it, then change a few lines in the exercises. You will not be asked to write programs from scratch. Evidence you keep: your Anscombe statistics table and plots with a two-sentence lesson, and one workplace decision rewritten as an analytical question. Part A: Guided practice (Core) ¶ A1. Google Colab in two minutes ¶ Google Colab is a free website for running Python notebooks. You need a Google account. Go to colab.research.google.com , or use the Open in Colab button above. To open a file you downloaded, choose File → Upload notebook and select the .ipynb file. A notebook is made of cells . Text cells explain; code cells run. Click inside a code cell and press Shift + Enter to run it. The result appears underneath. Run cells from top to bottom . Later cells use results from earlier ones. If something goes wrong Choose Runtime → Restart session and run all . This starts again from the top and fixes most problems. A2. Values and variables ¶ A variable is a name for a value. The = sign stores the value under that name. price = 120 quantity = 3 total = price * quantity total 360 The last line of a cell is shown as the output. You can also use print to show several things. discount = 0.10 print ( "Total before discount:" , total ) print ( "Total after discount:" , total * ( 1 - discount )) Total before discount: 360 Total after discount: 324.0 Text goes inside quotes, and a list holds several values in square brackets. segment = "Consumer" monthly_sales = [ 120 , 95 , 140 , 180 ] print ( segment , "sales in four months:" , monthly_sales ) print ( "Total:" , sum ( monthly_sales )) print ( "Number of months:" , len ( monthly_sales )) Consumer sales in four months: [120, 95, 140, 180] Total: 535 Number of months: 4 Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # Change the numbers in the list, then run the cell again. monthly_sales = [ 120 , 95 , 140 , 180 ] print ( "Average monthly sales:" , sum ( monthly_sales ) / len ( monthly_sales )) Average monthly sales: 133.75 A3. Tables with pandas ¶ pandas is the Python library analysts use for tables. A table in pandas is called a DataFrame . We first import the library, then build a small made-up table of five orders. import pandas as pd orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "A1" , "A2" , "A3" , "A4" , "A5" ], "region" : [ "North" , "South" , "North" , "East" , "South" ], "sales" : [ 250.0 , 120.0 , 90.0 , 310.0 , 180.0 ], "items" : [ 3 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 2 ], }) orders .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id region sales items 0 A1 North 250.0 3 1 A2 South 120.0 1 2 A3 North 90.0 2 3 A4 East 310.0 4 4 A5 South 180.0 2 Each row is one order. Each column has a name. Useful first checks: print ( "Rows and columns:" , orders . shape ) print ( orders . dtypes ) Rows and columns: (5, 4) order_id object region object sales float64 items int64 dtype: object dtypes shows each column's type: object means text, int64 whole numbers, float64 decimals. A4. Select, filter, add up, count ¶ Select one column with its name in square brackets: orders [ "sales" ] 0 250.0 1 120.0 2 90.0 3 310.0 4 180.0 Name: sales, dtype: float64 Add up or average a column: print ( "Total sales:" , orders [ "sales" ] . sum ()) print ( "Average sales per order:" , orders [ "sales" ] . mean ()) Total sales: 950.0 Average sales per order: 190.0 Filter rows with a condition. This keeps only orders from the North region: north = orders [ orders [ "region" ] == "North" ] north .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id region sales items 0 A1 North 250.0 3 2 A3 North 90.0 2 Count how many rows, and how many different values a column has: print ( "Number of orders:" , len ( orders )) print ( "Number of different regions:" , orders [ "region" ] . nunique ()) Number of orders: 5 Number of different regions: 3 Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # Change "North" to "South" and run again. How many South orders are there, # and what are their total sales? selected = orders [ orders [ "region" ] == "North" ] print ( len ( selected ), "orders, total sales" , selected [ "sales" ] . sum ()) 2 orders, total sales 340.0 A5. Group and summarise ¶ groupby splits the table into groups and summarises each one. Here: total sales for each region. sales_by_region = orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum () sales_by_region region East 310.0 North 340.0 South 300.0 Name: sales, dtype: float64 agg computes several summaries for each group at once. Each line inside it reads: new column name = (column to use, summary to compute) . docs.text: Session 1 lecture: Why data analytics matters ¶ Data analytics means making decisions with evidence instead of guesswork, and explaining that evidence so people act on it. This lecture shows why that matters, how an analysis is organised, and why you must always look at the data, not only its summary numbers. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . What you will be able to do ¶ Name the four levels of analytics and give a business example of each. Explain, with a real story, how data changed a decision and how it can fail. Turn a vague request into a question with a decision , population , period and measure . Show with code why summary statistics are not enough, using Anscombe's quartet and the Datasaurus Dozen. Name the most common ways numbers mislead. This lecture uses the Foundations pages as its reading. In the Lab you practise the Python behind every demonstration here. How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first: being wrong is how you learn what to check. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words. Part 1: What is data analytics? ¶ Data analytics turns raw records into answers to business questions. It works at four levels, each building on the one before. Level Question it answers Everyday example Descriptive What happened? Sales fell last quarter. Diagnostic Why did it happen? The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened. Predictive What is likely to happen next? If nothing changes, that region will keep losing sales. Prescriptive What should we do about it? Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices. Most of this course works at the first two levels, done properly : a clear question, trustworthy data, correct calculations, honest charts and a recommendation a manager can act on. Later sessions add uncertainty and simple prediction. Check your understanding Which level is each statement? "Deliveries in the North got slower because the new carrier skips Saturday collections." "We expect about 400 returns in December." "Move the slow carrier's routes to the faster one for one month and measure the effect." "We shipped 12,000 parcels in October." Part 2: Real stories where data changed the outcome ¶ Each story teaches one habit you will use in every session. Read the full versions in Why data analytics matters . Story What happened The habit it teaches John Snow , London, 1854 Mapping cholera deaths showed them clustered around one water pump. Its handle was removed. A simple, well-chosen picture can overturn what "everyone knows". Florence Nightingale , 1850s Her diagrams showed most soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals, not of wounds. Analysis only changes things when decision-makers understand it. Moneyball , baseball, 2002 A low-budget team found undervalued players by measuring on-base percentage. Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money. Walmart , hurricane, 2004 Sales patterns before earlier storms guided what to stock before a new one. Past patterns can guide everyday operational decisions. Google Flu Trends , 2008–2015 Estimating flu from searches worked, then failed badly and was shut down. More data is not automatically better data. Every result needs validation. Predict, then reveal Four of these stories are successes; one is a failure. Before reading the last row, ask yourself: what could make a model that once worked stop working? Then read the last row and the full story in Foundations. Check your understanding Snow and Nightingale both drew their evidence. Why might a chart persuade a decision-maker when a table of the same numbers does not? Part 3: From question to recommendation ¶ Every analysis in this course follows the same seven steps. The full version is in the analytical workflow . Step Ask Keep as evidence 1. Business question Who must decide what, and by when? The decision and a one-sentence question 2. Data understanding What does each row represent? What is missing? Grain, keys, units, scope 3. Preparation What changes are needed, and can someone repeat them? Untouched original data and a change log 4. Analysis Which comparison or metric answers the question? Metric definition, filters, calculation 5. Validation Do totals reconcile? Can I explain odd values? Spot checks, count and total checks 6. Visualisation Can the audience see the key comparison at a glance? A labelled chart with period, units and population 7. Recommendation What action follows, and what is still uncertain? Action, one caveat, a follow-up measure Step 1 in detail: a question you can answer ¶ A manager says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups." That is a feeling, not a question. A question you can answer with data names four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the sales table Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Total sales by customer segment "Which customer segment had the highest total sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Check your understanding A colleague asks: "Is the new website working?" Which of the four parts are missing? Suggest one value for each. Part 4: Always plot your data — Anscombe's quartet ¶ In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe made four small datasets to make one point. We build them in code, compute their summary statistics, and only then look at them. The code below stores all four datasets in one table. Each row is one point: which set it belongs to ( set ), and its x and y values. import pandas as pd # Anscombe's quartet (1973): four small datasets, eleven points each. x = [ 10 , 8 , 13 , 9 , 11 , 14 , 6 , 4 , 12 , 7 , 5 ] anscombe = pd . concat ([ pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "I" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 8.04 , 6.95 , 7.58 , 8.81 , 8.33 , 9.96 , 7.24 , 4.26 , 10.84 , 4.82 , 5.68 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "II" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 9.14 , 8.14 , 8.74 , 8.77 , 9.26 , 8.10 , 6.13 , 3.10 , 9.13 , 7.26 , 4.74 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "III" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 7.46 , 6.77 , 12.74 , 7.11 , 7.81 , 8.84 , 6.08 , 5.39 , 8.15 , 6.42 , 5.73 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "IV" , "x" : [ 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 19 , 8 , 8 , 8 ], "y" : [ 6.58 , 5.76 , 7.71 , 8.84 , 8.47 , 7.04 , 5.25 , 12.50 , 5.56 , 7.91 , 6.89 ]}), ], ignore_index = True ) print ( "Rows, columns:" , anscombe . shape ) anscombe . head () Rows, columns: (44, 3) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } set x y 0 I 10 8.04 1 I 8 6.95 2 I 13 7.58 3 I 9 8.81 4 I 11 8.33 Now the summary statistics for each set. groupby("set") splits the table into the four sets; agg computes several summaries for each one. summary = anscombe . groupby ( "set" ) . agg ( mean_x = ( "x" , "mean" ), mean_y = ( "y" , "mean" ), sd_x = ( "x" , "std" ), sd_y = ( "y" , "std" ), ) summary [ "correlation" ] = anscombe . groupby ( "set" )[[ "x" , "y" ]] . apply ( lambda d : d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) summary . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mean_x mean_y sd_x sd_y correlation set I 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 II 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 III 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 IV 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 Finally, the straight line that best fits each set. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope and the intercept of that line. import numpy as np for name , points in anscombe . groupby ( "set" ): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) print ( f "Set { name : >3 } : best-fit line y = { intercept : .2f } + { slope : .3f } x" ) Set I: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set II: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set III: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set IV: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Predict, then reveal Read the outputs above. The four sets share their means, spreads, correlation and best-fit line. Sketch what you think a scatter plot of each set looks like. Will the four pictures be similar? Then run the next cell. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 8 , 6.5 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) line_x = np . array ([ 2 , 20 ]) for ax , ( name , points ) in zip ( axes . flat , anscombe . groupby ( "set" )): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) ax . plot ( line_x , intercept + slope * line_x , color = "#d95f02" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . scatter ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], s = 40 , color = "#1f78b4" , zorder = 3 ) ax . set_title ( f "Set { name } " ) for ax in axes [ 1 ]: ax . set_xlabel ( "x" ) for ax in axes [:, 0 ]: ax . set_ylabel ( "y" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same statistics, same trend line, four different stories" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Set What the picture shows What the statistics hide I A loose, roughly straight-line relationship Nothing: the summary describes it well II A smooth curve The relationship is not a straight line III A perfect line except for one outlier One unusual point drags the trend line IV Almost every point has the same x; one far point creates the "trend" Remove that point and there is no trend to measure Remember Summary statistics compress data, and compression throws information away. A chart shows you what was thrown away. Plot first, then summarise. Check your understanding In set IV, what happens to the correlation if the one point far to the right is a data-entry error and you remove it? Why can you not even compute it? Part 5: The Datasaurus Dozen ¶ In 2017 Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice pushed Anscombe's idea further. Starting from a dinosaur drawn with data points, they nudged the points step by step into twelve other shapes while keeping the summary statistics almost identical. The next cell downloads their data from a fixed public address and checks the file's fingerprint, so everyone gets exactly the same version. import hashlib import io import urllib.request import pandas as pd # The Datasaurus Dozen (Matejka and Fitzmaurice, 2017), from the open-source # datasauRus package (MIT licence). The link points to one fixed version, and the # fingerprint check confirms we got exactly that file. DATASAURUS_URL = ( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jumpingrivers/datasauRus/" "94f3c3a82660e256b84f70961f50dc0e216757de/inst/extdata/DatasaurusDozen-Long.tsv" ) DATASAURUS_SHA256 = "c8c4792c3ed15238ba07dad6ab778adc79d72e3e1324ead4d8c1ae52849780f8" file_bytes = urllib . request . urlopen ( DATASAURUS_URL ) . read () assert hashlib . sha256 ( file_bytes ) . hexdigest () == DATASAURUS_SHA256 , "Unexpected file: ask your instructor." dozen = pd . read_csv ( io . BytesIO ( file_bytes ), sep = " \t " ) print ( "Rows, columns:" , dozen . shape ) print ( "Datasets:" , dozen [ "dataset" ] . nunique ()) dozen . head () Rows, columns: (1846, 3) Datasets: 13 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dataset x y 0 dino 55.3846 97.1795 1 dino 51.5385 96.0256 2 dino 46.1538 94.4872 3 dino 42.8205 91.4103 4 dino 40.7692 88.3333 Predict, then reveal The table has thirteen datasets. Their names ( dino , star , circle , …) are a hint. First look at the statistics in the next cell. Would you have guessed the datasets had different shapes from these numbers alone? dozen_summary = dozen . groupby ( "dataset" ) . agg ( mean_x = ( "x" , "mean" ), mean_y = ( "y" , "mean" ), sd_x = ( "x" , "std" ), sd_y = ( "y" , "std" ), ) dozen_summary [ "correlation" ] = dozen . groupby ( "dataset" )[[ "x" , "y" ]] . apply ( lambda d : d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) dozen_summary . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mean_x mean_y sd_x sd_y correlation dataset away 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.06 bullseye 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.07 circle 54.27 47.84 16.76 26.93 -0.07 dino 54.26 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.06 dots 54.26 47.84 16.77 26.93 -0.06 h_lines 54.26 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.06 high_lines 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.94 -0.07 slant_down 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.94 -0.07 slant_up 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.07 star 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.93 -0.06 v_lines 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.94 -0.07 wide_lines 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.07 x_shape 54.26 47.84 16.77 26.93 -0.07 Now draw one small scatter plot per dataset. Charts like this, one per group on the same axes, are called small multiples . import matplotlib.pyplot as plt names = dozen [ "dataset" ] . unique () fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 3 , 5 , figsize = ( 12 , 7 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) for ax in axes . flat : ax . set_visible ( False ) for ax , name in zip ( axes . flat , names ): points = dozen [ dozen [ "dataset" ] == name ] ax . set_visible ( True ) ax . scatter ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], s = 8 ) ax . set_title ( name . replace ( "_" , " " )) fig . suptitle ( "The Datasaurus Dozen: one scatter plot per dataset" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () A report saying "x and y are essentially unrelated, centred around the same values" would be true for every panel, including the dinosaur. At work You will rarely meet a dinosaur in a sales report. You will meet the same problem in everyday forms: an average delivery time that hides a group of customers waiting weeks; one huge order that makes a quiet month look like growth; two stores with the same average sales but very different patterns. See Statistics are not enough . Check your understanding Why are the thirteen panels drawn with the same axes? What could go wrong if each panel chose its own axis range? Part 6: A preview of how numbers mislead ¶ Numbers feel objective, but the same data can tell very different stories depending on how it is summarised and drawn. Here is one trap, live. Both charts below show the same two numbers . products = [ "Product A" , "Product B" ] satisfaction = [ 96 , 98 ] # made-up percentages fig , ( left , right ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 3.5 )) left . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#1f78b4" ) left . set_ylim ( 95 , 98.5 ) left . set_title ( "Axis starts at 95" ) right . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#1f78b4" ) right . set_ylim ( 0 , 100 ) right . set_title ( "Axis starts at 0" ) for ax in ( left , right ): ax . set_ylabel ( "Satisfied customers (%)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same data, two impressions (made-up numbers)" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () We judge bars by their length , so bar charts should start at zero. On the left, Product B looks several times better; on the right you see the truth: two products almost the same. The full list of traps is in How statistics can mislead . Later sessions return to each one with real data. Trap One-line warning Where we meet it again Correlation is not causation Two things moving together may share a hidden cause Correlation and regression Simpson's paradox A total can reverse the story of every part Metrics and KPIs Misleading axes Where the axis starts changes the impression Visualisation principles Cherry-picked time windows The chosen start and end dates can create any trend Time series and trends Which average? Mean and median can tell different stories Descriptive statistics Percentages without the base "Up 200%" means little without the counts Marketing case Survivorship bias The records you see may be only the survivors Business cases A checklist for any number you are shown Compared to what? Who or what is included? What is the denominator? Could something else explain it? How is it drawn? Summary ¶ Analytics answers four kinds of question: what happened, why, what next and what to do. Good analysis starts from a decision , and a good question names a decision, population, period and measure. The seven-step workflow keeps evidence at each step so someone else can check your work. Different data can share identical summary statistics. Always plot your data. Numbers mislead through causation claims, mixing groups, axes, time windows, averages, missing bases and survivors. Quiz ¶ Answer these in your own words. We go through them at the start of the next lecture. Name the four levels of analytics, and give a one-line business example of the diagnostic level. Google Flu Trends worked for a while and then failed. Give one reason, and the habit this teaches. Rewrite "How are our stores doing?" as an analytical question that names a decision, population, period and measure. Two datasets have the same mean, standard deviation and correlation. Can you conclude they look alike? What should you do? In Anscombe's set III, what single feature of the data changes the best-fit line? Why should a bar chart's value axis start at zero, while a line chart's axis may not? A report says "Customers who used our app spent 30% more." Give one explanation other than "the app made them spend more". In the seven-step workflow, what is the difference between analysis and validation ? docs.text: Every analysis in this course follows the same seven steps. The full version is in the analytical workflow . Step Ask Keep as evidence 1. Business question Who must decide what, and by when? The decision and a one-sentence question 2. Data understanding What does each row represent? What is missing? Grain, keys, units, scope 3. Preparation What changes are needed, and can someone repeat them? Untouched original data and a change log 4. Analysis Which comparison or metric answers the question? Metric definition, filters, calculation 5. Validation Do totals reconcile? Can I explain odd values? Spot checks, count and total checks 6. Visualisation Can the audience see the key comparison at a glance? A labelled chart with period, units and population 7. Recommendation What action follows, and what is still uncertain? Action, one caveat, a follow-up measure
docs.title: Part 3: From question to recommendation

docs.text: A manager says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups." That is a feeling, not a question. A question you can answer with data names four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the sales table Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Total sales by customer segment "Which customer segment had the highest total sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Check your understanding A colleague asks: "Is the new website working?" Which of the four parts are missing? Suggest one value for each.
docs.title: Step 1 in detail: a question you can answer

docs.text: In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe made four small datasets to make one point. We build them in code, compute their summary statistics, and only then look at them. The code below stores all four datasets in one table. Each row is one point: which set it belongs to ( set ), and its x and y values. import pandas as pd # Anscombe's quartet (1973): four small datasets, eleven points each. x = [ 10 , 8 , 13 , 9 , 11 , 14 , 6 , 4 , 12 , 7 , 5 ] anscombe = pd . concat ([ pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "I" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 8.04 , 6.95 , 7.58 , 8.81 , 8.33 , 9.96 , 7.24 , 4.26 , 10.84 , 4.82 , 5.68 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "II" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 9.14 , 8.14 , 8.74 , 8.77 , 9.26 , 8.10 , 6.13 , 3.10 , 9.13 , 7.26 , 4.74 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "III" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 7.46 , 6.77 , 12.74 , 7.11 , 7.81 , 8.84 , 6.08 , 5.39 , 8.15 , 6.42 , 5.73 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "IV" , "x" : [ 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 19 , 8 , 8 , 8 ], "y" : [ 6.58 , 5.76 , 7.71 , 8.84 , 8.47 , 7.04 , 5.25 , 12.50 , 5.56 , 7.91 , 6.89 ]}), ], ignore_index = True ) print ( "Rows, columns:" , anscombe . shape ) anscombe . head () Rows, columns: (44, 3) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } set x y 0 I 10 8.04 1 I 8 6.95 2 I 13 7.58 3 I 9 8.81 4 I 11 8.33 Now the summary statistics for each set. groupby("set") splits the table into the four sets; agg computes several summaries for each one. summary = anscombe . groupby ( "set" ) . agg ( mean_x = ( "x" , "mean" ), mean_y = ( "y" , "mean" ), sd_x = ( "x" , "std" ), sd_y = ( "y" , "std" ), ) summary [ "correlation" ] = anscombe . groupby ( "set" )[[ "x" , "y" ]] . apply ( lambda d : d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) summary . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mean_x mean_y sd_x sd_y correlation set I 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 II 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 III 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 IV 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 Finally, the straight line that best fits each set. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope and the intercept of that line. import numpy as np for name , points in anscombe . groupby ( "set" ): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) print ( f "Set { name : >3 } : best-fit line y = { intercept : .2f } + { slope : .3f } x" ) Set I: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set II: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set III: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set IV: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Predict, then reveal Read the outputs above. The four sets share their means, spreads, correlation and best-fit line. Sketch what you think a scatter plot of each set looks like. Will the four pictures be similar? Then run the next cell. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 8 , 6.5 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) line_x = np . array ([ 2 , 20 ]) for ax , ( name , points ) in zip ( axes . flat , anscombe . groupby ( "set" )): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) ax . plot ( line_x , intercept + slope * line_x , color = "#d95f02" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . scatter ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], s = 40 , color = "#1f78b4" , zorder = 3 ) ax . set_title ( f "Set { name } " ) for ax in axes [ 1 ]: ax . set_xlabel ( "x" ) for ax in axes [:, 0 ]: ax . set_ylabel ( "y" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same statistics, same trend line, four different stories" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Set What the picture shows What the statistics hide I A loose, roughly straight-line relationship Nothing: the summary describes it well II A smooth curve The relationship is not a straight line III A perfect line except for one outlier One unusual point drags the trend line IV Almost every point has the same x; one far point creates the "trend" Remove that point and there is no trend to measure Remember Summary statistics compress data, and compression throws information away. A chart shows you what was thrown away. Plot first, then summarise. Check your understanding In set IV, what happens to the correlation if the one point far to the right is a data-entry error and you remove it? Why can you not even compute it?
docs.title: Part 4: Always plot your data — Anscombe's quartet

docs.text: In 2017 Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice pushed Anscombe's idea further. Starting from a dinosaur drawn with data points, they nudged the points step by step into twelve other shapes while keeping the summary statistics almost identical. The next cell downloads their data from a fixed public address and checks the file's fingerprint, so everyone gets exactly the same version. import hashlib import io import urllib.request import pandas as pd # The Datasaurus Dozen (Matejka and Fitzmaurice, 2017), from the open-source # datasauRus package (MIT licence). The link points to one fixed version, and the # fingerprint check confirms we got exactly that file. DATASAURUS_URL = ( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jumpingrivers/datasauRus/" "94f3c3a82660e256b84f70961f50dc0e216757de/inst/extdata/DatasaurusDozen-Long.tsv" ) DATASAURUS_SHA256 = "c8c4792c3ed15238ba07dad6ab778adc79d72e3e1324ead4d8c1ae52849780f8" file_bytes = urllib . request . urlopen ( DATASAURUS_URL ) . read () assert hashlib . sha256 ( file_bytes ) . hexdigest () == DATASAURUS_SHA256 , "Unexpected file: ask your instructor." dozen = pd . read_csv ( io . BytesIO ( file_bytes ), sep = " \t " ) print ( "Rows, columns:" , dozen . shape ) print ( "Datasets:" , dozen [ "dataset" ] . nunique ()) dozen . head () Rows, columns: (1846, 3) Datasets: 13 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dataset x y 0 dino 55.3846 97.1795 1 dino 51.5385 96.0256 2 dino 46.1538 94.4872 3 dino 42.8205 91.4103 4 dino 40.7692 88.3333 Predict, then reveal The table has thirteen datasets. Their names ( dino , star , circle , …) are a hint. First look at the statistics in the next cell. Would you have guessed the datasets had different shapes from these numbers alone? dozen_summary = dozen . groupby ( "dataset" ) . agg ( mean_x = ( "x" , "mean" ), mean_y = ( "y" , "mean" ), sd_x = ( "x" , "std" ), sd_y = ( "y" , "std" ), ) dozen_summary [ "correlation" ] = dozen . groupby ( "dataset" )[[ "x" , "y" ]] . apply ( lambda d : d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) dozen_summary . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mean_x mean_y sd_x sd_y correlation dataset away 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.06 bullseye 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.07 circle 54.27 47.84 16.76 26.93 -0.07 dino 54.26 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.06 dots 54.26 47.84 16.77 26.93 -0.06 h_lines 54.26 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.06 high_lines 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.94 -0.07 slant_down 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.94 -0.07 slant_up 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.07 star 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.93 -0.06 v_lines 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.94 -0.07 wide_lines 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.07 x_shape 54.26 47.84 16.77 26.93 -0.07 Now draw one small scatter plot per dataset. Charts like this, one per group on the same axes, are called small multiples . import matplotlib.pyplot as plt names = dozen [ "dataset" ] . unique () fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 3 , 5 , figsize = ( 12 , 7 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) for ax in axes . flat : ax . set_visible ( False ) for ax , name in zip ( axes . flat , names ): points = dozen [ dozen [ "dataset" ] == name ] ax . set_visible ( True ) ax . scatter ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], s = 8 ) ax . set_title ( name . replace ( "_" , " " )) fig . suptitle ( "The Datasaurus Dozen: one scatter plot per dataset" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () A report saying "x and y are essentially unrelated, centred around the same values" would be true for every panel, including the dinosaur. At work You will rarely meet a dinosaur in a sales report. You will meet the same problem in everyday forms: an average delivery time that hides a group of customers waiting weeks; one huge order that makes a quiet month look like growth; two stores with the same average sales but very different patterns. See Statistics are not enough . Check your understanding Why are the thirteen panels drawn with the same axes? What could go wrong if each panel chose its own axis range?
docs.title: Part 5: The Datasaurus Dozen

docs.text: Numbers feel objective, but the same data can tell very different stories depending on how it is summarised and drawn. Here is one trap, live. Both charts below show the same two numbers . products = [ "Product A" , "Product B" ] satisfaction = [ 96 , 98 ] # made-up percentages fig , ( left , right ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 3.5 )) left . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#1f78b4" ) left . set_ylim ( 95 , 98.5 ) left . set_title ( "Axis starts at 95" ) right . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#1f78b4" ) right . set_ylim ( 0 , 100 ) right . set_title ( "Axis starts at 0" ) for ax in ( left , right ): ax . set_ylabel ( "Satisfied customers (%)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same data, two impressions (made-up numbers)" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () We judge bars by their length , so bar charts should start at zero. On the left, Product B looks several times better; on the right you see the truth: two products almost the same. The full list of traps is in How statistics can mislead . Later sessions return to each one with real data. Trap One-line warning Where we meet it again Correlation is not causation Two things moving together may share a hidden cause Correlation and regression Simpson's paradox A total can reverse the story of every part Metrics and KPIs Misleading axes Where the axis starts changes the impression Visualisation principles Cherry-picked time windows The chosen start and end dates can create any trend Time series and trends Which average? Mean and median can tell different stories Descriptive statistics Percentages without the base "Up 200%" means little without the counts Marketing case Survivorship bias The records you see may be only the survivors Business cases A checklist for any number you are shown Compared to what? Who or what is included? What is the denominator? Could something else explain it? How is it drawn?
docs.title: Part 6: A preview of how numbers mislead

docs.text: Analytics answers four kinds of question: what happened, why, what next and what to do. Good analysis starts from a decision , and a good question names a decision, population, period and measure. The seven-step workflow keeps evidence at each step so someone else can check your work. Different data can share identical summary statistics. Always plot your data. Numbers mislead through causation claims, mixing groups, axes, time windows, averages, missing bases and survivors.

docs.text: Session 2 lab: Can we trust the sales table? ¶ Turn a vague request into a clear question, take the retail table apart, and prove you can count its orders correctly before anyone draws a chart. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ The head of a retail business says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups. I need to know where to look first. But before you show me any chart: can I trust these numbers? How many orders did we actually have?" This is not yet a question you can answer with data, and a wrong count at this stage spoils every later chart. Today you turn the request into a question and build trust in the data. About the data We use the Superstore sample published by Tableau. It describes a fictitious company, not a real one. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units : the file does not state a currency, so we never label it as dollars, rupees or anything else. How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G7 Independent tasks Same skills, new questions, on your own or in pairs I1–I6 Challenge Harder reasoning and debugging C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Write a business question that names a decision, a population, a period and a measure. Explain what the setup cell's load_orders() does, step by step. State the grain of the table and count orders correctly with nunique() . Write a data dictionary and run a quality checklist across five dimensions. Explain what the returns flag does and does not tell you. Check one order by hand and keep a preparation log . Evidence you keep: your question, grain statement, data dictionary, quality checklist, preparation log, one hand-checked order and a first chart with its filters written down. Before you start, work through the Session 2 lecture and the Session 1 lab , and have your evidence log open. Guided practice ¶ G1 (Core): From request to question ¶ A good analytical question answers four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the course data Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Sales by customer segment "Which customer segment had the highest Sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Your turn Rewrite the head's request as your own one-sentence question, using the four parts. Write it in your evidence log. G2 (Core): Load the data ¶ Run the setup cell first. It downloads the sample from Tableau's website, checks it is exactly the version this course was written for, and prepares the table. In G4 you will open it up and see what each step does. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. GBC Standard Plastic Binding Systems Combs 3.54 2 0.80 -5.49 0 1 0 4 2023-01-01 2 3 US-2023-112326 2023-01-04 2023-01-08 Standard Class PO-19195 Home Office United States Central Office Supplies ... Avery 508 11.78 3 0.20 4.27 0 1 0 4 2023-01-01 3 4 US-2023-112326 2023-01-04 2023-01-08 Standard Class PO-19195 Home Office United States Central Office Supplies ... SAFCO Boltless Steel Shelving 272.74 3 0.20 -64.77 0 1 0 4 2023-01-01 4 5 US-2023-141817 2023-01-05 2023-01-12 Standard Class MB-18085 Consumer United States East Office Supplies ... Avery Hi-Liter EverBold Pen Style Fluorescent ... 19.54 3 0.20 4.88 0 1 0 7 2023-01-01 5 rows × 22 columns G3 (Core): Size, column types and dates ¶ print ( "Rows, columns:" , df . shape ) df . dtypes Rows, columns: (6815, 22) row_id int64 order_id object order_date datetime64[ns] ship_date datetime64[ns] ship_mode object customer_id object segment object country_region object region object category object sub_category object product_id object product_name object sales float64 quantity int64 discount float64 profit float64 returned_order_flag int64 customer_analysis_eligible int64 customer_order_conflict int64 order_to_ship_days int64 order_month datetime64[ns] dtype: object Check the types make sense: order_id , segment , region are text ( object ). sales , profit , discount are decimals ( float64 ); quantity is a whole number. order_date , ship_date , order_month are dates ( datetime64 ). IDs are not amounts row_id is stored as a number, but adding it up means nothing. It is an identifier: a nominal variable, whatever its storage type. Which dates are included? print ( "First order date:" , df [ "order_date" ] . min () . date ()) print ( "Last order date: " , df [ "order_date" ] . max () . date ()) First order date: 2023-01-03 Last order date: 2025-12-31 G4 (Core): What load_orders() does ¶ So far you used load_orders() without looking inside. Now we open it up. You do not need to memorise this code; you need to know what was changed between the original file and df , so you can explain your numbers. The function does seven things: Step What happens Why 1 Reads the Orders and Returns sheets from the Excel file These are the raw tables 2 Finds orders that have more than one Customer ID A known data issue, flagged before filtering 3 Keeps orders placed from 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31 Gives the course a fixed, complete period 4 Renames columns to short lowercase names Easier to type: order_id instead of "Order ID" 5 Adds returned_order_flag Marks orders on the returns list 6 Adds customer_order_conflict and customer_analysis_eligible Marks the customer-ID issue from step 2 7 Adds order_to_ship_days and order_month , then keeps 22 columns sorted by row_id Handy derived columns The cells below repeat each step on its own so you can see the effect. Step 1: Read the raw sheets ¶ SOURCE_FILE is the Excel file the setup cell downloaded. pd.read_excel reads one sheet into a DataFrame. raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) print ( "Raw Orders sheet, rows and columns:" , raw . shape ) print ( "Returns sheet, rows and columns: " , returns . shape ) print ( "Order dates in the raw file:" , raw [ "Order Date" ] . min () . date (), "to" , raw [ "Order Date" ] . max () . date ()) Raw Orders sheet, rows and columns: (10194, 21) Returns sheet, rows and columns: (296, 2) Order dates in the raw file: 2023-01-03 to 2026-12-30 The raw file has more rows than df , and its dates run further. The Returns sheet is just a list of order IDs: returns . head ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Order ID Returned 0 US-2023-100762 Yes 1 US-2023-100867 Yes 2 US-2023-102652 Yes Step 2: Find orders with more than one customer ¶ Every order should belong to one customer. The code counts the different Customer IDs inside each order and keeps the orders where that count is above 1. This is done on the whole raw file , before any filtering, so no conflict is hidden by the date filter. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) conflict_orders {'CA-2025-121465', 'CA-2026-130494'} Step 3: Keep orders placed 2023 to 2025 ¶ The filter keeps rows whose Order Date is on or after 1 January 2023 and before 1 January 2026. It looks at the order date only. in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) print ( "Rows kept: " , in_scope . sum ()) print ( "Rows dropped:" , ( ~ in_scope ) . sum ()) Rows kept: 6815 Rows dropped: 3379 The ship date is not filtered. An order placed late in 2025 may ship in early 2026, and it stays in, because the order date defines the period: print ( "Lines in df that shipped in 2026:" , ( df [ "ship_date" ] >= "2026-01-01" ) . sum ()) Lines in df that shipped in 2026: 34 Step 4: Rename columns ¶ rename swaps the original names (with spaces and capitals) for short names. Four raw columns are not kept at all, because the course does not need them: kept_raw = [ "Row ID" , "Order ID" , "Order Date" , "Ship Date" , "Ship Mode" , "Customer ID" , "Segment" , "Country/Region" , "Region" , "Category" , "Sub-Category" , "Product ID" , "Product Name" , "Sales" , "Quantity" , "Discount" , "Profit" ] [ col for col in raw . columns if col not in kept_raw ] ['Customer Name', 'City', 'State/Province', 'Postal Code'] Step 5: The returns flag ¶ isin asks, for each row, "is this order ID on the returns list?". The answer True / False is turned into 1 / 0 . A three-line order on the list gets a 1 on all three lines . Step 6: The customer-conflict flags ¶ The same isin trick marks every line of a conflicted order with customer_order_conflict = 1 . customer_analysis_eligible is the opposite ( 1 - conflict ). These lines stay in all Sales and order counts; they are left out only when we later analyse individual customers. df . groupby ( "customer_order_conflict" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () customer_order_conflict 0 3387 1 1 Name: order_id, dtype: int64 Compare this with the output of Step 2: not every conflicted order in the raw file was placed inside the course period, so fewer of them appear in df . Step 7: Two derived date columns ¶ order_to_ship_days = ship date minus order date, in whole days. order_month = the first day of the order's month, used to group by month. df [[ "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" ]] . head ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id order_date ship_date order_to_ship_days order_month 0 US-2023-103800 2023-01-03 2023-01-07 4 2023-01-01 1 US-2023-112326 2023-01-04 2023-01-08 4 2023-01-01 2 US-2023-112326 2023-01-04 2023-01-08 4 2023-01-01 Remember The original Excel file is never changed. load_orders() builds a fresh, prepared copy every time you run it, so anyone can repeat your work and get the same table. G5 (Core): Find the grain and count orders ¶ Grain means: what does one row represent? Look at all the rows of one order: df [ df [ "order_id" ] == "US-2023-100762" ][[ "row_id" , "order_id" , "segment" , "category" , "product_id" , "sales" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } row_id order_id segment category product_id sales 1684 1685 US-2023-100762 Corporate Office Supplies OFF-AR-10000380 151.92 1688 1689 US-2023-100762 Corporate Office Supplies OFF-LA-10003930 196.62 1690 1691 US-2023-100762 Corporate Office Supplies OFF-PA-10001815 144.12 1691 1692 US-2023-100762 Corporate Office Supplies OFF-PA-10004082 15.96 Same order_id , different row_id and product: each row is one product line within an order . Predict before you run the next cell: will the number of rows equal the number of orders? print ( "Rows (order lines):" , len ( df )) print ( "Different orders: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Rows (order lines): 6815 Different orders: 3388 Remember len(df) counts rows . df["order_id"].nunique() counts different orders . Use the second one whenever a question is about orders. How many lines do orders usually have? groupby("order_id").size() counts the lines in each order; value_counts() then counts how many orders have 1 line, 2 lines, and so on. lines_per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" ) . size () . value_counts () . sort_index () lines_per_order . plot ( kind = "bar" , title = "How many lines each order has, orders placed 2023–2025" ) plt . xlabel ( "Lines in the order" ) plt . ylabel ( "Number of orders" ) plt . xticks ( rotation = 0 ) plt . show () Many orders have one line, but plenty have several. Be careful with what it does not tell you: It has no return date, quantity or refund amount. A 0 means not on the list . It does not prove the order was never returned. The flag repeats on every line of a listed order. The order you looked at in G5 is on the list. To count orders on the returns list, filter to flag 1 and use nunique() on order_id , as in the second line of the output above. Say "orders on the returns list", not "returned orders" or "return rate": the list tells us membership only. docs.text: The head of a retail business says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups. I need to know where to look first. But before you show me any chart: can I trust these numbers? How many orders did we actually have?" This is not yet a question you can answer with data, and a wrong count at this stage spoils every later chart. Today you turn the request into a question and build trust in the data. About the data We use the Superstore sample published by Tableau. It describes a fictitious company, not a real one. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units : the file does not state a currency, so we never label it as dollars, rupees or anything else.

Write your grain statement Complete this sentence in your log: "One row in df represents one ______ , identified by ______ ." Predict before you run the next cell: will the number of rows equal the number of orders? print ( "Rows (order lines):" , len ( df )) print ( "Different orders: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Rows (order lines): 6815 Different orders: 3388 Remember len(df) counts rows . df["order_id"].nunique() counts different orders . Use the second one whenever a question is about orders. How many lines do orders usually have? groupby("order_id").size() counts the lines in each order; value_counts() then counts how many orders have 1 line, 2 lines, and so on. lines_per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" ) . size () . value_counts () . sort_index () lines_per_order . plot ( kind = "bar" , title = "How many lines each order has, orders placed 2023–2025" ) plt . xlabel ( "Lines in the order" ) plt . ylabel ( "Number of orders" ) plt . xticks ( rotation = 0 ) plt . show () Many orders have one line, but plenty have several. That is why len(df) overstates the number of orders.

docs.text: returned_order_flag is 1 when an order is on the source's returns list . Be careful with what it does not tell you: It has no return date, quantity or refund amount. A 0 means not on the list . It does not prove the order was never returned. The flag repeats on every line of a listed order. The order you looked at in G5 is on the list. See how the flag repeats: df [ df [ "order_id" ] == "US-2023-100762" ][[ "row_id" , "order_id" , "returned_order_flag" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } row_id order_id returned_order_flag 1684 1685 US-2023-100762 1 1688 1689 US-2023-100762 1 1690 1691 US-2023-100762 1 1691 1692 US-2023-100762 1 Now compare two ways of counting: flagged = df [ df [ "returned_order_flag" ] == 1 ] print ( "Sum of the flag (counts LINES): " , df [ "returned_order_flag" ] . sum ()) print ( "Distinct orders on the returns list: " , flagged [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Sum of the flag (counts LINES): 511 Distinct orders on the returns list: 191 A common mistake Adding up returned_order_flag counts lines of listed orders, not orders. To count orders on the returns list, filter to flag 1 and use nunique() on order_id , as in the second line of the output above. Say "orders on the returns list", not "returned orders" or "return rate": the list tells us membership only.

In this table every order has exactly one segment, so the segment counts add up to the overall total. One order can contain products from several categories . That order is counted once in each category it touches, so the category counts add up to more than the overall total. Distinct counts do not always add up Sales and Profit can be added across groups. Distinct order counts can only be added when every order belongs to exactly one group. Always recount distinct orders at the level you display. Session 2 lecture: Data, grain and the DataFrame ¶ Before you add anything up, know what kind of data each column holds, what one row stands for, and whether the table can be trusted. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Start by answering the quiz at the end of the Session 1 lecture, 01_why_data_analytics_lecture.md . Write your answers down before the discussion. What you will be able to explain ¶ The four levels of measurement and which calculations make sense for each. What makes a table tidy . The grain of a table, and the job of primary and foreign keys . What a data dictionary records and why every analysis needs one. Five data-quality dimensions and a pandas check for each. Part Topic 1 Levels of measurement 2 Tidy data 3 Grain and keys 4 Data dictionaries 5 Data-quality dimensions 6 Worked case: the Superstore order lines How to use this notebook When you see Predict, then reveal , write your guess first and only then run the cell. Being wrong on paper is the fastest way to learn. Run the setup cell first. It prepares pandas, the chart style and the retail table used in Part 6. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. Part 1: Levels of measurement ¶ Not every number is a quantity. A postcode, a shirt size and a temperature are all written with digits or ordered labels, yet you cannot treat them the same way. Statisticians sort variables into four levels of measurement . Each level allows everything the level above it allows, plus something new. Level What the values do Examples What makes sense Nominal Name a group; no order Segment, region, product ID, postcode Count, share, mode Ordinal Name a group in order ; gaps not equal Shirt size, satisfaction 1–5, ship class + median, percentiles, "higher than" Interval Ordered with equal gaps , but zero is arbitrary Temperature in °C, calendar dates + differences, mean Ratio Equal gaps and a true zero Sales, quantity, days to ship, age + ratios: "twice as much" Nominal and ordinal variables are categorical . Interval and ratio variables are numeric (quantitative). Predict, then reveal: is 20 °C twice as hot as 10 °C? ¶ Write down yes or no , then run the cell. It converts both temperatures to Fahrenheit and compares the ratios. celsius = pd . Series ([ 10 , 20 ], index = [ "cool day" , "warm day" ]) fahrenheit = celsius * 9 / 5 + 32 print ( "Ratio in Celsius: " , celsius [ "warm day" ] / celsius [ "cool day" ]) print ( "Ratio in Fahrenheit:" , round ( fahrenheit [ "warm day" ] / fahrenheit [ "cool day" ], 2 )) print ( "Difference in Celsius:" , celsius [ "warm day" ] - celsius [ "cool day" ], "degrees" ) Ratio in Celsius: 2.0 Ratio in Fahrenheit: 1.36 Difference in Celsius: 10 degrees The ratio changes when the unit changes, because 0 °C is not "no temperature". So ratios on an interval scale mean nothing. The difference is meaningful in either unit. Sales is different: 0 really means no sales, so "Region A sold twice as much as Region B" stays true whatever the currency. That is a ratio scale. Predict, then reveal: numbers that are not quantities ¶ The table below is made up. pandas sees three numeric columns. Which of the three averages printed by the next cell actually mean something? survey = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" , "C4" , "C5" , "C6" ], "postcode" : [ 44600 , 44700 , 44600 , 33700 , 44600 , 44800 ], "satisfaction_1_to_5" : [ 5 , 4 , 5 , 1 , 4 , 2 ], "orders_last_year" : [ 3 , 1 , 6 , 2 , 0 , 4 ], }) print ( survey . dtypes , end = " 

 " ) survey [[ "postcode" , "satisfaction_1_to_5" , "orders_last_year" ]] . mean () customer object postcode int64 satisfaction_1_to_5 int64 orders_last_year int64 dtype: object postcode 42,833.33 satisfaction_1_to_5 3.50 orders_last_year 2.67 dtype: float64 Postcode is nominal. The average postcode is not a place. Satisfaction is ordinal. The gap between 1 and 2 need not equal the gap between 4 and 5, so the mean is risky. The median and the share of 4s and 5s are safer. Orders last year is ratio. Its mean is meaningful. The right summaries for the first two: print ( "Most common postcode:" , survey [ "postcode" ] . mode ()[ 0 ]) print ( "Median satisfaction: " , survey [ "satisfaction_1_to_5" ] . median ()) print ( "Share scoring 4 or 5:" , ( survey [ "satisfaction_1_to_5" ] >= 4 ) . mean ()) Most common postcode: 44600 Median satisfaction: 4.0 Share scoring 4 or 5: 0.6666666666666666 Telling pandas about order ¶ An ordinal column stored as text sorts alphabetically, which is wrong. An ordered categorical keeps the real order. sizes = pd . Series ([ "M" , "S" , "XL" , "L" , "S" , "M" ]) print ( "Alphabetical:" , sorted ( sizes . unique ())) sizes = pd . Categorical ( sizes , categories = [ "S" , "M" , "L" , "XL" ], ordered = True ) print ( "Real order: " , list ( sizes . categories )) print ( "Largest size:" , sizes . max ()) Alphabetical: ['L', 'M', 'S', 'XL'] Real order: ['S', 'M', 'L', 'XL'] Largest size: XL Check your understanding 1 Classify each Superstore column as nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio: segment , ship_mode , order_date , sales , quantity , order_to_ship_days , row_id . For one of them, explain why someone could reasonably argue for two levels. Remember The data type pandas shows ( int64 , object ) is about storage . The level of measurement is about meaning . An ID stored as a number is still nominal. Part 2: Tidy data ¶ A table is tidy when: Each variable is a column. Each observation is a row. Each value is a single cell. Spreadsheets for people are often not tidy: months spread across columns look good on a page but are awkward to filter, group and chart. wide = pd . DataFrame ({ "region" : [ "North" , "South" , "East" ], "Jan" : [ 120 , 95 , 80 ], "Feb" : [ 130 , 90 , 85 ], "Mar" : [ 150 , 110 , 70 ], }) wide .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } region Jan Feb Mar 0 North 120 130 150 1 South 95 90 110 2 East 80 85 70 Predict, then reveal ¶ The table has 3 rows and 3 month columns. After reshaping to one row per region and month , how many rows will there be? melt turns column names into values of a new column. tidy = wide . melt ( id_vars = "region" , var_name = "month" , value_name = "sales" ) print ( "Rows after melt:" , len ( tidy )) tidy Rows after melt: 9 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } region month sales 0 North Jan 120 1 South Jan 95 2 East Jan 80 3 North Feb 130 4 South Feb 90 5 East Feb 85 6 North Mar 150 7 South Mar 110 8 East Mar 70 Now "sales for March" is a filter and "sales by region" is a groupby , both one line of code: print ( tidy [ tidy [ "month" ] == "Mar" ]) print () print ( tidy . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum ()) region month sales 6 North Mar 150 7 South Mar 110 8 East Mar 70 region East 235 North 400 South 295 Name: sales, dtype: int64 The opposite move, long to wide, is pivot . Use wide tables for reading , tidy tables for analysing . A second untidy pattern: two values in one cell. messy = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "segment_region" : [ "Consumer/West" , "Corporate/East" , "Consumer/East" ]}) messy [[ "segment" , "region" ]] = messy [ "segment_region" ] . str . split ( "/" , expand = True ) messy .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer segment_region segment region 0 C1 Consumer/West Consumer West 1 C2 Corporate/East Corporate East 2 C3 Consumer/East Consumer East Check your understanding 2 A finance file has one row per department and a column for each of the 12 months' budgets, plus 12 columns for actual spend. Which tidy rule does it break? Sketch the column names of a tidy version. Part 3: Grain and keys ¶ The grain of a table is what one row represents: one order, one product within an order, one customer per month, one employee per day. Grain decides what simple counting means. If a row is a product within an order, then counting rows counts order lines , not orders. Two kinds of key make grain explicit: Key Meaning Check Primary key Column(s) that identify each row uniquely; never missing No duplicates, no blanks Foreign key Column that points to the primary key of another table Every value exists in that other table Here is a tiny made-up shop with three tables at three different grains. customers = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer_id" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "segment" : [ "Consumer" , "Corporate" , "Consumer" ]}) orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "O1" , "O2" , "O3" , "O4" ], "customer_id" : [ "C1" , "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "shipping_fee" : [ 5 , 5 , 10 , 5 ]}) order_lines = pd . DataFrame ({ "line_id" : [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ], "order_id" : [ "O1" , "O1" , "O2" , "O3" , "O3" , "O3" , "O4" ], "product" : [ "Pen" , "Desk" , "Chair" , "Pen" , "Lamp" , "Paper" , "Desk" ], "sales" : [ 4 , 200 , 150 , 4 , 30 , 8 , 220 ]}) order_lines .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product sales 0 1 O1 Pen 4 1 2 O1 Desk 200 2 3 O2 Chair 150 3 4 O3 Pen 4 4 5 O3 Lamp 30 5 6 O3 Paper 8 6 7 O4 Desk 220 Grain of each table: customers : one customer, primary key customer_id . orders : one order, primary key order_id ; customer_id is a foreign key. order_lines : one product within an order, primary key line_id ; order_id is a foreign key. Check the keys with code: print ( "line_id unique in order_lines? " , order_lines [ "line_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique in order_lines?" , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique in orders? " , orders [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "Every line's order exists? " , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . isin ( orders [ "order_id" ]) . all ()) print () print ( "Rows in order_lines:" , len ( order_lines )) print ( "Different orders: " , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) line_id unique in order_lines? True order_id unique in order_lines? False order_id unique in orders? True Every line's order exists? True Rows in order_lines: 7 Different orders: 4 Predict, then reveal: the shipping fee trap ¶ We want total shipping fees. The fee lives in orders (one per order). A colleague joins it onto the order lines and adds it up. Look at the orders table above and work out the true total fee by hand. Will the colleague's number be the same? joined = order_lines . merge ( orders , on = "order_id" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" ) print ( "True total fee (orders table): " , orders [ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) print ( "Colleague's total (after the join):" , joined [ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) joined [[ "line_id" , "order_id" , "product" , "shipping_fee" ]] True total fee (orders table): 25 Colleague's total (after the join): 50 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product shipping_fee 0 1 O1 Pen 5 1 2 O1 Desk 5 2 3 O2 Chair 5 3 4 O3 Pen 10 4 5 O3 Lamp 10 5 6 O3 Paper 10 6 7 O4 Desk 5 After the join, each order's fee appears on every line of that order, so summing it counts the fee once per line. The join changed the grain of the fee. Two habits prevent this: Before adding up a column, ask: at what grain is this value recorded? Use validate= in merge to state the relationship you expect ( "one_to_one" , "many_to_one" , "one_to_many" ). pandas raises an error if the keys break it. The correct total, taken back at the order grain: print ( "Fee, one per order:" , joined . drop_duplicates ( "order_id" )[ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) Fee, one per order: 25 Check your understanding 3 A table has one row per employee per month. What is its primary key? If you sum headcount = 1 over the whole year, what have you counted? Part 4: Data dictionaries ¶ A data dictionary describes every column so that anyone can use the table correctly without asking you. Field Example for sales Name sales Meaning Sales reported for the order line Type (storage) float64 Level of measurement Ratio Unit Source monetary units; currency not stated Allowed values Zero or more Can you add it up? Yes, across lines and groups Source and changes Orders sheet, column "Sales"; not changed pandas can fill in the mechanical fields for you. The human fields (meaning, unit, "can you add it up?") need your judgement. def profile_columns ( data ): """One row per column: storage type, missing values, distinct values and an example.""" return pd . DataFrame ({ "dtype" : data . dtypes . astype ( str ), "missing" : data . isna () . sum (), "distinct" : data . nunique (), "example" : data . iloc [ 0 ], }) profile_columns ( order_lines ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dtype missing distinct example line_id int64 0 7 1 order_id object 0 4 O1 product object 0 5 Pen sales int64 0 6 4 Check your understanding 4 profile_columns says line_id is int64 with as many distinct values as rows. Which human fields of the dictionary would you add for it, and what would you write under "Can you add it up?" Part 5: Data-quality dimensions ¶ "Is the data good?" is too vague to check. Break it into dimensions , each with a test you can run. Dimension Question Example pandas check Completeness Are values missing that should be present? df.isna().sum() Validity Do values follow the rules (type, range, allowed list)? (df["quantity"] > 0).all() Consistency Do related values agree, within and across tables? Ship date not before order date Uniqueness Is each real-world thing recorded once? df["id"].is_unique , df.duplicated() Timeliness Is the data recent enough, and is the period complete? df["date"].max() versus the reporting date Here is a small made-up extract with a problem planted in each dimension. Read it first and try to spot them. extract = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "A1" , "A2" , "A3" , "A3" , "A5" , "A6" ], "region" : [ "West" , "west" , "East" , "East" , None , "South" ], "order_date" : pd . to_datetime ([ "2025-03-01" , "2025-03-02" , "2025-03-02" , "2025-03-02" , "2025-03-04" , "2025-03-05" ]), "ship_date" : pd . to_datetime ([ "2025-03-03" , "2025-03-01" , "2025-03-05" , "2025-03-05" , "2025-03-06" , "2025-03-07" ]), "quantity" : [ 2 , 1 , 3 , 3 , - 4 , 1 ], }) extract .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id region order_date ship_date quantity 0 A1 West 2025-03-01 2025-03-03 2 1 A2 west 2025-03-02 2025-03-01 1 2 A3 East 2025-03-02 2025-03-05 3 3 A3 East 2025-03-02 2025-03-05 3 4 A5 None 2025-03-04 2025-03-06 -4 5 A6 South 2025-03-05 2025-03-07 1 print ( "Completeness: missing values per column" ) print ( extract . isna () . sum (), end = "

Timestamp ( "2025-03-31" ) print ( "Timeliness: last order" , extract [ "order_date" ] . max () . date (), "| days before the reporting date:" , ( reporting_date - extract [ "order_date" ] . max ()) . days ) Completeness: missing values per column order_id 0 region 1 order_date 0 ship_date 0 quantity 0 dtype: int64 Validity: rows with quantity not above zero order_id region order_date ship_date quantity 4 A5 None 2025-03-04 2025-03-06 -4 Consistency (labels): region spellings -> ['East', 'South', 'West', 'west'] Consistency (dates): rows shipped before they were ordered order_id region order_date ship_date quantity 1 A2 west 2025-03-02 2025-03-01 1 Uniqueness: is order_id unique? For each one, decide and record whether to fix, flag, exclude or keep, and why. Session 3 is about those decisions.
