Part 6: Worked case — the Superstore order lines ¶ Now apply every idea to the course data. The question from the business: "How many orders did we have, and can I trust the number?" Step 1: Load and profile ¶ df = load_orders () print ( "Rows, columns:" , df . shape ) profile_columns ( df ) Rows, columns: (6815, 22) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dtype missing distinct example row_id int64 0 6815 1 order_id object 0 3388 US-2023-103800 order_date datetime64[ns] 0 918 2023-01-03 00:00:00 ship_date datetime64[ns] 0 989 2023-01-07 00:00:00 ship_mode object 0 4 Standard Class customer_id object 0 793 DP-13000 segment object 0 3 Consumer country_region object 0 2 United States region object 0 4 Central category object 0 3 Office Supplies sub_category object 0 17 Paper product_id object 0 1803 OFF-PA-10000174 product_name object 0 1794 Message Book, Wirebound, Four 5 1/2" X 4" Form... sales float64 0 4640 16.45 quantity int64 0 14 2 discount float64 0 12 0.20 profit float64 0 5471 5.55 returned_order_flag int64 0 2 0 customer_analysis_eligible int64 0 2 1 customer_order_conflict int64 0 2 0 order_to_ship_days int64 0 9 4 order_month datetime64[ns] 0 36 2023-01-01 00:00:00 Step 2: Predict, then reveal — what is the grain? ¶ Is the primary key order_id or row_id ? Predict, then check both. print ( "row_id unique? " , df [ "row_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique?" , df [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print () print ( "Rows (order lines):" , len ( df )) print ( "Different orders: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) row_id unique? True order_id unique? False Rows (order lines): 6815 Different orders: 3388 row_id is unique and order_id repeats: one row is one product line within an order , identified by row_id . order_id behaves like a foreign key to an (invisible) orders table. So the answer to "how many orders?" is nunique() on order_id , never len(df) . Step 3: Which attributes belong to the order, and which to the line? ¶ If a column is an attribute of the order , it should take exactly one value within each order. The next cell counts, for each column, the largest number of different values found inside one order. columns_to_test = [ "order_date" , "ship_mode" , "segment" , "region" , "category" , "product_id" , "sales" ] values_per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ columns_to_test ] . nunique () . max () values_per_order . rename ( "max distinct values within one order" ) order_date 1 ship_mode 1 segment 1 region 1 category 3 product_id 11 sales 11 Name: max distinct values within one order, dtype: int64 Where the maximum is 1, the column is recorded at order grain (repeated on every line). Where it is above 1, it is recorded at line grain . This matters for counting. Distinct orders add up across groups of an order-grain column, but not across groups of a line-grain column: for column in [ "segment" , "category" ]: orders_per_group = df . groupby ( column )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () print ( f " { column : 9s } : group order counts add up to { orders_per_group . sum () } " f " | overall distinct orders { df [ 'order_id' ] . nunique () } " ) segment : group order counts add up to 3388 | overall distinct orders 3388 category : group order counts add up to 4779 | overall distinct orders 3388 Step 4: Five quality dimensions in one cell ¶ print ( "Completeness | missing values:" , df . isna () . sum () . sum ()) print ( "Validity | quantity always above zero:" , ( df [ "quantity" ] > 0 ) . all (), "| sales never negative:" , ( df [ "sales" ] >= 0 ) . all ()) print ( "Consistency | ship date never before order date:" , ( df [ "ship_date" ] >= df [ "order_date" ]) . all ()) print ( "Uniqueness | row_id unique:" , df [ "row_id" ] . is_unique , "| fully duplicated rows:" , df . duplicated () . sum ()) print ( "Timeliness | order dates from" , df [ "order_date" ] . min () . date (), "to" , df [ "order_date" ] . max () . date (), "| months present:" , df [ "order_month" ] . nunique ()) Completeness | missing values: 0 Validity | quantity always above zero: True | sales never negative: True Consistency | ship date never before order date: True Uniqueness | row_id unique: True | fully duplicated rows: 0 Timeliness | order dates from 2023-01-03 to 2025-12-31 | months present: 36 Read the output line by line. Each line is one entry for a quality checklist, with its evidence. One known consistency issue A few orders in the raw file carry more than one customer ID. The setup cell flags them in customer_order_conflict . They stay in all order and Sales counts; they are excluded only when analysing individual customers. You will explore this in the lab. Summary ¶ Idea One-line takeaway Levels of measurement Nominal → ordinal → interval → ratio; only ratio data supports "twice as much" Tidy data One variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell Grain Say what one row is before you count anything Keys Primary key unique and complete; foreign keys point to another table; validate= guards joins Data dictionary Meaning, type, level, unit, rules, additivity and source for each column Quality dimensions Completeness, validity, consistency, uniqueness, timeliness, each with a check and a decision Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the next lecture. Write short answers. Give one example each of a nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio variable from a business you know. Why is "the average satisfaction score rose from 3.9 to 4.1" weaker evidence than "the share of customers scoring 4 or 5 rose from 62% to 70%"? A table lists one row per store with columns sales_2024 and sales_2025 . Is it tidy? What would the tidy version look like? In the Superstore table, why does len(df) not answer "how many orders?" What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key? A delivery fee recorded once per order is joined onto order lines and summed. What goes wrong, and how do you avoid it? Name the quality dimension each check belongs to: (a) no ship date before its order date, (b) row_id has no duplicates, (c) no blank region , (d) last order date is close to today. Why are distinct order counts by category not additive, while those by segment are? Lab briefing ¶ In the Session 2 lab you will turn a vague request into a question, take the Superstore table apart, write its grain statement and data dictionary, run a five-dimension quality checklist, hand-check one order and fix a colleague's counting mistakes. docs.text: Not every number is a quantity. A postcode, a shirt size and a temperature are all written with digits or ordered labels, yet you cannot treat them the same way. Statisticians sort variables into four levels of measurement . Each level allows everything the level above it allows, plus something new. Level What the values do Examples What makes sense Nominal Name a group; no order Segment, region, product ID, postcode Count, share, mode Ordinal Name a group in order ; gaps not equal Shirt size, satisfaction 1–5, ship class + median, percentiles, "higher than" Interval Ordered with equal gaps , but zero is arbitrary Temperature in °C, calendar dates + differences, mean Ratio Equal gaps and a true zero Sales, quantity, days to ship, age + ratios: "twice as much" Nominal and ordinal variables are categorical . Interval and ratio variables are numeric (quantitative).
docs.title: Part 1: Levels of measurement

docs.text: Write down yes or no , then run the cell. It converts both temperatures to Fahrenheit and compares the ratios. celsius = pd . Series ([ 10 , 20 ], index = [ "cool day" , "warm day" ]) fahrenheit = celsius * 9 / 5 + 32 print ( "Ratio in Celsius: " , celsius [ "warm day" ] / celsius [ "cool day" ]) print ( "Ratio in Fahrenheit:" , round ( fahrenheit [ "warm day" ] / fahrenheit [ "cool day" ], 2 )) print ( "Difference in Celsius:" , celsius [ "warm day" ] - celsius [ "cool day" ], "degrees" ) Ratio in Celsius: 2.0 Ratio in Fahrenheit: 1.36 Difference in Celsius: 10 degrees The ratio changes when the unit changes, because 0 °C is not "no temperature". So ratios on an interval scale mean nothing. The difference is meaningful in either unit. Sales is different: 0 really means no sales, so "Region A sold twice as much as Region B" stays true whatever the currency. That is a ratio scale.

docs.text: The table below is made up. pandas sees three numeric columns. Which of the three averages printed by the next cell actually mean something? survey = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" , "C4" , "C5" , "C6" ], "postcode" : [ 44600 , 44700 , 44600 , 33700 , 44600 , 44800 ], "satisfaction_1_to_5" : [ 5 , 4 , 5 , 1 , 4 , 2 ], "orders_last_year" : [ 3 , 1 , 6 , 2 , 0 , 4 ], }) print ( survey . dtypes , end = " \n\n " ) survey [[ "postcode" , "satisfaction_1_to_5" , "orders_last_year" ]] . mean () customer object postcode int64 satisfaction_1_to_5 int64 orders_last_year int64 dtype: object postcode 42,833.33 satisfaction_1_to_5 3.50 orders_last_year 2.67 dtype: float64 Postcode is nominal. The average postcode is not a place. Satisfaction is ordinal. The gap between 1 and 2 need not equal the gap between 4 and 5, so the mean is risky. The median and the share of 4s and 5s are safer. Orders last year is ratio. Its mean is meaningful. The right summaries for the first two: print ( "Most common postcode:" , survey [ "postcode" ] . mode ()[ 0 ]) print ( "Median satisfaction: " , survey [ "satisfaction_1_to_5" ] . median ()) print ( "Share scoring 4 or 5:" , ( survey [ "satisfaction_1_to_5" ] >= 4 ) . mean ()) Most common postcode: 44600 Median satisfaction: 4.0 Share scoring 4 or 5: 0.6666666666666666

docs.text: A table is tidy when: Each variable is a column. Each observation is a row. Each value is a single cell. Spreadsheets for people are often not tidy: months spread across columns look good on a page but are awkward to filter, group and chart. wide = pd . DataFrame ({ "region" : [ "North" , "South" , "East" ], "Jan" : [ 120 , 95 , 80 ], "Feb" : [ 130 , 90 , 85 ], "Mar" : [ 150 , 110 , 70 ], }) wide .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } region Jan Feb Mar 0 North 120 130 150 1 South 95 90 110 2 East 80 85 70

After reshaping to one row per region and month , how many rows will there be? melt turns column names into values of a new column. tidy = wide . melt ( id_vars = "region" , var_name = "month" , value_name = "sales" ) print ( "Rows after melt:" , len ( tidy )) tidy Rows after melt: 9 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } region month sales 0 North Jan 120 1 South Jan 95 2 East Jan 80 3 North Feb 130 4 South Feb 90 5 East Feb 85 6 North Mar 150 7 South Mar 110 8 East Mar 70 Now "sales for March" is a filter and "sales by region" is a groupby , both one line of code: print ( tidy [ tidy [ "month" ] == "Mar" ]) print () print ( tidy . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum ()) region month sales 6 North Mar 150 7 South Mar 110 8 East Mar 70 region East 235 North 400 South 295 Name: sales, dtype: int64 The opposite move, long to wide, is pivot . Use wide tables for reading , tidy tables for analysing . A second untidy pattern: two values in one cell. messy = pd . docs.text: The grain of a table is what one row represents: one order, one product within an order, one customer per month, one employee per day. Grain decides what simple counting means. If a row is a product within an order, then counting rows counts order lines , not orders. Two kinds of key make grain explicit: Key Meaning Check Primary key Column(s) that identify each row uniquely; never missing No duplicates, no blanks Foreign key Column that points to the primary key of another table Every value exists in that other table Here is a tiny made-up shop with three tables at three different grains. customers = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer_id" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "segment" : [ "Consumer" , "Corporate" , "Consumer" ]}) orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "O1" , "O2" , "O3" , "O4" ], "customer_id" : [ "C1" , "C1" , "C2" , "C3" ], "shipping_fee" : [ 5 , 5 , 10 , 5 ]}) order_lines = pd . DataFrame ({ "line_id" : [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ], "order_id" : [ "O1" , "O1" , "O2" , "O3" , "O3" , "O3" , "O4" ], "product" : [ "Pen" , "Desk" , "Chair" , "Pen" , "Lamp" , "Paper" , "Desk" ], "sales" : [ 4 , 200 , 150 , 4 , 30 , 8 , 220 ]}) order_lines .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product sales 0 1 O1 Pen 4 1 2 O1 Desk 200 2 3 O2 Chair 150 3 4 O3 Pen 4 4 5 O3 Lamp 30 5 6 O3 Paper 8 6 7 O4 Desk 220 Grain of each table: customers : one customer, primary key customer_id . orders : one order, primary key order_id ; customer_id is a foreign key. order_lines : one product within an order, primary key line_id ; order_id is a foreign key. Check the keys with code: print ( "line_id unique in order_lines? " , order_lines [ "line_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique in order_lines?" , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique in orders? " , orders [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "Every line's order exists? " , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . isin ( orders [ "order_id" ]) . all ()) print () print ( "Rows in order_lines:" , len ( order_lines )) print ( "Different orders: " , order_lines [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) line_id unique in order_lines? True order_id unique in order_lines? False order_id unique in orders? True Every line's order exists? True Rows in order_lines: 7 Different orders: 4

docs.text: We want total shipping fees. The fee lives in orders (one per order). A colleague joins it onto the order lines and adds it up. Look at the orders table above and work out the true total fee by hand. Will the colleague's number be the same? joined = order_lines . merge ( orders , on = "order_id" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" ) print ( "True total fee (orders table): " , orders [ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) print ( "Colleague's total (after the join):" , joined [ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) joined [[ "line_id" , "order_id" , "product" , "shipping_fee" ]] True total fee (orders table): 25 Colleague's total (after the join): 50 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product shipping_fee 0 1 O1 Pen 5 1 2 O1 Desk 5 2 3 O2 Chair 5 3 4 O3 Pen 10 4 5 O3 Lamp 10 5 6 O3 Paper 10 6 7 O4 Desk 5 After the join, each order's fee appears on every line of that order, so summing it counts the fee once per line. The join changed the grain of the fee. Two habits prevent this: Before adding up a column, ask: at what grain is this value recorded? Use validate= in merge to state the relationship you expect ( "one_to_one" , "many_to_one" , "one_to_many" ). pandas raises an error if the keys break it. The correct total, taken back at the order grain: print ( "Fee, one per order:" , joined . drop_duplicates ( "order_id" )[ "shipping_fee" ] . sum ()) Fee, one per order: 25 Check your understanding 3 A table has one row per employee per month. What is its primary key? If you sum headcount = 1 over the whole year, what have you counted?

docs.text: A data dictionary describes every column so that anyone can use the table correctly without asking you. Field Example for sales Name sales Meaning Sales reported for the order line Type (storage) float64 Level of measurement Ratio Unit Source monetary units; currency not stated Allowed values Zero or more Can you add it up? Yes, across lines and groups Source and changes Orders sheet, column "Sales"; not changed pandas can fill in the mechanical fields for you. The human fields (meaning, unit, "can you add it up?") need your judgement. def profile_columns ( data ): """One row per column: storage type, missing values, distinct values and an example.""" return pd . DataFrame ({ "dtype" : data . dtypes . astype ( str ), "missing" : data . isna () . sum (), "distinct" : data . nunique (), "example" : data . iloc [ 0 ], }) profile_columns ( order_lines ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dtype missing distinct example line_id int64 0 7 1 order_id object 0 4 O1 product object 0 5 Pen sales int64 0 6 4 Check your understanding 4 profile_columns says line_id is int64 with as many distinct values as rows. Which human fields of the dictionary would you add for it, and what would you write under "Can you add it up?"

docs.text:
"Is the data good?" is too vague to check. Break it into dimensions , each with a test you can run. Dimension Question Example pandas check Completeness Are values missing that should be present? df.isna().sum() Validity Do values follow the rules (type, range, allowed list)? (df["quantity"] > 0).all() Consistency Do related values agree, within and across tables? Ship date not before order date Uniqueness Is each real-world thing recorded once? df["id"].is_unique , df.duplicated() Timeliness Is the data recent enough, and is the period complete? df["date"].max() versus the reporting date Here is a small made-up extract with a problem planted in each dimension. docs.text: Is the primary key order_id or row_id ? Predict, then check both. print ( "row_id unique? " , df [ "row_id" ] . is_unique ) print ( "order_id unique?" , df [ "order_id" ] . is_unique ) print () print ( "Rows (order lines):" , len ( df )) print ( "Different orders: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) row_id unique? True order_id unique? False Rows (order lines): 6815 Different orders: 3388 row_id is unique and order_id repeats: one row is one product line within an order , identified by row_id . order_id behaves like a foreign key to an (invisible) orders table. docs.text: If a column is an attribute of the order , it should take exactly one value within each order. The next cell counts, for each column, the largest number of different values found inside one order. columns_to_test = [ "order_date" , "ship_mode" , "segment" , "region" , "category" , "product_id" , "sales" ] values_per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ columns_to_test ] . nunique () . max () values_per_order . rename ( "max distinct values within one order" ) order_date 1 ship_mode 1 segment 1 region 1 category 3 product_id 11 sales 11 Name: max distinct values within one order, dtype: int64 Where the maximum is 1, the column is recorded at order grain (repeated on every line). Where it is above 1, it is recorded at line grain . This matters for counting. Distinct orders add up across groups of an order-grain column, but not across groups of a line-grain column: for column in [ "segment" , "category" ]: orders_per_group = df . groupby ( column )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () print ( f " { column : 9s } : group order counts add up to { orders_per_group . sum () } " f " | overall distinct orders { df [ 'order_id' ] . nunique () } " ) segment : group order counts add up to 3388 | overall distinct orders 3388 category : group order counts add up to 4779 | overall distinct orders 3388

docs.text: Idea One-line takeaway Levels of measurement Nominal → ordinal → interval → ratio; only ratio data supports "twice as much" Tidy data One variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell Grain Say what one row is before you count anything Keys Primary key unique and complete; foreign keys point to another table; validate= guards joins Data dictionary Meaning, type, level, unit, rules, additivity and source for each column Quality dimensions Completeness, validity, consistency, uniqueness, timeliness, each with a check and a decision

docs.text: Answer these at the start of the next lecture. Write short answers. Give one example each of a nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio variable from a business you know. Why is "the average satisfaction score rose from 3.9 to 4.1" weaker evidence than "the share of customers scoring 4 or 5 rose from 62% to 70%"? A table lists one row per store with columns sales_2024 and sales_2025 . Is it tidy? What would the tidy version look like? In the Superstore table, why does len(df) not answer "how many orders?" What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key? A delivery fee recorded once per order is joined onto order lines and summed. What goes wrong, and how do you avoid it? Name the quality dimension each check belongs to: (a) no ship date before its order date, (b) row_id has no duplicates, (c) no blank region , (d) last order date is close to today. Why are distinct order counts by category not additive, while those by segment are?

docs.text: In the Session 2 lab you will turn a vague request into a question, take the Superstore table apart, write its grain statement and data dictionary, run a five-dimension quality checklist, hand-check one order and fix a colleague's counting mistakes. Evidence to keep: your question, grain statement, data dictionary, quality checklist, preparation log and one hand-checked order.

docs.text: Session 3 lab: Clean it, check it, log it ¶ Three files from three sources, each with its own problems: repeated football matches, a usage file with most of its dates missing, and a retail workbook whose sheets must be joined without losing or doubling anything. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ The head of analytics says: "We have been handed three files for next quarter's reports. Before anyone builds a chart on them: what is wrong with each one, what did you fix, and can I see the proof?" Your job today is not to find insights. It is to make each file fit for use , show the evidence, and say clearly what still cannot be trusted. About the data World Cup results : compiled for Sports Viz Sundays 2018 and published in Tableau's sample-data catalog. We download it from that source for learning; we do not redistribute it, and the course does not claim a licence for it. Mobile OS usage : from Statcounter Global Stats (licence CC BY-SA 3.0), via Tableau's sample-data catalog. Each percentage is a share of page views on the websites Statcounter tracks, not a share of devices sold or of people. Superstore : Tableau's sample for a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units; no currency is stated. How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G5 Independent tasks Same skills, new questions, on your own or in pairs I1–I6 Challenge Harder reasoning and debugging C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Profile a new file: size, types, missing values and duplicates. Find exact duplicates and confirm the fix against an independent total. Detect stray spaces, broken characters and inconsistent names. Diagnose missing dates and choose a subset you can defend. Join three tables with validate= , indicator=True and row-count checks. Keep a cleaning log with before and after counts. Evidence you keep: your cleaning log, the duplicate check against official totals, your Mobile OS decision with its reason, the Superstore join checks and your fix for the debugging challenge. Before you start, work through the Session 3 lecture . Guided practice ¶ G1 (Core): Load the three files ¶ The first cell is the course setup cell you know from Session 2: it downloads the Superstore workbook and checks it. The second cell defines fetch , which downloads a file into memory and checks its fingerprint, and then loads the other two files. Nothing is saved over the originals: every change today happens to a copy in Python. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. import hashlib import io def fetch ( url , expected_sha256 ): """Download a file into memory and check its SHA-256 fingerprint.""" with urllib . request . urlopen ( url ) as response : data = response . read () if hashlib . sha256 ( data ) . hexdigest () != expected_sha256 : print ( "WARNING: this file has changed since the course was written:" , url ) print ( "Your numbers may differ from the lab. Ask your facilitator." ) return data world_cup_bytes = fetch ( "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/world_cup_results.xlsx" , "dbad641c16c914c14fef0c95bf6f918fa5d2746671e4dc269b6a1ec3e2a3cc45" , ) mobile_bytes = fetch ( "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/mobile_os_usage.csv" , "0db44110e84a31c06491af89a30949cd8ced1c42fac56488cb04ca4f9e449995" , ) matches_raw = pd . read_excel ( io . BytesIO ( world_cup_bytes ), sheet_name = "WorldCupMatches" ) cups = pd . read_excel ( io . BytesIO ( world_cup_bytes ), sheet_name = "WorldCups" ) mobile_raw = pd . read_csv ( io . BytesIO ( mobile_bytes )) print ( "World Cup matches:" , matches_raw . shape ) print ( "World Cup tournaments:" , cups . shape ) print ( "Mobile OS usage:" , mobile_raw . shape ) World Cup matches: (852, 12) World Cup tournaments: (20, 10) Mobile OS usage: (1898, 3) Start the cleaning log now. Every step you take today adds one row to it. cleaning_log = [] def log_step ( dataset , change , why , before , after ): """Add one row to the cleaning log.""" cleaning_log . append ({ "dataset" : dataset , "change" : change , "why" : why , "rows_before" : before , "rows_after" : after }) print ( "Cleaning log ready." ) Cleaning log ready. G2 (Core): Profile the match results ¶ Before fixing anything, look. What does one row represent, what types are the columns, and is anything missing? matches_raw . head () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Year Date Time Round Stadium City Country HomeTeam HomeGoals AwayGoals AwayTeam Observation 0 1930 1930-07-13 15:00 Group 1 Pocitos Montevideo Uruguay France 4 1 Mexico 1 1930 1930-07-13 15:00 Group 4 Parque Central Montevideo Uruguay USA 3 0 Belgium 2 1930 1930-07-14 12:45 Group 2 Parque Central Montevideo Uruguay Yugoslavia 2 1 Brazil 3 1930 1930-07-14 14:50 Group 3 Pocitos Montevideo Uruguay Romania 3 1 Peru 4 1930 1930-07-15 16:00 Group 1 Parque Central Montevideo Uruguay Argentina 1 0 France print ( matches_raw . dtypes ) print () print ( "Missing values per column:" ) print ( matches_raw . isna () . sum ()) Year int64 Date datetime64[ns] Time object Round object Stadium object City object Country object HomeTeam object HomeGoals int64 AwayGoals int64 AwayTeam object Observation object dtype: object Missing values per column: Year 0 Date 0 Time 0 Round 0 Stadium 0 City 0 Country 0 HomeTeam 0 HomeGoals 0 AwayGoals 0 AwayTeam 0 Observation 0 dtype: int64 One row is one match : a year, a date, two teams and their goals. The Observation column holds notes such as "win after extra time". isna() reports no missing values at all, yet most matches have no note. Blanks can be stored as empty text instead of NaN , and then isna() cannot see them: empty_notes = matches_raw [ "Observation" ] . astype ( str ) . str . strip () == "" print ( "Observation cells that are empty text:" , empty_notes . sum (), "of" , len ( matches_raw )) Observation cells that are empty text: 787 of 852 Here an empty note is expected (most matches end normally), so we leave it. The lesson: check for empty text as well as NaN before you call a column complete. The WorldCups sheet records the official number of matches and goals for each tournament. That gives us an independent check : count the match rows per year and compare. check = pd . DataFrame ({ "match_rows" : matches_raw . groupby ( "Year" ) . size (), "official_matches" : cups . set_index ( "Year" )[ "MatchesPlayed" ], }) check [ "difference" ] = check [ "match_rows" ] - check [ "official_matches" ] check [ check [ "difference" ] != 0 ] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } match_rows official_matches difference Year 2014 80 64 16 Predict before you continue Only one tournament disagrees, and it has more rows than matches played. Write down two possible explanations before you run G3. G3 (Core): Find and remove the duplicates ¶ duplicated() marks rows that are identical, in every column, to an earlier row. is_copy = matches_raw . duplicated () print ( "Exact duplicate rows:" , is_copy . sum ()) print ( "Years affected:" , matches_raw . loc [ is_copy , "Year" ] . value_counts () . to_dict ()) Exact duplicate rows: 16 Years affected: {2014: 16} Look at both copies of a few of them. keep=False marks the first copy too, so you can see the pairs side by side. pairs = matches_raw [ matches_raw . duplicated ( keep = False )] pairs . sort_values ([ "Date" , "HomeTeam" ])[[ "Year" , "Date" , "Round" , "HomeTeam" , "HomeGoals" , "AwayGoals" , "AwayTeam" ]] . head ( 6 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Year Date Round HomeTeam HomeGoals AwayGoals AwayTeam 820 2014 2014-06-28 Round of 16 Brazil 1 1 Chile 836 2014 2014-06-28 Round of 16 Brazil 1 1 Chile 821 2014 2014-06-28 Round of 16 Colombia 2 0 Uruguay 837 2014 2014-06-28 Round of 16 Colombia 2 0 Uruguay 833 2014 2014-06-29 Round of 16 Costa Rica 1 1 Greece 839 2014 2014-06-29 Round of 16 Costa Rica 1 1 Greece Same teams, same date, same score, same stadium: the same match recorded twice. Each match is one real event, so these are true duplicates . Remove them from a copy, log the step, and run the independent check again. before = len ( matches_raw ) matches = matches_raw . drop_duplicates () . copy () log_step ( "World Cup matches" , "Removed exact duplicate rows" , "Same match recorded twice; match count exceeded the official total" , before , len ( matches )) check [ "match_rows_clean" ] = matches . groupby ( "Year" ) . size () print ( "Years where clean rows differ from the official count:" , ( check [ "match_rows_clean" ] != check [ "official_matches" ]) . sum ()) Years where clean rows differ from the official count: 0 Remember The fix is confirmed by a number that came from somewhere else (the official match count), not just by "the duplicates are gone". Copy the before and after counts into your evidence log. G4 (Core): Text problems — spaces, broken characters, names ¶ Text columns hide problems that are invisible when you look at a few rows. Start with stray spaces. for column in [ "City" , "Stadium" , "HomeTeam" , "AwayTeam" ]: text = matches [ column ] . astype ( str ) print ( f " { column : 9 } values with leading or trailing spaces: { ( text != text . str . strip ()) . sum () } " ) City values with leading or trailing spaces: 836 Stadium values with leading or trailing spaces: 0 HomeTeam values with leading or trailing spaces: 0 AwayTeam values with leading or trailing spaces: 0 Every City value ends with a space. That is harmless until you join on city or type "Paris" in a filter. Strip it and log it (a text fix does not change the row count, so before and after are the same). matches [ "City" ] = matches [ "City" ] . str . strip () log_step ( "World Cup matches" , "Stripped spaces from City" , "Every City value ended in a space" , len ( matches ), len ( matches )) print ( "Cities with spaces left:" , ( matches [ "City" ] != matches [ "City" ] . str . strip ()) . sum ()) Cities with spaces left: 0 Next, broken characters . The symbols ï¿½ are what is left of letters such as ô or é after the file passed through the wrong encoding. The original letter is gone. text_columns = [ "City" , "Stadium" , "HomeTeam" , "AwayTeam" ] broken = matches [ text_columns ] . apply ( lambda column : column . astype ( str ) . str . contains ( "ï¿½" )) print ( "Rows with a broken character:" , broken . any ( axis = 1 ) . sum ()) pd . Series ( pd . unique ( matches [ text_columns ] . where ( broken ) . stack ())) . head ( 12 ) Rows with a broken character: 73 0 Stade Vï¿½lodrome 1 Maracanï¿½ - Estï¿½dio Jornalista Mï¿½rio Filho 2 Malmï¿½ 3 Norrkï¿½Ping 4 Nou Camp - Estadio Leï¿½n 5 Dï¿½Sseldorf 6 Estadio Josï¿½ Marï¿½a Minella 7 Estadio Olï¿½mpico Chateau Carreras 8 Estadio Municipal de Balaï¿½dos 9 La Coruï¿½A 10 Estadio Olï¿½mpico Universitario 11 Cï¿½te d'Ivoire dtype: object Some of these are easy to read ( Cï¿½te d'Ivoire is Côte d'Ivoire), others are not. We flag the affected rows rather than guessing; correcting them needs a trusted reference list. matches [ "text_broken_flag" ] = broken . any ( axis = 1 ) . astype ( int ) log_step ( "World Cup matches" , "Flagged rows with broken characters (not corrected)" , "Encoding damage; original letters cannot be recovered from the file" , len ( matches ), len ( matches )) matches [ "text_broken_flag" ] . value_counts () text_broken_flag 0 763 1 73 Name: count, dtype: int64 Finally, names . Look for teams that might be the same country under two names. teams = pd . concat ([ matches [ "HomeTeam" ], matches [ "AwayTeam" ]]) teams [ teams . str . contains ( "Iran|Germany" )] . value_counts () Germany FR 62 Germany 44 Iran 6 IR Iran 6 Name: count, dtype: int64 Not every difference is an error Iran and IR Iran are the same team written two ways: a candidate for a documented mapping. Germany FR (West Germany), German DR (East Germany) and Germany are historically different teams. Merging them is an analytical choice, not a fix, and must be stated if you make it. You decide how to treat each one in I4. G5 (Core): Join the three Superstore sheets safely ¶ The Superstore workbook has three sheets. Read them raw from the file the setup cell downloaded. orders_raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns_raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) people_raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "People" ) print ( "Orders: " , orders_raw . shape ) print ( "Returns:" , returns_raw . shape ) print ( "People: " , people_raw . shape ) people_raw Orders: (10194, 21) Returns: (296, 2) People: (4, 2) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Regional Manager Region 0 Sadie Pawthorne West 1 Chuck Magee East 2 Roxanne Rodriguez Central 3 Fred Suzuki South Step 1: before the join, check the keys. Orders will be joined to Returns on Order ID and to People on Region . Each key must be unique on the Returns and People side, or rows will multiply. print ( "Returns: is Order ID unique?" , returns_raw [ "Order ID" ] . is_unique ) print ( "People: is Region unique? " , people_raw [ "Region" ] . is_unique ) print ( "Returns: values in Returned:" , returns_raw [ "Returned" ] . unique ()) Returns: is Order ID unique? True People: is Region unique? True Returns: values in Returned: ['Yes'] Step 2: join with validate and indicator . Each order line has at most one returns row and exactly one region manager, so both joins are many-to-one . step1 = orders_raw . merge ( returns_raw , on = "Order ID" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" , indicator = "returns_match" ) step2 = step1 . merge ( people_raw , on = "Region" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" , indicator = "people_match" ) print ( "Rows: orders" , len ( orders_raw ), "| after Returns" , len ( step1 ), "| after People" , len ( step2 )) print () print ( step2 [ "returns_match" ] . value_counts ()) print () print ( step2 [ "people_match" ] . value_counts ()) Rows: orders 10194 | after Returns 10194 | after People 10194 returns_match left_only 9394 both 800 right_only 0 Name: count, dtype: int64 people_match both 10194 left_only 0 right_only 0 Name: count, dtype: int64 Step 3: after the join, check a total and the unmatched rows. print ( "Sales before joins:" , round ( orders_raw [ "Sales" ] . sum (), 2 )) print ( "Sales after joins: " , round ( step2 [ "Sales" ] . sum (), 2 )) print ( "Lines without a manager:" , step2 [ "Regional Manager" ] . isna () . sum ()) print ( "Listed orders found in Orders:" , returns_raw [ "Order ID" ] . isin ( orders_raw [ "Order ID" ]) . sum (), "of" , len ( returns_raw )) Sales before joins: 2326534.35 Sales after joins: 2326534.35 Lines without a manager: 0 Listed orders found in Orders: 296 of 296 Read the output above: The row count and the Sales total did not change, so neither join multiplied anything. Lines whose order is not on the returns list get a blank Returned . Blank here means "not listed", not "unknown": that is why load_orders() turns it into a 0/1 flag. Every line found a manager. Turn the blank into an explicit flag, and log the join. orders_joined = step2 . drop ( columns = [ "returns_match" , "people_match" ]) orders_joined [ "returned_listed" ] = orders_joined [ "Returned" ] . eq ( "Yes" ) . astype ( int ) log_step ( "Superstore" , "Left-joined Returns (on Order ID) and People (on Region)" , "Add returns listing and regional manager to each line; validated many-to-one" , len ( orders_raw ), len ( orders_joined )) orders_joined [[ "Order ID" , "Region" , "Regional Manager" , "Returned" , "returned_listed" ]] . head () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Order ID Region Regional Manager Returned returned_listed 0 US-2023-103800 Central Roxanne Rodriguez NaN 0 1 US-2023-112326 Central Roxanne Rodriguez NaN 0 2 US-2023-112326 Central Roxanne Rodriguez NaN 0 3 US-2023-112326 Central Roxanne Rodriguez NaN 0 4 US-2023-141817 East Chuck Magee NaN 0 Independent tasks ¶ I1 (Core): Profile the Mobile OS file ¶ The file has three columns: a month, an operating system and its percentage of page views. Profile it the same way you profiled the matches. print ( mobile_raw . dtypes ) print () print ( "Missing values per column:" ) print ( mobile_raw . isna () . sum ()) mobile_raw . head () Date object Mobile Operating System object Percent of Usage float64 dtype: object Missing values per column: Date 1772 Mobile Operating System 0 Percent of Usage 0 dtype: int64 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Date Mobile Operating System Percent of Usage 0 2008-12-01 Android 0.00 1 2008-12-01 iOS 32.56 2 2008-12-01 SymbianOS 42.02 3 2008-12-01 Series 40 0.00 4 2008-12-01 BlackBerry OS 0.00 Most dates are missing. Which months do have dates, how many operating systems does each have, and do their percentages add up to about 100? dated = mobile_raw . dropna ( subset = [ "Date" ]) dated . groupby ( "Date" ) . agg ( systems = ( "Mobile Operating System" , "nunique" ), percent_total = ( "Percent of Usage" , "sum" ), ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } systems percent_total Date 2008-12-01 26 100.00 2009-01-01 26 100.00 2009-02-01 26 100.01 2009-03-01 26 99.99 2009-04-01 22 99.17 Record in your evidence log: How many rows have a date, and how many do not. Which months are dated, and which of them look complete (all systems present, total close to 100). One month that looks incomplete , and how you can tell. I2 (Core): Choose a subset you can defend ¶ The undated rows cannot be placed in time. It is tempting to give them dates based on their position in the file, but row order is not evidence: a file can be sorted, filtered or appended in any order. The defensible choice is to keep only the dated rows , and to mark the month that is incomplete. before = len ( mobile_raw ) mobile = mobile_raw . dropna ( subset = [ "Date" ]) . copy () mobile [ "Date" ] = pd . to_datetime ( mobile [ "Date" ]) month_totals = mobile . groupby ( "Date" )[ "Percent of Usage" ] . sum () complete_months = month_totals [( month_totals - 100 ) . abs () < 0.5 ] . index mobile [ "complete_month" ] = mobile [ "Date" ] . isin ( complete_months ) . astype ( int ) log_step ( "Mobile OS" , "Kept only rows with a date; flagged incomplete months" , "Undated rows cannot be placed in time; row order is not evidence" , before , len ( mobile )) mobile . groupby ( "Date" )[ "complete_month" ] . first () Date 2008-12-01 1 2009-01-01 1 2009-02-01 1 2009-03-01 1 2009-04-01 0 Name: complete_month, dtype: int64 Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell: it charts the share of page views for two systems, complete months only. # 2. Change the list to two or three other systems, for example "BlackBerry OS" or "Android". # 3. Rewrite the title so it says exactly what the chart shows, including the period. selected = [ "iOS" , "SymbianOS" ] subset = mobile [( mobile [ "complete_month" ] == 1 ) & mobile [ "Mobile Operating System" ] . isin ( selected )] chart = subset . pivot ( index = "Date" , columns = "Mobile Operating System" , values = "Percent of Usage" ) ax = chart . plot ( marker = "o" , title = "Share of mobile page views, Dec 2008 – Mar 2009 (Statcounter)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Percent of page views" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Write one sentence describing your chart and one sentence on what the file cannot tell you (think about what a page-view share measures, and about the period covered). I3 (Core): How much did the duplicates matter? ¶ Compare goals per match for each tournament using the raw and the clean match tables. Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Run the cell and find the tournament where raw and clean differ. # 2. Change "goals_per_match" to "matches" to compare match counts instead. # 3. Then compare the clean goals with the official GoalsScored column in cups. def per_tournament ( table ): goals = table [ "HomeGoals" ] + table [ "AwayGoals" ] return pd . DataFrame ({ "matches" : table . groupby ( "Year" ) . size (), "goals" : goals . groupby ( table [ "Year" ]) . sum (), }) . assign ( goals_per_match = lambda t : t [ "goals" ] / t [ "matches" ]) comparison = pd . DataFrame ({ "raw" : per_tournament ( matches_raw )[ "goals_per_match" ], "clean" : per_tournament ( matches )[ "goals_per_match" ], }) comparison . tail ( 5 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } raw clean Year 1998 2.67 2.67 2002 2.52 2.52 2006 2.30 2.30 2010 2.27 2.27 2014 2.58 2.67 Did the duplicates change the average much? Would they have changed a total (all goals scored in 2014) more or less? Write your answer, with the numbers, in your log. I4 (Core): Finish the cleaning log ¶ Decide how to treat Iran / IR Iran and the German teams from G4. Add one row to the log for your decision, even if the decision is "leave unchanged". Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # 1. Edit the mapping: add or remove names you decide to combine. # 2. Fill in the reason in log_step. If you change nothing, log that decision too. name_map = { "IR Iran" : "Iran" } before_names = pd . concat ([ matches [ "HomeTeam" ], matches [ "AwayTeam" ]]) . nunique () matches [ "HomeTeam" ] = matches [ "HomeTeam" ] . replace ( name_map ) matches [ "AwayTeam" ] = matches [ "AwayTeam" ] . replace ( name_map ) after_names = pd . concat ([ matches [ "HomeTeam" ], matches [ "AwayTeam" ]]) . nunique () log_step ( "World Cup matches" , f "Renamed teams: { name_map } " , "Write your reason here" , len ( matches ), len ( matches )) print ( "Different team names before:" , before_names , "| after:" , after_names ) Different team names before: 83 | after: 82 Now print the whole log. This table is your main evidence for today. pd . DataFrame ( cleaning_log ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dataset change why rows_before rows_after 0 World Cup matches Removed exact duplicate rows Same match recorded twice; match count exceede... 852 836 1 World Cup matches Stripped spaces from City Every City value ended in a space 836 836 2 World Cup matches Flagged rows with broken characters (not corre... Encoding damage; original letters cannot be re... 836 836 3 Superstore Left-joined Returns (on Order ID) and People (... docs.text: Three files from three sources, each with its own problems: repeated football matches, a usage file with most of its dates missing, and a retail workbook whose sheets must be joined without losing or doubling anything. docs.text: The head of analytics says: "We have been handed three files for next quarter's reports. Before anyone builds a chart on them: what is wrong with each one, what did you fix, and can I see the proof?" Your job today is not to find insights. It is to make each file fit for use , show the evidence, and say clearly what still cannot be trusted. About the data World Cup results : compiled for Sports Viz Sundays 2018 and published in Tableau's sample-data catalog. We download it from that source for learning; we do not redistribute it, and the course does not claim a licence for it. Mobile OS usage : from Statcounter Global Stats (licence CC BY-SA 3.0), via Tableau's sample-data catalog. Each percentage is a share of page views on the websites Statcounter tracks, not a share of devices sold or of people. Superstore : Tableau's sample for a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units; no currency is stated.

Each match is one real event, so these are true duplicates . Remove them from a copy, log the step, and run the independent check again. before = len ( matches_raw ) matches = matches_raw . drop_duplicates () . copy () log_step ( "World Cup matches" , "Removed exact duplicate rows" , "Same match recorded twice; match count exceeded the official total" , before , len ( matches )) check [ "match_rows_clean" ] = matches . groupby ( "Year" ) . size () print ( "Years where clean rows differ from the official count:" , ( check [ "match_rows_clean" ] != check [ "official_matches" ]) . sum ()) Years where clean rows differ from the official count: 0 Remember The fix is confirmed by a number that came from somewhere else (the official match count), not just by "the duplicates are gone". docs.text: Text columns hide problems that are invisible when you look at a few rows. Start with stray spaces. for column in [ "City" , "Stadium" , "HomeTeam" , "AwayTeam" ]: text = matches [ column ] . astype ( str ) print ( f " { column : 9 } values with leading or trailing spaces: { ( text != text . str . strip ()) . sum () } " ) City values with leading or trailing spaces: 836 Stadium values with leading or trailing spaces: 0 HomeTeam values with leading or trailing spaces: 0 AwayTeam values with leading or trailing spaces: 0 Every City value ends with a space. That is harmless until you join on city or type "Paris" in a filter. Strip it and log it (a text fix does not change the row count, so before and after are the same). matches [ "City" ] = matches [ "City" ] . str . strip () log_step ( "World Cup matches" , "Stripped spaces from City" , "Every City value ended in a space" , len ( matches ), len ( matches )) print ( "Cities with spaces left:" , ( matches [ "City" ] != matches [ "City" ] . str . strip ()) . sum ()) Cities with spaces left: 0 Next, broken characters . The symbols ï¿½ are what is left of letters such as ô or é after the file passed through the wrong encoding. The original letter is gone. text_columns = [ "City" , "Stadium" , "HomeTeam" , "AwayTeam" ] broken = matches [ text_columns ] . apply ( lambda column : column . astype ( str ) . str . contains ( "ï¿½" )) print ( "Rows with a broken character:" , broken . any ( axis = 1 ) . sum ()) pd . Series ( pd . unique ( matches [ text_columns ] . where ( broken ) . stack ())) . head ( 12 ) Rows with a broken character: 73 0 Stade Vï¿½lodrome 1 Maracanï¿½ - Estï¿½dio Jornalista Mï¿½rio Filho 2 Malmï¿½ 3 Norrkï¿½Ping 4 Nou Camp - Estadio Leï¿½n 5 Dï¿½Sseldorf 6 Estadio Josï¿½ Marï¿½a Minella 7 Estadio Olï¿½mpico Chateau Carreras 8 Estadio Municipal de Balaï¿½dos 9 La Coruï¿½A 10 Estadio Olï¿½mpico Universitario 11 Cï¿½te d'Ivoire dtype: object Some of these are easy to read ( Cï¿½te d'Ivoire is Côte d'Ivoire), others are not. We flag the affected rows rather than guessing; correcting them needs a trusted reference list. matches [ "text_broken_flag" ] = broken . any ( axis = 1 ) . astype ( int ) log_step ( "World Cup matches" , "Flagged rows with broken characters (not corrected)" , "Encoding damage; original letters cannot be recovered from the file" , len ( matches ), len ( matches )) matches [ "text_broken_flag" ] . value_counts () text_broken_flag 0 763 1 73 Name: count, dtype: int64 Finally, names . Look for teams that might be the same country under two names. teams = pd . concat ([ matches [ "HomeTeam" ], matches [ "AwayTeam" ]]) teams [ teams . str . contains ( "Iran|Germany" )] . value_counts () Germany FR 62 Germany 44 Iran 6 IR Iran 6 Name: count, dtype: int64 Not every difference is an error Iran and IR Iran are the same team written two ways: a candidate for a documented mapping.
